Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! Ahem! Let me clear my throat! I've been thinking about it ever since, and that laugh is the final conclusion. Why? Because a laugh is the wisest, easiest answer to everything that's strange. And come what may, one comfort always remains: it's all predestined. I didn't hear all his talk with Starbuck, but to my eye, Starbuck looked the way I felt the other evening. You can be sure the old sultan has got him, too. I caught it, knew it — if I had the gift, I could have prophesied it easily. Because when I got a good look at his skull, I saw it. Well, Stubb, wise Stubb — that's my title — well, Stubb, what of it? Here's a body. I don't know all that may be coming, but whatever it is, I'll go to meet it laughing. What a mischievous leer lurks in all your horrors! I feel funny. Fa la! La la! What's my sweet little wife doing at home right now? Crying her eyes out? Giving a party for the latest harpooners, I'd wager, cheerful as a ship's pennant, and so am I — fa la! La la! Oh —
We'll drink tonight with hearts as light, to love, as gay and fleeting as bubbles that swim on the beaker's brim, and break on the lips while meeting.
A brave song that — who calls? Mr. Starbuck? Yes, yes, sir — (Aside) he's my superior, and he has his too, if I'm not mistaken. — Yes, yes, sir, just finishing this job — coming.

chapters.title: Chapter 40 — Midnight, Forecastle
paragraphs: HARPOONERS AND SAILORS.
(The foresail rises and reveals the watch standing, lounging, leaning, and lying in various positions, all singing in chorus.)
Farewell and goodbye to you, Spanish ladies! Farewell and goodbye to you, ladies of Spain! Our captain's commanded —
1ST NANTUCKET SAILOR. Oh, boys, don't be sentimental — it's bad for the digestion! Have a drink, follow me!
(Sings, and all follow.)

Our captain stood upon the deck, a spyglass in his hand, surveying all those splendid whales that spouted near the strand. Oh, your tubs in your boats, my boys, and by your braces stand, and we'll take one of those fine whales, hand, boys, over hand! So be cheerful, my lads! May your hearts never fail! While the bold harpooner is striking the whale!
MATE'S VOICE FROM THE QUARTER-DECK. Eight bells there, forward!

2ND NANTUCKET SAILOR. Stop the singing! Eight bells! Do you hear, bell-boy? Strike the bell eight, Pip, you little rascal! And let me call the watch. I've got the right kind of mouth for that — a barrel-sized mouth. So, so — (Thrusts his head down the hatch.) Starboard watch, ahoy! Eight bells down below! Get up!

DUTCH SAILOR. Great sleeping tonight, mate — a fat night for it. I credit our old sultan's wine for that. It puts some to sleep as much as it livens up others. We sing, they sleep — yes, lying down there like barrels in a cellar. At them again! Here, take this copper tube and shout through it. Tell them to stop dreaming about their girls. Tell them it's Judgment Day — they've got to kiss their sweethearts goodbye and face the reckoning. That's the way — that's it! Your throat hasn't been ruined by eating Amsterdam butter.

FRENCH SAILOR. Listen, boys! Let's have a jig or two before we anchor in Blanket Bay. What do you say? Here comes the other watch. Everybody on your feet! Pip! Little Pip! Come on with your tambourine!
PIP. (Sulky and sleepy.) Don't know where it is.

FRENCH SAILOR. Beat your belly, then, and flap your ears. Dance, men, I say! Merry's the word — hurrah! Damn me, won't you dance? Line up, single file, and gallop into the double-shuffle! Throw yourselves into it! Legs! Legs!
ICELAND SAILOR. I don't like your dance floor, mate — it's too springy for my taste. I'm used to ice. Sorry to dampen the mood, but excuse me.
MALTESE SAILOR. Me too. Where are your girls? Who but a fool would take his own left hand in his right and say, 'How do you do?' Partners! I need partners!
SICILIAN SAILOR. That's right — girls and a green lawn! Then I'll dance with you — yes, I'll leap like a grasshopper!
LONG-ISLAND SAILOR. Well, well, you grumblers, there's plenty of us willing. Make hay while you can, I say. All legs go to the harvest soon enough. Ah! Here comes the music — now we're in business!

AZORE SAILOR. (Climbing up and tossing the tambourine through the hatch.) Here you go, Pip — and there's the windlass post. Climb up! Now, boys! (Half of them dance to the tambourine; some go below; some sleep or lie among the coils of rigging. Plenty of cursing.)
AZORE SAILOR. (Dancing.) Go, Pip! Bang it, bell-boy! Rig it, dig it, jig it, bell-boy! Make sparks fly! Break those jinglers!
PIP. Jinglers, you say? There goes another one — fell off. I'm pounding it too hard.
CHINA SAILOR. Rattle your teeth, then, and keep pounding — make a pagoda of yourself.
FRENCH SAILOR. Wild and merry! Hold up your hoop, Pip, so I can jump through it! Rip the sails! Tear loose!
TASHTEGO. (Quietly smoking.) That's a white man for you. He calls that fun. Humph! I'll save my sweat.

OLD MANX SAILOR. I wonder whether those cheerful lads realize what they're dancing over. 'I'll dance on your grave' — that's the bitterest curse of your night-witches, those who beat headwinds round corners. O Christ! To think of the green sea-bottoms and the green-skulled crews! Well, well — maybe the whole world is a ball, as you scholars say, and so it's only right to make one ballroom of it. Dance on, lads — you're young. I was once.
3RD NANTUCKET SAILOR. Break time! Whew! This is harder work than rowing after whales in a calm. Give us a puff, Tash.
(They stop dancing and gather in groups. Meanwhile, the sky darkens — the wind rises.)
LASCAR SAILOR. By Brahma! Boys, it'll be time to take in sail soon. The heaven-born, high-tide Ganges has turned to wind! You show your black brow, Shiva!

MALTESE SAILOR. (Reclining and shaking his cap.) It's the waves — the whitecaps are dancing now. They'll shake their foam-caps soon. If only all the waves were women — then I'd gladly go drown, and dance with them forever! There's nothing so sweet on earth — heaven itself can't match it — as those swift glances from warm, wild women's bosoms in the dance, when their arching arms hide such ripe, bursting grapes.

SICILIAN SAILOR. (Reclining.) Don't tell me about it! Listen, lad — those fleet interlacings of limbs — lithe swayings — flirtings — flutterings! Lip! Heart! Hip! All graze each other: unceasing touch and go! Not a full taste, mind you, or satisfaction would come. Eh, Pagan? (Nudging.)

TAHITIAN SAILOR. (Reclining on a mat.) Hail, holy nakedness of our dancing girls — the Heeva-Heeva! Ah, low-veiled, palm-crowned Tahiti! I still rest on your mat, but the soft earth has shifted! I saw you woven in the forest, my mat! Green the first day I carried you home; now worn and wilted. Ah me! Neither you nor I can bear the change! How would it be, then, if transplanted to that sky? Can I hear the roaring streams from Pirohitee's peak of spears, when they leap down the cliffs and drown the villages? — The blast! The blast! Up, spine, and face it! (Leaps to his feet.)
PORTUGUESE SAILOR. How the sea crashes against the hull! Stand by for reefing, lads! The winds are just crossing swords — soon they'll go lunging at each other.

DANISH SAILOR. Crack, crack, old ship! As long as you're cracking, you're holding! Well done! The mate keeps you to it firmly. He's no more afraid than the island fortress at Kattegat, built to fight the Baltic with storm-battered guns, crusted with sea salt!
4TH NANTUCKET SAILOR. He has his orders, mind you. I heard old Ahab tell him he must always kill a squall, the way you burst a waterspout with a pistol — fire your ship right into it!
ENGLISH SAILOR. Bloody hell, but that old man's a grand old fellow! We're the lads to hunt up his whale!
ALL. Yes! Yes!

OLD MANX SAILOR. How the three masts shake! Pine trees are the hardest to keep alive when transplanted to foreign soil, and here there's none but the crew's cursed clay. Steady, helmsman! Steady. This is the sort of weather when brave hearts break on shore, and hulls split at sea. Our captain has his birthmark. Look there, boys — there's another one in the sky — glowing like that, see? Everything else pitch black.
DAGGOO. What of that? Whoever's afraid of black is afraid of me! I'm carved out of it!

SPANISH SAILOR. (Aside.) He wants a fight, does he? The old grudge makes me touchy. (Stepping forward.) Yes, harpooner, your race is the undeniable dark side of mankind — devilishly dark, at that. No offense.
DAGGOO. (Grimly.) None.
ST. JAGO'S SAILOR. That Spaniard is either mad or drunk. But it can't be drink, or else our old sultan's liquor takes a long time to work in his case.
5TH NANTUCKET SAILOR. What's that I see — lightning? Yes.
SPANISH SAILOR. No. Daggoo showing his teeth.
DAGGOO. (Springing forward.) Swallow yours, runt! White skin, white liver!
SPANISH SAILOR. (Meeting him.) I'll carve you up! Big body, small soul!
ALL. A fight! A fight! A fight!
TASHTEGO. (Taking a puff.) A fight below and a fight aloft — gods and men, both brawlers! Humph!
BELFAST SAILOR. A fight! Arrah, a fight! The Virgin be blessed, a fight! Dive right in!
ENGLISH SAILOR. Fair play! Grab the Spaniard's knife! Make a ring, a ring!
OLD MANX SAILOR. Already formed — look! The ringed horizon. In that ring, Cain struck Abel. Sweet work, proper work! No? Then why, God, did you make the ring?
MATE'S VOICE FROM THE QUARTER-DECK. Hands to the halyards! Take in topgallant sails! Stand by to reef topsails!
ALL. The squall! The squall! Jump, lads! (They scatter.)

PIP. (Shrinking under the windlass.) Lads? Lord help such lads! Crash, smash! There goes the jib-stay! Bang-whang! God! Duck lower, Pip — here comes the royal yard! It's worse than being in the whirling woods on the last day of the year! Who'd go climbing after chestnuts now? But there they go, all cursing, and here I don't. Fine prospects for them — they're on the road to heaven. Hold on tight! Lord, what a squall! But those fellows up there are worse than any storm — they're your white squalls, they are. White squalls? White whale, shh! Shh! Here I've heard all their talk just now, and the white whale — shh! Shh! — mentioned only once! And only this evening — it makes me jingle all over like my tambourine — that snake of an old man swore them all in to hunt it! Oh, great white God up there somewhere in the darkness, have mercy on this small black boy down here. Protect him from all men who have no hearts to feel fear!

chapters.title: Chapter 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts had gone up with the rest. My oath had been welded with theirs. And I shouted louder and hammered my oath harder because of the dread in my soul. A wild, mystical, sympathetic feeling was in me. Ahab's unquenchable feud seemed like my own. With eager ears I learned the history of that murderous monster against whom I and all the others had sworn our oaths of violence and revenge.

For some time, though only at intervals, the solitary White Whale had haunted those uncivilized seas mostly visited by sperm whale hunters. But not all of them knew of his existence. Only a few had knowingly seen him, and the number who had actually and deliberately fought him was very small. Because of the large number of whale ships, their scattered positions across the entire ocean, with many of them pushing their hunt along lonely latitudes where they might not encounter another vessel for a full year or more, and because of the great length of each voyage and the irregular sailing schedules from home — all of these factors, along with others, had long prevented the news about Moby Dick from spreading through the entire worldwide whaling fleet. It was reasonable to suspect that several ships reported to have encountered, at such and such a time or on such and such a line of longitude, a sperm whale of unusual size and ferocity — which, after doing great damage to its attackers, had completely escaped — that this whale must have been none other than Moby Dick. Yet since the sperm whale fishery had recently seen many instances of great ferocity, cunning, and malice from the whales being hunted, those who had unknowingly fought Moby Dick were mostly content to blame the particular terror he inspired on the general dangers of the sperm whale fishery rather than on this individual creature. That was how most people had understood the disastrous encounter between Ahab and the whale.

As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or horrific amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who eventually heard the story of the White Whale.

Nor did wild rumors fail to exaggerate and further horrify the true accounts of these deadly encounters. For not only do fantastic rumors naturally grow from the very body of all shocking events, the way a damaged tree sprouts fungi, but in maritime life, far more than on land, wild rumors flourish wherever there is any real foundation for them to cling to. And just as the sea surpasses the land in this respect, so the whale fishery surpasses every other kind of seafaring life in the wonder and terror of the rumors that circulate. For whalemen as a group are no more free from the ignorance and superstition that all sailors inherit than anyone else. But of all sailors, they are by far the most directly exposed to whatever is terrifyingly astonishing in the sea. Face to face they encounter its greatest marvels, and hand to jaw they fight them. Alone, in such remote waters that you could sail a thousand miles past a thousand shores without finding a single welcoming hearth — in such places, doing the work he does, the whaleman is surrounded by influences that make his imagination pregnant with mighty creations.

No wonder, then, that as the rumors of the White Whale gathered force from merely crossing the widest ocean spaces, they eventually absorbed all manner of morbid suggestions and half-formed hints of supernatural forces. In the end, these invested Moby Dick with new terrors borrowed from nothing visible. So much panic did he finally inspire that few who had heard of the White Whale through these rumors alone were willing to face the danger of his jaws.

But there were still other, more practical influences at work. Even today, the original fearsome reputation of the sperm whale, as terrifyingly different from all other whale species, has not died out among whalemen. There are those among them who, though intelligent and brave enough to fight a Greenland or right whale, would perhaps — from inexperience, incompetence, or fear — refuse a battle with the sperm whale. In any case, plenty of whalemen, especially those not sailing under the American flag, have never fought a sperm whale at all. Their knowledge of whales is limited to the less dangerous species hunted in the North. Sitting on their deck hatches, these men listen with childlike wonder and awe to the wild, strange tales of southern whaling. And the supreme terribleness of the great sperm whale is nowhere more deeply understood than aboard the ships that face him.

And as if the now proven reality of his power had, in earlier legendary times, cast its shadow before it, we find some naturalist-authors — Olassen and Povelson — declaring the sperm whale not only to be a terror to every other creature in the sea but so incredibly ferocious as to be perpetually thirsting for human blood. Even as late as Cuvier's time, these or similar impressions persisted. In his Natural History, the Baron himself states that at the sight of the sperm whale, all fish (sharks included) are "struck with the most vivid terror" and "often, in the panic of their flight, dash themselves against rocks so violently as to cause instant death." And however much general fishing experience may correct such reports, in their full terribleness — even down to Povelson's bloodthirsty detail — the superstitious belief in them is, in certain crises, revived in the hunters' minds.

So, overawed by the rumors and omens surrounding him, not a few fishermen recalled, regarding Moby Dick, the earliest days of the sperm whale fishery, when it was often hard to persuade experienced right-whale men to join this new and daring trade. Such men insisted that while other whales might be safely pursued, to chase and lance something as terrifying as the sperm whale was not for mortal man. To attempt it would be to be instantly torn into eternity. On this point, some remarkable documents survive.

Nevertheless, some there were who, even knowing all this, were ready to chase Moby Dick. And an even greater number, having only heard of him vaguely and at a distance, without specific details of any particular disaster and without the supernatural embellishments, were tough enough not to flee from the fight if it came to them.

One of the wild ideas I mentioned, which eventually became linked with the White Whale in superstitious minds, was the eerie notion that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had actually been encountered in opposite latitudes at the very same instant.

Nor, credulous as such people must have been, was this idea entirely without some faint basis in fact. For since the secrets of ocean currents have never been fully revealed, even by the most advanced research, the hidden movements of the sperm whale below the surface remain largely unexplained to his pursuers. From time to time, these mysteries have produced the most curious and contradictory theories, especially about the means by which, after diving to enormous depth, the whale transports himself with such incredible speed to the most distant points.

It is a fact well known to both American and English whale ships, and recorded authoritatively years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with harpoon barbs in their bodies that were thrown in the Greenland seas. And in some cases, the interval between the two attacks could not have been more than a few days. From this, some whalemen have concluded that the Northwest Passage, so long a puzzle to man, was never a puzzle to the whale. So that here, in the real lived experience of living men, the legendary wonders told in ancient times — about the inland Strello mountain in Portugal, near whose top there was said to be a lake where shipwrecks floated to the surface, and the even more marvelous story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse, whose waters were believed to flow underground all the way from the Holy Land — these fabulous tales are nearly equaled by the whalemen's realities.

Forced into familiarity with such wonders, and knowing that after repeated, fearless attacks the White Whale had escaped alive, it can hardly be surprising that some whalemen went further in their superstition. They declared Moby Dick not only everywhere at once but immortal (for immortality is just everywhere-ness in time). Though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed. Or if he should ever be made to spout thick blood, that sight would be only a ghostly deception. For again, in unstained waves hundreds of leagues away, his pure white spout would be seen once more.

But even stripped of these supernatural rumors, there was enough in the earthly reality and undeniable character of the monster to strike the imagination with extraordinary power. It was not so much his uncommon size that distinguished him from other sperm whales, but — as mentioned elsewhere — a peculiar snow-white, wrinkled forehead and a high, pyramid-shaped white hump. These were his prominent features, the marks by which, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity at a great distance to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, spotted, and marbled with the same ghostly hue that he had earned his distinctive name of the White Whale. A name literally justified by his vivid appearance when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all sparkling with golden gleams.

It was not his unusual size, nor his remarkable color, nor even his deformed lower jaw that invested the whale with such natural terror, but rather an unprecedented, intelligent malice that, according to specific accounts, he had displayed over and over in his attacks. Most of all, his treacherous retreats struck more fear than perhaps anything else. For when swimming ahead of his triumphant pursuers, showing every sign of alarm, he had been known several times to turn around suddenly and, bearing down on them, either smash their boats to splinters or drive them back in panic to their ship.

Several deaths had already attended his chase. Though similar disasters, however little publicized on shore, were by no means unusual in the fishery, in most cases the White Whale's actions seemed to show such infernal premeditation that every maiming or death he caused was not regarded as the work of a mindless animal.

Judge, then, to what peaks of inflamed, desperate fury the minds of his more determined hunters were driven when, amid the splinters of shattered boats and the sinking limbs of torn companions, they swam out of the white foam of the whale's terrible rage into the serene, maddening sunlight that smiled on, as if at a birth or a wedding.

His three boats smashed around him, oars and men whirling in the eddies, one captain seized the line-knife from his broken bow and lunged at the whale like an Arkansas duelist at his enemy, blindly trying with a six-inch blade to reach the life buried fathoms deep in the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was that Moby Dick, sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, reaped away Ahab's leg the way a mower cuts a blade of grass. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay assassin could have struck him with more apparent malice. There was little reason to doubt that ever since that nearly fatal encounter, Ahab had nursed a savage hatred for the whale — all the fiercer because in his frenzied state of mind, he eventually came to identify with Moby Dick not just all his physical suffering but all his intellectual and spiritual torments. The White Whale swam before him as the living embodiment of all those malicious forces that some deep-thinking men feel eating away at them until they are left living with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible evil which has existed from the beginning — to whose rule even modern Christians assign half the world, and which the ancient Ophites of the East worshipped in their statue of the devil — Ahab did not bow down before it like them. Instead, deliriously transferring the idea to the hated white whale, he hurled himself, broken as he was, against it. All that most enrages and torments, all that stirs up the dregs of things, all truth laced with malice, all that cracks the sinews and clots the brain, all the subtle demonisms of life and thought — to crazy Ahab, all evil was visibly concentrated and made physically attackable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale's white hump the sum of all the rage and hatred felt by his entire race from Adam onward. And then, as if his chest were a cannon, he fired his burning heart's shell upon it.

It is unlikely that this obsession in him sprang up at the precise moment he lost his leg. Then, lunging at the monster, knife in hand, he had only been giving vent to a sudden, passionate, physical fury. And when he received the blow that tore him apart, he probably felt nothing but the agonizing bodily wound. Yet when, forced by this collision to turn homeward, Ahab and his anguish lay stretched together in one hammock for long months of days and weeks, rounding in mid-winter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape — then it was that his torn body and wounded soul bled into each other, and the mingling drove him mad. That this final obsession seized him only then, on the homeward voyage after the encounter, seems nearly certain from the fact that at intervals during the passage, he was a raving lunatic. Though missing a leg, such vital strength still lurked in his powerful chest, and was intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lash him down even as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a straitjacket he swung to the mad rocking of the gales. And when, running into calmer latitudes, the ship floated with gentle sails spread across the tranquil tropics, and his madness appeared to have been left behind with the Cape Horn swells, and he came out of his dark den into the blessed light and air — even then, when he showed that firm, composed face, however pale, and gave his calm orders again, and his mates thanked God the terrible madness was gone — even then, deep within his hidden self, Ahab still raved on. Human madness is often a cunning, cat-like thing. When you think it has fled, it may have only transformed itself into some subtler form. Ahab's full lunacy did not subside but contracted and deepened, like the Hudson River, which does not diminish but flows narrowly and unfathomably through the Highland gorge. And just as in his narrowed obsession not one drop of Ahab's broader madness was left behind, so in that broader madness not one drop of his great natural intellect had been destroyed. What had been the living agent now became the living instrument. His particular lunacy had stormed his general sanity and captured it, turning all its concentrated firepower on its own mad target. So far from having lost his strength, Ahab, for that single purpose, now possessed a thousand times more power than he had ever sanely brought to bear on any reasonable goal.

This is much, yet Ahab's larger, darker, deeper part remains only hinted at. But it is useless to try to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked fortress where we now stand — however grand and wonderful, now leave it — take your way, you nobler, sadder souls, down to those vast Roman halls beneath, where far below the fantastic towers of man's upper world, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits enthroned in bearded state — an ancient buried beneath antiquities, seated on broken statues! So with a cracked throne, the great gods mock that captive king. So, like a pillar built to support a temple, he sits patiently, holding up on his frozen brow the piled weight of ages. Wind your way down there, you prouder, sadder souls! Question that proud, sad king! There is a family resemblance — yes, he begat you, you young exiled royals. And from your grim father alone will the old state secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this — namely, that all his means were sane, but his motive and his object mad. Yet without power to kill, change, or escape the fact, he also knew that he had long been deceiving mankind about it — and in some ways still was. But his deception was only subject to his awareness, not to his deliberate will. Nevertheless, he succeeded so well in it that when he stepped ashore on his ivory leg at last, no Nantucketer thought him anything other than naturally grief-stricken, and deeply so, by the terrible accident that had befallen him.

The reports of his undeniable madness at sea were likewise popularly attributed to the same cause. And so too was all the added brooding that had settled on his brow from that day onward, right up to the day he sailed on the Pequod for the present voyage. And it is not so unlikely that, far from doubting his fitness for another whaling voyage because of such dark signs, the calculating people of that practical island were inclined to think that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed from within and burned from without, with the fixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea — such a man, if he could be found, would seem the very one to drive his iron and raise his lance against the most terrifying of all beasts. Or if for any reason thought to be physically unable, such a man would seem supremely fit to urge and howl his crew onward to the attack. But whatever the truth, this much is certain: with the mad secret of his undiminished rage locked and bolted inside him, Ahab had deliberately sailed on this voyage with one single, all-consuming purpose — hunting the White Whale. Had any of his old acquaintances on shore even half-guessed what was lurking inside him, how quickly their horrified and righteous souls would have torn the ship from such a fiendish man! They had signed on for profitable cruises, the profits counted in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, implacable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this gray-headed, ungodly old man, chasing a Biblical whale with curses around the world, at the head of a crew mainly made up of mongrel renegades, castaways, and cannibals — morally weakened, too, by the helplessness of mere unaided virtue in Starbuck, the bulletproof cheerfulness of Stubb, and the pervasive mediocrity of Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially selected and assembled by some infernal fate to help him in his obsessive revenge. How they responded so completely to the old man's fury — by what dark magic their souls were possessed, so that at times his hatred seemed almost to be theirs, and the White Whale as much their unbearable enemy as his — how all this came to be — what the White Whale meant to them, or how, to their unconscious minds, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life — to explain all this would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The underground miner that works in all of us — how can anyone tell where his shaft leads by the ever-shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who doesn't feel the irresistible arm pulling? What skiff, towed behind a warship, can stand still? For my part, I gave myself up to the madness of the time and place. But while rushing headlong to confront the whale, I could see nothing in that brute but the deadliest evil.

chapters.title: Chapter 42 — The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: What the white whale meant to Ahab has been hinted at. What he was to me, at times, remains unsaid.

Beyond the more obvious fears that Moby Dick could stir in any man's soul, there was another thought — or rather a vague, nameless horror about him — that sometimes overpowered everything else with its intensity. Yet it was so mystical, so nearly impossible to put into words, that I almost despair of making it comprehensible. It was the whiteness of the whale that appalled me above all things. But how can I hope to explain myself here? And yet, in some dim, fumbling way, explain myself I must, or all these chapters will have been for nothing.

In many natural objects, whiteness enhances beauty, as if adding some special virtue of its own — in marble, in japonicas, in pearls. Various nations have recognized a royal superiority in this color. The grand old kings of Pegu placed the title "Lord of the White Elephants" above all their other titles of dominion. The modern kings of Siam unfurled the same snow-white creature on their royal banner. The Hanoverian flag bore the figure of a snow-white horse. The great Austrian Empire, heir to imperial Rome, chose the same imperial color. This supremacy extends even to the human race itself, granting the white man an assumed mastery over every darker people. Beyond all this, whiteness has been made a symbol of gladness — among the Romans, a white stone marked a joyful day. In other human customs and symbols, this same color represents many touching, noble things: the innocence of brides, the gentleness of old age. Among the Red Men of America, the gift of a white wampum belt was the deepest pledge of honor. In many lands, whiteness represents the majesty of Justice in the judge's ermine, and adds to the daily grandeur of kings and queens drawn by milk-white horses. Even in the highest mysteries of the most solemn religions, it has been made the symbol of divine purity and power. The Persian fire worshippers held the white forked flame holiest on the altar. In Greek mythology, great Jove himself took the form of a snow-white bull. Among the noble Iroquois, the midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog was by far the holiest festival of their faith — that spotless, loyal creature being held the purest messenger they could send to the Great Spirit with the yearly news of their devotion. Directly from the Latin word for white, all Christian priests derive the name of one part of their sacred clothing — the alb, or tunic worn beneath the cassock. Among the holy ceremonies of the Roman Catholic faith, white is specially used in celebrating the Passion of our Lord. In the Vision of St. John, white robes are given to the redeemed, and the twenty-four elders stand clothed in white before the great white throne, and the Holy One sitting there is white like wool. Yet for all these accumulated associations with whatever is sweet, honorable, and sublime, there lurks something elusive in the deepest idea of this color that strikes more panic into the soul than the redness that frightens us in blood.

It is this elusive quality that causes the thought of whiteness, when separated from kinder associations and paired with any object terrible in itself, to heighten that terror to its furthest limits. Consider the white bear of the poles and the white shark of the tropics. What but their smooth, flaky whiteness makes them the supreme horrors they are? That ghastly whiteness gives them an awful mildness, even more repulsive than outright ferocity, in their dumb, gloating stare. The fierce-fanged tiger in his striped coat cannot stagger courage the way the white-shrouded bear or shark can.

Regarding the polar bear, someone might argue that it is not the whiteness alone that heightens the intolerable hideousness of that beast. Analyzed carefully, one might say that heightened horror only arises because the creature's mindless ferocity is dressed in the fleece of heavenly innocence and love. By bringing together two such opposite emotions in our minds, the polar bear frightens us with so unnatural a contrast. But even granting all this — without the whiteness, you would not feel that intensified terror.

As for the white shark, the white gliding ghostliness of that creature at rest, when seen in its ordinary moods, strangely matches the same quality in the polar bear. The French capture this perfectly in the name they give that fish. The Roman Catholic mass for the dead begins with "Requiem eternam" — eternal rest — from which "Requiem" names the mass itself and any other funeral music. In reference to the white, silent stillness of death in this shark, and the mild deadliness of its habits, the French call it Requin.

Think of the albatross. Where do those clouds of spiritual wonder and pale dread come from, in which that white phantom sails through every imagination? It was not Coleridge who first cast that spell, but God's great, unsparing poet laureate: Nature.

I remember the first albatross I ever saw. It was during a long gale, in waters near the Antarctic seas. From my morning watch below, I climbed to the cloud-covered deck. There, thrown upon the main hatches, I saw a regal, feathery thing of spotless whiteness, with a hooked, noble bill. At intervals, it spread its vast archangel wings as if to embrace some holy ark. Wonderful flutterings and throbbings shook it. Though physically unharmed, it cried out like some king's ghost in supernatural anguish. Through its indescribable, strange eyes, I felt I glimpsed secrets known only to God. Like Abraham before the angels, I bowed. The white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those forever-exiled waters, I had lost all the warped memories of customs and civilization. I gazed long at that miracle of feathers. I cannot describe — only hint at — the things that shot through me then. But at last I stirred and asked a sailor what bird this was. A goney, he said. Goney! I had never heard the name. Could this glorious creature be utterly unknown to people ashore? Never! But later I learned that "goney" was a seaman's name for albatross. So Coleridge's wild Rhyme could have had nothing to do with the mystical impressions I felt when I saw that bird on our deck. I had not then read the poem, nor knew the bird to be an albatross. Yet in saying this, I only shine a brighter light on the noble merit of both poem and poet.

I maintain, then, that in the bird's wondrous bodily whiteness chiefly lurks the secret of its spell. This is further proven by the fact that there are birds called grey albatrosses. I have seen them often, but never with the emotions I felt when I beheld the Antarctic fowl.

But how had the mystical creature been caught? Whisper it not, and I will tell you: with a treacherous hook and line, as the bird floated on the sea. Eventually the Captain made a postman of it, tying a lettered leather tag around its neck with the ship's time and position, then letting it go free. But I have no doubt that leather tag, meant for human hands, was removed in Heaven when the white bird flew up to join the wing-folding, worshipping cherubim.

Most famous in Western history and Native American traditions is the White Steed of the Prairies — a magnificent milk-white horse, large-eyed, small-headed, broad-chested, with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his proud, scornful bearing. He was the chosen king of vast herds of wild horses whose pastures were bounded only by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghenies. At their blazing head he led them westward like that chosen star which every evening guides the hosts of light. The flashing waterfall of his mane, the curving comet of his tail, dressed him in finery more splendid than anything gold and silver workers could have furnished. He was a supreme, archangelic vision of that unfallen western world, which to the eyes of old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those first days when Adam walked as majestic as a god, bold-browed and fearless as this mighty horse. Whether marching with his lieutenants and generals at the head of endless columns streaming across the plains like a river, or whether with his surrounding subjects grazing all around at the horizon, reviewing them at a gallop with warm nostrils reddening through his cool milky whiteness — in whatever form he appeared, he was always an object of trembling reverence and awe to the bravest Indians. And it cannot be questioned, from what legendary records tell of this noble horse, that it was his spiritual whiteness above all that clothed him with divinity. And that divinity contained something which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.
But there are other cases where whiteness loses all that added strange glory it possesses in the White Steed and the Albatross.

What is it about the albino man that so particularly repels and often shocks the eye, so that he is sometimes despised by his own family? It is the whiteness that covers him, the very thing expressed by his name. The albino is as well-built as other men — he has no real deformity — and yet this all-pervading whiteness makes him more strangely hideous than the ugliest birth defect. Why should this be?

In quite different ways, Nature in her subtlest but no less vicious workings does not fail to enlist this supreme attribute of the terrible among her forces. From its snowy appearance, the armored ghost of the Southern Seas has been called the White Squall. And in some historical cases, human cruelty has not overlooked so powerful a tool. How wildly it heightens the effect of that passage in Froissart, when, masked in the snowy emblem of their faction, the desperate White Hoods of Ghent murder their magistrate in the marketplace.

In certain things, the common inherited experience of all humanity bears witness to the supernatural quality of this color. It can hardly be doubted that the one visible quality in the appearance of the dead that most horrifies the viewer is the marble paleness lingering there — as if that pallor were as much the mark of terror in the next world as it is of mortal fear in this one. From the pallor of the dead, we borrow the color of the shroud we wrap them in. Even in our superstitions we throw the same snowy cloak around our ghosts — all phantoms rise in a milk-white fog. And while these terrors grip us, let us add that even the king of terrors himself, as portrayed by the evangelist, rides on a pale horse.

Therefore, whatever grand or gracious thing a person may symbolize through whiteness in other moods, no one can deny that in its deepest, most idealized meaning, it summons a peculiar specter to the soul.

But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it seems impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all associations meant to make it fearful, yet still found to work the same spell on us, however softened — can we hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

Let us try. But in a matter like this, subtlety speaks to subtlety, and without imagination, no one can follow another into these halls. And though many of the imaginative impressions about to be presented may have been shared by most people, few were probably fully aware of them at the time, and therefore may not be able to recall them now.

Why does the man of untrained imagination, who happens to know little about the particular character of the holiday, find that the mere mention of Whitsuntide conjures in his mind such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-walking pilgrims, downcast and hooded in fresh-fallen snow? Or why does the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the American heartland find that the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun summons such an eyeless statue in his soul?

Or what is it — beyond the traditions of imprisoned warriors and kings, which do not fully explain it — that makes the White Tower of London strike the imagination of an untraveled American so much more powerfully than its neighboring landmarks, the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody Tower? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire — why does their bare mention send, in certain moods, such a gigantic ghostliness over the soul, while the thought of Virginia's Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, regardless of all geography, does the name of the White Sea cast such a spectral pall over the imagination, while the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long, mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the most brilliant yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a purely fanciful example, why does "the tall pale man" of the Harz forests in old Central European fairy tales, whose unchanging pallor glides silently through the green of the groves — why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping demons of the Blocksberg?

It is not entirely the memory of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes, nor the stampedes of her frantic seas, nor the dryness of skies that never weep rain, nor the sight of her wide fields of leaning spires, wrenched capstones, and drooping crosses — like the tilted yards of anchored fleets — and her suburban avenues of house-walls fallen against each other like a tossed deck of cards. These things alone do not make tearless Lima the strangest, saddest city you can see. For Lima has taken the white veil. And there is a higher horror in the whiteness of her grief. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins forever new. It admits no cheerful green of natural decay. It spreads over her broken walls the rigid pallor of a stroke that freezes its own distortions.

I know that to ordinary perception, whiteness is not admitted to be the prime agent in heightening the terror of things already terrible. Nor does the unimaginative mind find any terror in those sights whose awfulness, to another mind, consists almost entirely in this one quality — especially when displayed in any form approaching silence or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be clarified by the following examples.

First: The sailor, when approaching foreign coasts, if he hears the roar of breakers at night, snaps to alertness and feels just enough fear to sharpen all his senses. But under exactly the same conditions, let him be called from his hammock to see his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness — as if herds of combed white bears were swimming around him from encircling headlands — and he feels a silent, superstitious dread. The shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is as horrible to him as a real ghost. In vain the sounding lead assures him he is still in deep water. Heart and helm both fail him. He never rests until blue water is beneath him again. Yet where is the sailor who will tell you, "Sir, it was not so much the fear of hitting hidden rocks as the fear of that hideous whiteness that shook me"?

Second: To the native peoples of Peru, the constant sight of the snow-crowned Andes holds no dread, except perhaps in imagining the eternal frozen desolation that reigns at such heights, and the natural thought of how terrifying it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same goes for the frontiersman of the West, who views with relative indifference an endless prairie sheeted in driven snow, with no shadow of tree or branch to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the Antarctic seas. There, by some infernal trick of frost and air, he — shivering and half-shipwrecked — instead of seeing rainbows that speak of hope and comfort in his misery, beholds what looks like a boundless graveyard grinning at him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But you say, I think, that this bleached chapter about whiteness is just a white flag flown by a coward's soul. You surrender to despair, Ishmael.

Tell me, then — why does a strong young colt, born in some peaceful Vermont valley, far from all predators — why is it that on the sunniest day, if you shake a fresh buffalo hide behind him so he cannot even see it but only smells its wild animal musk — why will he bolt, snort, and paw the ground in frenzy with bulging eyes? He has no memory of being attacked by wild creatures in his green northern home. The strange muskiness cannot remind him of any past danger. What does this New England colt know of the black bison herds of distant Oregon?

Nothing. But here you see, even in a speechless animal, the instinct of knowing the demonic forces in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, when he smells that savage musk, the charging, goring bison herds are as real to him as they are to the abandoned wild foal on the prairies, which at this very moment they may be trampling into dust.

So it is: the muffled rolling of a milky sea, the bleak rustling of frosted mountain peaks, the desolate shifting of windblown prairie snows — all these are to Ishmael what the shaking of that buffalo robe is to the frightened colt.

Though neither of us knows where the nameless things lie, of which these mystic signs give such hints — yet with me, as with the colt, somewhere those things must exist. In many of its aspects, this visible world seems formed in love. The invisible spheres were formed in fright.

But we have not yet solved the spell of this whiteness or learned why it appeals with such power to the soul. And stranger still, far more ominous — why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaningful symbol of spiritual things, the very veil of the Christian's God, and yet at the same time the intensifying agent in things most appalling to humanity.

Is it that by its vagueness it hints at the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and so stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation when we gaze into the white depths of the Milky Way? Or is it that whiteness, in its essence, is not so much a color as the visible absence of color — and at the same time the sum of all colors? Is that why there is such a meaningful blankness in a wide landscape of snow — a colorless all-color of atheism from which we recoil? And when we consider the theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly colors — every stately or lovely display, the sweet tints of sunset skies and woods, the gilded velvets of butterflies, the rosy cheeks of young girls — are all merely surface illusions, not actually part of the substances themselves, but only painted on from outside? So that all of glorified Nature paints herself like a prostitute, whose attractions conceal nothing but the charnel-house within? And when we go further and consider that the mystical cosmetic that produces every one of her colors — the great principle of light — forever remains white or colorless in itself, and if it touched all objects without any medium, would paint even tulips and roses with its own blank shade? Considering all this, the paralyzed universe lies before us like a leper. And like stubborn travelers in Lapland who refuse to wear tinted protective glasses, the wretched unbeliever stares himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps the entire view around him. And of all these things, the albino whale was the symbol. Do you wonder, then, at the fiery hunt?

chapters.title: Chapter 43 — Hark!
paragraphs: "Hey! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"

It was the middle watch. A fair moonlit night. The seamen were standing in a line, passing buckets from one of the freshwater barrels amidships to the drinking cask near the stern. Standing mostly on the sacred ground of the quarterdeck, they were careful not to speak or scuffle their feet. From hand to hand the buckets went in the deepest silence, broken only by the occasional flap of a sail and the steady hum of the never-stopping engine room of the sea.
It was in the midst of this quiet that Archy, one of the line, whose post was near the after-hatches, whispered to his neighbor, a Chilean, the words above.
"Hey! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"
"Take the bucket, will you, Archy? What noise do you mean?"
"There it is again — under the hatches — don't you hear it — a cough — it sounded like a cough."
"Cough be damned! Pass along that return bucket."
"There again — there it is! — it sounds like two or three sleepers turning over!"
"Good lord! Knock it off, shipmate, will you? It's the three soaked biscuits you ate for supper turning over inside you — nothing else. Watch the bucket!"
"Say what you want, shipmate. I've got sharp ears."
"Right, you're the one, aren't you, who heard the hum of the old Quaker lady's knitting needles fifty miles at sea from Nantucket. You're the one."

"Grin away. We'll see what turns up. Listen, Cabaco — there is somebody down in the after-hold who has not yet been seen on deck. And I suspect our old captain knows something about it too. I heard Stubb tell Flask, one morning watch, that there was something of that sort going on."
"Nonsense! The bucket!"

chapters.title: Chapter 44 — The Chart
paragraphs: If you had followed Captain Ahab down into his cabin after the squall that took place the night after that wild ratification of his purpose with the crew, you would have seen him go to a locker in the stern, bring out a large wrinkled roll of yellowish sea charts, and spread them before him on his bolted-down table. Then, sitting down before them, you would have seen him intently studying the various lines and shadings that met his eye, and with slow but steady pencil tracing additional courses over spaces that already showed a maze of such markings. At intervals he would refer to stacks of old log-books beside him, where the records of past voyages of various ships chasing the Sperm Whale were set down in faded entries.

While he worked this way, the heavy pewter lamp suspended in chains overhead rocked constantly with the ship's motion, throwing shifting gleams and shadows of lines across his wrinkled brow. It almost seemed that while he himself was marking out lines and courses on the wrinkled charts, some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.

But it was not this particular night that Ahab pondered over his charts alone in his cabin. Almost every night they were brought out. Almost every night some pencil marks were erased and others substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans spread before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, all with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

Now, to anyone not fully acquainted with the ways of whales, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task to seek out one solitary creature in the boundless oceans of this planet. But not so to Ahab. He knew the patterns of all tides and currents. By calculating the drifting of the sperm whale's food, and by recalling the regular, established seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes, he could arrive at reasonable estimates — almost approaching certainty — about the best times for finding his prey in any given stretch of water.

So well-established is the fact of the sperm whale's regular return to given waters that many hunters believe if he could be closely observed and studied worldwide, and if the logs of every voyage of the entire whale fleet were carefully compiled, then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found as predictable as the herring shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migration charts of the sperm whale.

Since the above was written, the statement is happily confirmed by an official circular issued by Lieutenant Maury, of the National Observatory, Washington, April 16th, 1851. By that circular, it appears that precisely such a chart is being completed, and portions of it are presented in the circular. "This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each district are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen."

Besides, when making a passage from one feeding-ground to another, the sperm whales — guided by some infallible instinct, or rather secret intelligence from God himself — mostly swim in veins, as they are called. They continue their way along a given ocean-line with such unwavering precision that no ship ever sailed her course by any chart with one tenth of such marvelous accuracy. Though any one whale's direction may be straight as a surveyor's line, and though the path of many may run broadly parallel along the same route, yet the individual whale rarely deviates more than a few miles from its exact course. This is because the ocean highways along which they travel provide the specific feeding opportunities the whales require.

And so, not only at known times, upon well-known separate feeding-grounds, could Ahab hope to encounter his prey. Even in crossing the widest expanses of water between those grounds, he could, by his skill, so position and time himself along the way as to still have some prospect of a meeting.

There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to undermine his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you cannot generally conclude that the herds found at such-and-such a latitude this year will be identically the same as those found there last season. There are peculiar and undeniable cases in which the opposite has proven true. In general, however, this is not the rule. So, Ahab could not hope, by tracking one known whale herd in any particular season, to find Moby Dick — as some lonely hunter would search the woods for some solitary elk. The key was this: by matching the time of year to the places where sperm whales had most often been encountered, Ahab could put himself in the best possible position, narrowing the odds against him enormously.

Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No effort could have enabled her commander to make the great passage southward, double Cape Horn, and then run down sixty degrees of latitude to reach the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore he had to wait for the next season. Yet the early departure of the Pequod had perhaps been shrewdly calculated by Ahab with exactly this in mind. Because by making a wide sweep along the northern waters, spending time among the Azores, down off the Cape de Verdes, off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata, and along the Carrol Ground — a hunting area known to be productive at that time of year — and then working his way across the Indian Ocean past the Seychelles and into the full fury of the Japanese cruising ground — by following this path, Ahab could hope that in some one of these areas, at the right moment, Moby Dick might be spotted.

But granting all this, considered calmly and coolly, does it not still seem a mad idea — that in the broad boundless ocean, one solitary whale, even if encountered, could be individually recognized by his hunter, as easily as a white-bearded man in the crowded streets of Constantinople? Yes. For the distinctive snow-white brow of Moby Dick, and his snow-white hump, could not be mistaken. And haven't I marked the whale? Ahab would mutter to himself as, after poring over his charts until long after midnight, he would lean back in his swinging chair and stare at the smoldering flame in his lamp. I've marked him, and he's marked me. He's marked me, too, he thought, touching his leg. But I'll chase him around Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of perdition before I give him up.

Often, when forced from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — which, feeding on his intense daytime thoughts, carried them forward amid a clash of frenzies and whirled them round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life became unbearable agony — and when, as sometimes happened, these spiritual torments heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him from which forked flames and lightning shot up, and fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a savage cry would be heard through the ship. Then with glaring eyes, Ahab would burst from his stateroom as though escaping a bed on fire. Yet these — perhaps — were only the outward reflections of the inner turmoil, projected beyond him by the torment inside. For at such times, mad Ahab, that thinking agent that called itself "I" was unhoused. Ahab's deeper self was a thing apart. God knows, in sleep it may have been some thinking thing within, escaping from the scorching containment of the frenzied outer mind, that vaguely tried to escape from the fire by seeking the open air of the ship's deck. But all this gave no relief. The frenzy of the mind fed on those limbs. And while his own living body lay a prisoner in its own extremity, Ahab's eternal, living principle walked among the unsleeping crew. Ahab was a sleepwalker in his own body.

chapters.title: Chapter 45 — The Affidavit
paragraphs: As far as there may be a narrative in this book — and indeed, as it indirectly touches on one or two very interesting and curious details about the habits of sperm whales — the foregoing chapter, in its earlier part, is as important as any in this volume. But the central matter requires still further and more familiar explanation, in order to be properly understood, and moreover to remove any disbelief that a profound ignorance of the entire subject might cause in some minds when they learn that I am earnest in setting down the story of a particular whale.

I do not care to do this part methodically, but will be content to make my point through separate examples of things practically or reliably known to me as a whaleman. From these examples, I trust, the conclusion I aim at will follow naturally.

First: I have personally known three instances where a whale, after receiving a harpoon, has effected a complete escape; and, after an interval (in one instance of three years), has been again struck by the same hand, and slain — when the two irons, both marked by the same private cypher, have been taken from the body. In the instance where three years intervened between the flinging of the two harpoons — and I think it may have been something more than that — the man who darted them happening, in the interval, to go in a trading ship on a voyage to Africa, went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and penetrated far into the interior, where he travelled for a period of nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, with all the other common perils incident to wandering in the heart of unknown regions. Meanwhile, the whale he had struck must also have been on its travels; no doubt it had thrice circumnavigated the globe, brushing with its flanks all the coasts of Africa; but to no purpose. This man and this whale again came together, and the one vanquished the other. I say I, myself, have known three instances similar to this; that is, in two of them I saw the whales struck; and, upon the second attack, saw the two irons with the respective marks cut in them afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so fell out that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time distinctly recognized a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale's eye, which I had observed there three years previous. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here are three instances, then, which I personally know the truth of; but I have heard of many other instances from persons whose veracity in the matter there is no good ground to impeach.

Secondly: It is well known in the Sperm Whale Fishery, however ignorant the world ashore may be of it, that there have been several memorable historical instances where a particular whale in the ocean has been at distant times and places popularly cognizable. Why such a whale became thus marked was not altogether and originally owing to his bodily peculiarities as distinguished from other whales; for however peculiar in that respect any chance whale may be, they soon put an end to his peculiarities by killing him, and boiling him down into a peculiarly valuable oil. No: the reason was this — that from the fatal experiences of the fishery there hung a terrible prestige of perilousness about such a whale as there did about Rinaldo Rinaldini, insomuch that most fishermen were content to recognize him by merely touching their tarpaulins when he would be discovered lounging by them on the sea, without seeking to cultivate a more intimate acquaintance. Like some poor devils ashore that happen to know an irascible great man, they make distant unobtrusive salutations to him in the street, lest if they pursued the acquaintance further, they might receive a summary thump for their presumption.

And not only did each of these famous whales enjoy great individual celebrity — indeed, you might call it ocean-wide renown — not only was each famous in life and now immortal in forecastle stories after death, but each was admitted into all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name. They had names as real as Cambyses or Caesar. Was it not so, Timor Tom! You famed leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who so long lurked in the oriental straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palm-shaded shore of Ombay! Was it not so, New Zealand Tom! You terror of all cruisers who crossed their wakes in the vicinity of the Tattoo Land! Was it not so, Morquan! King of Japan, whose lofty jet they say was at times spotted even from the peak of distant Donan! And was it not so, Don Miguel, you Chilean whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics on your back!

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times causing great havoc among the boats of different ships, were finally hunted down, systematically pursued, and killed by valiant whaling captains who raised their anchors with that express purpose in mind — just as Captain Butler of old set out through the Narragansett Woods specifically to capture that notorious murderous warrior Annawon, the chief fighter of the Indian King Philip.

I cannot find a better place than right here to mention one or two other things which seem important to me. In printed form, they establish the reasonableness of the whole story of the White Whale, especially the catastrophe. For this is one of those discouraging cases where truth requires as much supporting evidence as error. So ignorant are most landsmen of some of the plainest and most obvious wonders of the sea, that without some hints touching the plain facts, historical and otherwise, of the fishery, they might scoff at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or worse still, a hideous and intolerable allegory.

First: Though most men have some vague flitting ideas of the general perils of the grand fishery, yet they have nothing like a fixed, vivid conception of those perils, and the frequency with which they recur. One reason perhaps is that not one in fifty of the actual disasters and deaths by casualties in the fishery ever finds a public record at home, however transient and immediately forgotten that record. Do you suppose that that poor fellow there, who this moment perhaps caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan — do you suppose that that poor fellow's name will appear in the newspaper obituary you will read tomorrow at your breakfast? No: because the mails are very irregular between here and New Guinea. In fact, did you ever hear what might be called regular news direct or indirect from New Guinea? Yet I tell you that upon one particular voyage which I made to the Pacific, among many others we spoke thirty different ships, every one of which had had a death by a whale, some of them more than one, and three that had each lost a boat's crew. For God's sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! — not a gallon you burn, but at least one drop of man's blood was spilled for it.

Second: People ashore have indeed some vague idea that a whale is an enormous creature of enormous power. But I have always found that when describing some specific example of this twofold enormousness, they flatter me on my facetiousness — when, I declare upon my soul, I was no more trying to be funny than Moses when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

But fortunately the specific point I seek here can be established on testimony entirely independent of my own. That point is this: The Sperm Whale is in some cases sufficiently powerful, intelligent, and deliberately malicious to deliberately stave in, utterly destroy, and sink a large ship. And what is more, the Sperm Whale has done it.

First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Ere long, several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, issued from the shoal, and bore directly down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he so stove her in that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the severest exposure, part of the crew reached the land in their boats. Being returned home at last, Captain Pollard once more sailed for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again upon unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and forthwith forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. At this day Captain Pollard is a resident of Nantucket. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have conversed with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.

The following are extracts from Chace's narrative: "Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two separate attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact maneuvers which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the school which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions; as if fired with revenge for their sufferings." Furthermore, Captain Pollard himself — to whom I have been personally introduced — confirmed every word of this mate's account. And despite his disaster, Captain Pollard was given another command, and once more sailed for the Pacific. But on this second voyage the gods and fate again fell upon him — another ship was lost beneath him, and flung forth once more on the sea, Captain Pollard at last came home to Nantucket for good, becoming a night watchman. From those who knew him personally, I learned that he is the most impressive man, though entirely unassuming, even humble, that I ever encountered.

Here are his reflections some time after abandoning the ship, during a black night in an open boat, when almost despairing of reaching any hospitable shore. "The dark ocean and swelling waters were nothing; the fears of being swallowed up by some dreadful tempest, or dashed upon hidden rocks, with all the other ordinary subjects of fearful contemplation, seemed scarcely entitled to a moment's thought; the dismal looking wreck, and the horrid aspect and revenge of the whale, wholly engrossed my reflections, until day again made its appearance."
In another place — page 45 — he speaks of "the mysterious and mortal attack of the animal."

Second: The ship Union, also of Nantucket, was totally lost off the Azores in 1807 by a similar attack, but the authentic details of this catastrophe I have never happened to encounter, though from whale hunters I have now and then heard passing references to it.

Third: Some eighteen or twenty years ago, Commodore J——, then commanding an American warship of the first class, happened to be dining with a party of whaling captains, aboard a Nantucket ship in the harbor of Oahu, Sandwich Islands. When conversation turned to whales, the Commodore was pleased to be skeptical about the amazing strength attributed to them by the professional gentlemen present. He flatly denied, for example, that any whale could strike his stout warship so as to cause it to leak badly. Very good. Some weeks later, the Commodore set sail in that very ship. In the open sea, a great sperm whale struck the warship with such tremendous force as to throw the Commodore and every man to the deck. The sloop sprang a bad leak from the blow, and was forced to put in for repairs at the nearest port. I am not sure the Commodore has ever been entirely cured of his skepticism.

I will now refer you to Langsdorff's Voyages for a small detail particularly interesting to me. Langsdorff, you should know, was attached to the Russian Admiral Krusenstern's famous Discovery Expedition at the beginning of the current century. Captain Langsdorff begins his seventeenth chapter thus:

"By the thirteenth of May our ship was ready to sail, and the next day we were out in the open sea, on our way to Okhotsk. The weather was very clear and fine, but so intolerably cold that we were obliged to keep on our fur clothing. For some days we had very little wind; it was not till the nineteenth that a brisk gale from the northwest sprang up. An uncommon large whale, the body of which was larger than the ship itself, lay almost at the surface of the water, but was not perceived by any one on board till the moment when the ship, which was in full sail, was almost upon him, so that it was impossible to prevent the ship's striking him. We were thus placed in the most imminent danger, as this gigantic creature, setting up its back, raised the ship three feet at least out of the water. The masts reeled, and the sails fell altogether, while we who were below all sprang instantly upon the deck, concluding that we had struck upon some rock; instead of this, we saw the monster sailing off with the utmost gravity and solemnity. Captain D'Wolf applied immediately to the pumps to examine whether or not the vessel had received any damage from the shock, but we found that very happily it had escaped entirely uninjured."

Now, the Captain D'Wolf referred to as commanding the ship in question is a New Englander, who, after a long life of unusual adventures as a sea-captain, now resides in the village of Dorchester near Boston. I have the honor of being his nephew. I have specifically questioned him about this passage in Langsdorff. He confirms every word. The ship, however, was by no means large — a Russian craft built on the Siberian coast, purchased by my uncle after trading away the vessel he had originally sailed from home. He bargained it from the Russians as one might buy a used pony cart in the woods.

In that straightforward, manly book of old-fashioned adventure — so full of honest wonders — the voyage of Lionel Wafer, one of old Dampier's companions — I found a small incident set down so like what I just quoted from Langsdorff that I cannot resist inserting it here as a supporting example, if one is needed.

Lionel, it seems, was on his way to "John Ferdinando," as he calls the modern Juan Fernandez. "In our way thither," he says, "about four o'clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck upon a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin." Lionel then goes on to say that the shock was caused by "a large whale, the body of which, as the captain said, seemed larger than the ship itself."

I might proceed with several more examples, one way or another known to me, of the great power and malice at times of the sperm whale. In more than one instance, he has been known, not only to chase the assailing boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself, and long withstand all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that head; and, as for his strength, let me say that there have been examples where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship, and secured there — the whale towing her great hull through the water, as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that, if the sperm whale, once struck, is allowed time to rally, he then acts, not so often with blind rage, as with wilful, deliberate designs of destruction to his pursuers; nor is it without conveying some eloquent indication of his character, that upon being attacked he will frequently open his mouth, and retain it in that dread expansion for several consecutive minutes. But I must be content with only one more and a concluding illustration; a remarkable and most significant one, by which you will not fail to see, that not only is the most marvellous event in this book corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — Verily there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth century of the Christian era lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius was general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work of uncommon value in every way. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unsensational historian, except in one or two particulars that do not affect the matter I am about to mention.

Now, in this history of his, Procopius mentions that during the term of his prefecture at Constantinople, a great sea-monster was captured in the neighboring Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after having destroyed vessels at intervals in those waters for a period of more than fifty years. A fact thus set down in substantial history cannot easily be gainsaid. Nor is there any reason it should be. Of what precise species this sea-monster was is not mentioned. But as he destroyed ships, as well as for other reasons, he must have been a whale; and I am strongly inclined to think a sperm whale. And I will tell you why. For a long time I fancied that the sperm whale had been always unknown in the Mediterranean and the deep waters connecting with it. Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort. But further investigations have recently proved to me that in modern times there have been isolated instances of the presence of the sperm whale in the Mediterranean. I am told, on good authority, that on the Barbary coast, a Commodore Davis of the British navy found the skeleton of a sperm whale. Now, as a vessel of war readily passes through the Dardanelles, hence a sperm whale could, by the same route, pass out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that kind, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century staved ships and lay on the surface of the sea, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

chapters.title: Chapter 46 — Surmises
