paragraphs: Though, consumed with the hot fire of his purpose, Ahab in all his thoughts and actions ever had in view the ultimate capture of Moby Dick; though he seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion; nevertheless it may have been that he was by nature and long habituation far too wedded to a fiery whaleman's ways altogether to abandon the collateral prosecution of the voyage. Or at least, if this were otherwise, there were not wanting other motives much more influential with him. It would be refining too much, perhaps, even considering his monomania, to hint that his vindictiveness towards the White Whale might have possibly extended itself in some degree to all sperm whales, and that the more monsters he slew, by so much the more he multiplied the chances that each subsequently encountered whale would prove to be the hated one he hunted. But if such a hypothesis be indeed exceptionable, there were still additional considerations which, though not so strictly according with the wildness of his ruling passion, yet were by no means incapable of swaying him.

To accomplish his object Ahab must use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendency in some respects was over Starbuck, yet that ascendency did not cover the complete spiritual man any more than mere corporeal superiority involves intellectual mastership; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual but stand in a sort of corporeal relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still he knew that for all this the chief mate, in his soul, abhorred his captain's quest, and could he, would joyfully disintegrate himself from it, or even frustrate it. It might be that a long interval would elapse ere the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would ever be apt to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear upon him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab respecting Moby Dick was noways more significantly manifested than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should in some way be stripped of that strange imaginative impiousness which naturally invested it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept withdrawn into the obscure background (for few men's courage is proof against protracted meditation unrelieved by action); that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think of than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, yet all sailors of all sorts are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the varying outer weather, and they inhale its fickleness — and when retained for any object remote and blank in the pursuit, however promissory of life and passion in the end, it is above all things requisite that temporary interests and employments should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

Nor was Ahab unmindful of another thing. In times of strong emotion mankind disdain all base considerations; but such times are evanescent. The permanent constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness. Granting that the White Whale fully incites the hearts of this my savage crew, and playing round their savageness even breeds a certain generous knight-errantism in them — still, while for the love of it they give chase to Moby Dick, they must also have food for their more common, daily appetites. For even the high lifted and chivalric Crusaders of old times were not content to traverse two thousand miles of land to fight for their holy sepulchre, without committing burglaries, picking pockets, and gaining other pious perquisites by the way. Had they been strictly held to their one final and romantic object — that final and romantic object, too many would have turned from in disgust. I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hopes of cash — aye, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by, and no perspective promise of it to them, and then this same quiescent cash all at once mutinying in them, this same cash would soon cashier Ahab.

Nor was there wanting still another precautionary motive more related to Ahab personally. Having impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely, revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod's voyage, Ahab was now entirely conscious that, in so doing, he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation; and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew, if so disposed, and to that end competent, could refuse all further obedience to him, and even violently wrest from him the command. From even the barely hinted imputation of usurpation, and the possible consequences of such a suppressed impression gaining ground, Ahab must of course have been most anxious to protect himself. That protection could only consist in his own predominating brain and heart and hand, backed by a heedful, closely calculating attention to every minute atmospheric influence which it was possible for his crew to be subjected to.

For all these reasons, and others perhaps too subtle to spell out here, Ahab plainly saw that he must still in good measure stay true to the natural, stated purpose of the Pequod's voyage — observe all customary practices, and not only that, but force himself to show all his well-known passionate interest in the general pursuit of his profession.

Be all this as it may, his voice was now often heard hailing the three mastheads and warning them to keep a sharp lookout, and not to skip reporting even a porpoise. This vigilance was not long without reward.

chapters.title: Chapter 47 — The Mat-Maker
paragraphs: It was a cloudy, sultry afternoon. The seamen were lazily lounging about the decks or gazing vacantly over the rail into the lead-colored waters. Queequeg and I were quietly weaving what is called a sword-mat, to use as an additional lashing for our boat. So still and subdued was the whole scene, and yet somehow so full of anticipation, and such a spell of daydreaming lurked in the air, that each silent sailor seemed dissolved into his own invisible self.

I was the attendant or assistant to Queequeg while he worked at the mat. As I kept passing the filling thread of marline back and forth between the long strands of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads, idly looking off at the water while he carelessly drove each yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess ruled over the ship and the sea, broken only by the intermittent thumping of that great sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself were a shuttle mechanically weaving the unchangeable pattern of my own destiny. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one unchanging vibration, which merely allowed for the crosswise interweaving of other threads. This warp seemed like necessity. And here, thought I, with my own hand I weave my own fate into these unalterable strands. Meanwhile, Queequeg's indifferent sword — sometimes hitting the woof slantingly, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be — and with each weaving creating a corresponding contrast in the final fabric — this savage's sword, thought I, which thus strikes the woof at random, must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity — all three interwoven — none working separately. If chance freely determines the pattern, necessity sets its laws. Free will works somewhere between them. And chance, though limited in its range by both, has the final shaping power over all events.

We were weaving and weaving away when I was startled by a sound so strange, so long-drawn, so musically wild and unearthly, that the ball of free will dropped from my hand, and I stood gazing up at the clouds from which that voice fell like a wing. High aloft in the crosstrees was that mad Gay-Header, Tashtego. His body was reaching eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and at brief, sudden intervals he continued his cries. To be sure, the same sound was perhaps being heard from the mastheads of three other whaling vessels in the same waters at that very moment. But to us, hearing it for the first time, it hardly seemed possible that anything could make such sounds.

As he stood hovering over you, half-suspended in air, peering so wildly and eagerly toward the horizon, you would have thought him some prophet or seer beholding the shadows of Fate, and announcing their coming with those wild cries.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"Where away?"
"On the lee beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
Instantly all was commotion.
The Sperm Whale blows as a clock ticks, with the same unwavering and reliable regularity. And by this the whalemen distinguish this fish from other species of his kind.
"There go flukes!" was now the cry from Tashtego, and the whales disappeared.
"Quick, steward!" cried Ahab. "Time! Time!"
Dough-Boy hurried below, glanced at the watch, and reported the exact minute to Ahab.

The ship was now steered away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Tashtego reporting that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bow. For that peculiar trick sometimes used by the Sperm Whale — when, diving with his head in one direction, he nevertheless wheels around underwater and swiftly swims off the opposite way — could not now be at work. There was every reason to believe the whales were heading steadily downwind. And so it proved. Suddenly Tashtego gave a tremendous shout from the masthead.

But at this critical instant a sudden exclamation was heard that drew every eye from the whale. With a start, all stared at dark Ahab, who was surrounded by five dusky phantoms that seemed freshly formed out of thin air.

chapters.title: Chapter 48 — The First Lowering
paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they then seemed, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and, with a noiseless celerity, were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat which swung there. This boat had always been deemed one of the spare boats, though technically called the captain's, on account of its hanging from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bows was tall and swart, with one white tooth evilly protruding from its steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton funereally invested him, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning this ebonness was a glistening white plaited turban, the living hair braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less swart in aspect, the companions of this figure were of that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manillas — a race notorious for a certain diabolism of subtlety, and by some honest white mariners supposed to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents on the water of the devil, their lord, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" shouting across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a daring agility unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," drawlingly and soothingly sighed Stubb to his crew, some of whom still showed signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you stare at? Those chaps in yonder boat? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good fellows enough. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil fetch ye, ye ragamuffin rapscallions; ye are all asleep. Stop snoring, ye sleepers, and pull. Pull, will ye? pull, can't ye? pull, won't ye? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't ye pull? — pull and break something! pull, and start your eyes out! Here!" — whipping out the sharp knife from his girdle — "every mother's son of ye draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now ye do something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's exordium to his crew is given here at large because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in inculcating the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this specimen of his sermonizings that he ever flew into downright passions with his congregation. Not at all; and therein consisted his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrific things to his crew in a tone so strangely compounded of fun and fury, and the fury seemed so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such queer invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides he all the time looked so easy and indolent himself, so loungingly managed his steering-oar, and so broadly gaped — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, acted like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sort of humorists, whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous, as to put all inferiors on their guard in the matter of obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's barrels of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what we came for. (Pull, boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the advent of these outlandish strangers at such a critical instant as the lowering of the boats from the deck had not unreasonably awakened a sort of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company; but Archy's fancied discovery having some time previous got abroad among them, though indeed not credited then, this had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took off the extreme edge of their wonder; and so what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for their appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious surmisings; though the affair still left abundant room for all manner of wild conjectures as to dark Ahab's precise agency in the matter from the beginning. For me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod during the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the enigmatical hintings of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meantime, Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having sided the furthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a circumstance bespeaking how potent a crew was pulling him. Those tiger yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone; like five trip-hammers they rose and fell with regular strokes of strength, which periodically started the boat along the water like a horizontal burst boiler out of a Mississippi steamer. As for Fedallah, who was seen pulling the harpooneer oar, he had thrown aside his black jacket, and displayed his naked chest with the whole part of his body above the gunwale, clearly cut against the alternating depressions of the watery horizon; while at the other end of the boat Ahab, with one arm, like a fencer's, thrown half backward into the air, as if to counterbalance any tendency to trip, Ahab was seen steadily managing his steering oar as in a thousand boat lowerings ere the White Whale had torn him. All at once the outstretched arm gave a peculiar motion and then remained fixed, while the boat's five oars were seen simultaneously peaked. Boat and crew sat motionless on the sea. Instantly the three spread boats in the rear paused on their way. The whales had irregularly settled bodily down into the blue, thus giving no distantly discernible token of the movement, though from his closer vicinity Ahab had observed it.
"Every man look out along his oars!" cried Starbuck. "You, Queequeg, stand up!"

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised platform in the bow, the harpooner stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off toward the spot where the chase had last been seen. Likewise upon the extreme stern of the boat, where it was also triangularly raised level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and skillfully balancing himself against the jerking tosses of his chip of a craft, silently scanning the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far off, Flask's boat was also lying breathlessly still. Its commander was recklessly standing upon the top of the loggerhead, a stout post rooted in the keel and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is no bigger than the palm of a man's hand, and standing on such a base, Flask seemed perched at the masthead of some ship that had sunk to all but her topmost spars. But little King-Post was a resourceful fellow. Not a man to be long kept down by anything. And though the huge Daggoo loomed behind him like a dark mountain, Flask would still be the first to see a whale.
"I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand on the gunwale to steady himself, swiftly slid to the stern, and then straightening up, volunteered his lofty shoulders as a pedestal.
"Good a masthead as any, sir. Will you mount?"
"That I will, and thank you very much, my fine fellow. Only I wish you were fifty feet taller."

Whereupon, planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic harpooner stooped a little, presented his flat palm to Flask's foot, and then, putting Flask's hand on his plumed head and telling him to spring as he himself should toss, with one skillful fling landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And there was Flask now standing, with Daggoo's one lifted arm providing him with a chest-strap to lean against and steady himself.

At any time it is a strange sight for the newcomer to see with what marvelous habitual skill the whaleman will keep an upright posture in his boat, even when pitched about by the most violently contrary seas. Stranger still to see him perched giddily on the loggerhead itself under such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was even more remarkable. For supporting himself with a cool, indifferent, effortless, almost savage majesty, the noble black — to all appearances — bore little Flask on his shoulders with as much easy pride as though the little man were simply a badge or ornament he wore. So that they seemed like the black figure on the front of some enormous hearse, bearing a white coffin.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, betrayed no such far-gazing anxieties. The whales might have made one of their regular deep dives, not a temporary plunge from mere fright. And if so, Stubb, as was his habit in such cases, was resolved to comfort the waiting interval with his pipe. He pulled it from his hatband, where he always wore it at an angle like a feather. He loaded it and tamped down the tobacco with his thumb. But he had barely lit his match on the rough sandpaper of his hand when Tashtego, his harpooner, whose eyes had been set on a level with the water like two floated pistols, gave a sharp shout and declared that the whale was just below. Instantly, Stubb's pipe went out of his mouth.

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment — nothing but a troubled patch of greenish-white water and thin scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it, blowing off to leeward like confused spray from white-capped waves. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it does above intensely heated iron plates. Beneath this atmospheric wavering and curling, and partially beneath a thin layer of water too, the whales were swimming. Seen through the warped air and water, their vast dim shapes looked strangely magnified, like the full-length reflections in a thin mirror. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, transported and bewildered by such an enchanted sight, had fatally mistaken the size of the whale and struck too close. And so been dragged down into the deep, crushed by the weight of the rising monster.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it seemed ready to outrun them. It flew on and on, like a mass of merging bubbles swept down a swift stream from the hills.

"Pull, pull, my good boys," said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but most intensely concentrated whisper to his men. The sharp fixed glance from his eyes, aimed straight ahead of the bow, seemed almost like two visible needles in two unerring compasses. He did not say much to his crew, nor did they say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals piercingly broken by one of his peculiar whispers — now harsh with command, now soft with pleading.

How different the loud little King-Post. "Sing out and say something, my hearties! Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys! Only do that for me, and I'll sign over my Martha's Vineyard plantation to you, boys — including wife and children! Lay me on — lay me on! Oh Lord, Lord! I'll go stark, staring mad! See! See that white water!" And shouting, he pulled his hat from his head and stomped up and down on it. Then he picked it up and flung it far off upon the sea. And still he shrieked: "Lay me on — lay me on! Lay me on, sir!" he cried to Daggoo. "Break something! Break your back! Burst yourself! Only get me there!"

"Look at that fellow now," Stubb drawled philosophically, following along at a short distance with his unlit pipe still mechanically clamped between his teeth. "He's got fits, that Flask has. Fits? Yes, give him fits — that's the very word — pitch fits into them. Merrily, merrily, hearts alive! Pudding for supper, you know — merry's the word. Pull, babes — pull, sucklings — pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling. Nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two — that's all. Take it easy — why don't you take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!"

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his — those are words best left unspoken here, for you live under the blessed light of the Christian land. Only the godless sharks in the lawless seas may hear such words, when, with a tornado brow and eyes of red murder and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. The repeated specific references Flask made to "that whale" — as he called the imaginary monster he declared was constantly teasing his boat's bow with its tail — these references were at times so vivid and lifelike that they would cause one or two of his men to steal a fearful look over their shoulders. But this was against all rules. The oarsmen must row blindly, their eyes shut and a skewer through their necks — custom dictating that they must have no sight of the terror facing them. Well enough for them. But what about us in the bow? We could see the whole thing.

It was a sight full of sudden wonder and awe! The vast swells of the all-powerful sea, the surging hollow roar they made as they rolled along the eight gunwales like gigantic bowls in a boundless bowling green, the brief suspended agony of the boat as it tipped for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves that almost seemed about to cut it in two, the sudden profound plunge into the watery valleys, the keen goading surges to gain the top of the opposite hill — all this was thrilling. Not a man breathed. A thin mist of sweat covered every face. The chests heaved as if laboring at the forge. Not one word was spoken.

Not the raw recruit, marching from the arms of his wife into the fever heat of his first battle — not the dead man's ghost encountering the first unknown phantom in the other world — neither of these can feel stranger and stronger emotions than the man who for the first time finds himself pulling into the charmed, churning circle of the hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water made by the chase was now becoming more and more visible, owing to the deepening darkness of the cloud-shadows on the sea. The jets of spray no longer blended, but tilted everywhere to right and left. The whales seemed to be separating their paths. The boats were pulled farther apart. Starbuck gave chase to three whales running dead to leeward. Our sail was now set, and with the still-rising wind we rushed along — the boat going with such fury through the water that the lee oars could barely be dipped in time to escape being torn from the row-locks.
Soon we were running through a wide, drifting veil of mist. Neither ship nor boat to be seen.
"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding steam shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

Though completely swamped, the boat was nearly unharmed. Swimming around it, we picked up the floating oars, and lashing them across the gunwale, tumbled back to our places. There we sat up to our knees in the sea, the water covering every rib and plank, so that to our downward-gazing eyes the suspended craft seemed a coral boat grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl. The waves dashed their shields together. The whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire upon the prairie, in which, unconsumed, we were burning — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats. You might as well roar down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, scud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night. No sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea made an eerie sound against the half-submerged gunwale. At times we had to bail the boat with our hats. The oars were useless as propellers. We were forced to use them as paddles, guiding the boat through the breakers. Each man sat with his back to the sea, his face turned upon the others, and each flashing cheek was his companion's lightning-rod.

Wet, drenched through, and shivering cold, despairing of ship or boat, we lifted our eyes as dawn came. The mist still spread over the sea. The empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg started to his feet, cupping his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, as of ropes and masts hidden by the storm. The sound came nearer and nearer. The thick mists were dimly parted by a huge, vague form. Terrified, we all sprang into the sea as the ship, which at last had been searching for us after the other boats returned, bore directly down upon us within a distance of not much more than its own length.

Floating on the waves we watched the abandoned boat as it tossed and gaped beneath the ship's bow like a wood chip at the base of a waterfall. Then the vast hull rolled over it, and it was seen no more until it came up wallowing astern. Again we swam for it, were dashed against it by the seas, and were at last pulled up and safely landed on board. Before the squall hit, the other boats had cut loose from their fish and returned to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up, but was still cruising back and forth in case any sign of us should appear. It was only the morning after that we were recovered.

chapters.title: Chapter 49 — The Hyena
paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange mixed affair we call life when a man takes the whole universe for a vast practical joke, though the humor of it he can only dimly see, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. However, nothing discourages him, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He swallows down all events, all creeds, all beliefs, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how lumpy — as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And just as the ostrich blindly swallows these things, so does this man greedily consume the strangest opinions.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the entire situation. Considering, therefore, that squalls and capsizings and consequent campouts on the deep were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life — considering that at the supremely critical moment of approaching the whale, I must trust my life to the man who steered the boat, often a fellow who at that very instant was so reckless as to nearly sink the craft with his own excitement — considering that the particular danger of my situation was that I always belonged to the harpooner's boat, and the harpooner's duty was to approach nearest to the whale's head — and considering finally that in these critical moments the harpooner's task was to stand up and throw his weapon from a frantically rocking boat — considering all this, I say, it seemed to me that making a rough draft of my last will and testament was the sensible thing to do.

It may seem strange that of all men, sailors should be so fond of tinkering at their last wills and testaments, but there are no people in the world more devoted to that pastime. This was the fourth time in my nautical career that I had done the same thing. After the ceremony was concluded, I felt much easier. A stone was rolled away from my heart. Besides, all the days I should now live would be as good as the days that Lazarus lived after his resurrection — a supplementary clean gain of so many months or weeks as the case might be. I survived myself. My death and burial were locked up in my chest. I looked around me, calm and collected, and made up my mind to be coolly brave from that moment forward.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.

chapters.title: Chapter 50 — Ahab’s Boat and Crew. Fedallah
paragraphs: "Who would have thought it, Flask!" cried Stubb. "If I had only one leg, you wouldn't catch me in a boat — unless maybe to plug the drain-hole with my wooden toe. Oh! He's a wonderful old man!"

"I don't think it so strange, on that account," said Flask. "If his leg were off at the hip, now, that would be a different thing. That would disable him. But he has one knee, and a good part of the other left, you know."
"I don't know about that, little man. I've never yet seen him kneel."

Among whale-wise people it has often been debated whether, considering the supreme importance of his life to the success of the voyage, it is right for a whaling captain to risk that life in the active dangers of the chase. So Tamerlane's soldiers often argued, with tears in their eyes, whether that invaluable life of his ought to be carried into the thickest of the fight.

But with Ahab the question took on a different angle. Considering that even with two legs a man is but a hobbling creature in times of danger — considering that the pursuit of whales is always conducted under great and extraordinary difficulties, and that every individual moment involves peril — under these circumstances, is it wise for any maimed man to enter a whale-boat in the hunt? As a general rule, the joint-owners of the Pequod must plainly have thought not.

Ahab well knew that although his friends at home would think little of his entering a boat in certain comparatively harmless vicissitudes of the chase, for the sake of being near the scene of action and giving his orders in person, yet for Captain Ahab to have a boat actually apportioned to him as a regular headsman in the hunt — above all, for Captain Ahab to be supplied with five extra men as that same boat's crew — he well knew that such generous conceits never entered the heads of the owners of the Pequod. Therefore he had not solicited a boat's crew from them, nor had he in any way hinted his desires on that head. Nevertheless, he had taken private measures of his own touching all that matter. Until Cabaco's published discovery, the sailors had little foreseen it, though to be sure when, after being a little while out of port, all hands had concluded the customary business of fitting the whaleboats for service; when some time after this Ahab was now and then found bestirring himself in the matter of making thole-pins with his own hands for what was thought to be one of the spare boats, and even solicitously cutting the small wooden skewers which, when the line is running out, are pinned over the groove in the bow; when all this was observed in him, and particularly his solicitude in having an extra coat of sheathing in the bottom of the boat, as if to make it better withstand the pointed pressure of his ivory limb; and also the anxiety he evinced in exactly shaping the thigh-board, or clumsy cleat, as it is sometimes called, the horizontal piece in the boat's bow for bracing the knee against in darting or stabbing at the whale; when it was observed how often he stood up in that boat with his solitary knee fixed in the semi-circular depression in the cleat, and with the carpenter's chisel gouged out a little here and straightened it a little there — all these things, I say, had awakened much interest and curiosity at the time. But almost everybody supposed that this particular preparative heedfulness in Ahab must only be with a view to the ultimate chase of Moby Dick; for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. But such a supposition did by no means involve the remotest suspicion as to any boat's crew being assigned to that boat.

Now, as for the subordinate phantoms, whatever wonder remained soon faded. For in a whaler, wonders quickly lose their shine. Besides, now and then such unaccountable odds and ends of strange nationalities come up from the unknown corners of the earth to man these floating outlaws among whalers, and the ships themselves often pick up such strange castaway creatures found tossing about the open sea on planks, bits of wreck, oars, whale-boats, canoes, blown-off Japanese junks, and what not — that the Devil himself could hardly have been surprised at Fedallah's crew.

But be all this as it may, certain it is that while the subordinate phantoms soon found their place among the crew, though still as it were somehow distinct from them, yet that hair-turbaned Fedallah remained a muffled mystery to the last. Whence he came in a mannerly world like this, by what sort of unaccountable tie he soon evinced himself to be linked with Ahab's peculiar fortunes; nay, so far as to have some sort of a half-hinted influence — Heaven knows, but it might have been even authority over him — all this none knew. But one cannot sustain an indifferent air concerning Fedallah. He was such a creature as civilized, domestic people in the temperate zone only see in their dreams, and that but dimly; but the like of whom now and then glide among the unchanging Asiatic communities, especially the Oriental isles to the east of the continent — those insulated, immemorial, unalterable countries, which even in these modern days still preserve much of the ghostly aboriginalness of earth's primal generations, when the memory of the first man was a distinct recollection, and all men his descendants, unknowing whence he came, eyed each other as real phantoms, and asked of the sun and the moon why they were created and to what end; when, though, according to Genesis, the angels indeed consorted with the daughters of men, the devils also, add the uncanonical Rabbins, indulged in mundane amours.

chapters.title: Chapter 51 — The Spirit-Spout
paragraphs: Days, weeks passed, and under easy sail, the ivory Pequod had slowly swept across four separate cruising-grounds: the one off the Azores, the one off the Cape Verdes, the Plate — so called because it lies off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata — and the Carrol Ground, an unmarked watery expanse south of St. Helena.

It was while gliding through these last waters that one serene and moonlit night, when all the waves rolled by like scrolls of silver, and by their soft, spreading murmur made what seemed a silvery silence rather than a solitude — on such a silent night a silvery jet was seen far ahead of the white bubbles at the bow. Lit up by the moon, it looked celestial — like some plumed and glittering god rising from the sea. Fedallah first spotted this jet. For on these moonlit nights, it was his habit to climb to the main masthead and stand lookout there with the same precision as if it had been day. And the crew would find him there in the morning, still standing in the same posture, his fixed gaze aimed at the same advancing point. No matter how still the night, his thin lips moved on and on, as if muttering some endless prayer.

Walking the deck with quick, side-lunging strides, Ahab ordered the topgallant sails and royals set, and every studding-sail spread. The best helmsman on the ship was put at the wheel. Then, with every masthead manned, the loaded ship rolled down before the wind. The strange uplifting force of the stern breeze filling the hollows of so many sails made the buoyant, hovering deck feel like air beneath the feet. Still she rushed along, as if two opposing forces struggled within her — one to soar straight to heaven, the other to drive her toward some horizontal goal. And all the while the phantom jet kept rising ahead.

This midnight spout had almost become a forgotten thing when, some days later — there it was again: at the same silent hour, announced again, spotted by all. But when we set sail to overtake it, it once more vanished as if it had never existed. And so it served us night after night, until no one paid it any attention except to marvel at it. Mysteriously thrown into the clear moonlight or starlight, disappearing again for one, two, or three whole days, and somehow seeming at every new appearance to be advancing still further ahead of us — this solitary jet seemed forever beckoning us on.

Nor, given the ancient superstition of their race and the supernatural aura that seemed in many ways to surround the Pequod, were there lacking some seamen who swore that whenever and wherever that spout appeared — however far apart in time and place — it was cast by one and the same whale: Moby Dick. For a time, there also reigned a sense of peculiar dread at this flitting apparition, as if it were treacherously beckoning us on and on so that the monster might turn around upon us and tear us apart at last in some remote and savage sea.

These temporary fears, so vague but so awful, drew a strange power from the contrasting calm of the weather. Beneath all its blue gentleness, some thought there lurked a devilish charm, as for days upon days we voyaged through seas so wearily, so lonesomely mild that all of space, repelled by our vengeful mission, seemed to be emptying itself of life before our funeral-urn prow.

But at last, when we turned eastward, the Cape winds began howling around us, and we rose and fell upon the long, troubled seas that lie there. When the ivory-tusked Pequod bowed sharply to the blast and drove into the dark waves in her fury, until showers of silver chips — the foam-flakes — flew over her bulwarks, then all this desolate emptiness of life went away, but gave place to sights more dismal than before.

Close to our bow, strange shapes darted back and forth in the water before us, while thick behind us flew inscrutable sea-ravens. Every morning, perched on our rigging, rows of these birds were seen. Despite our shouting, they stubbornly clung to the ropes for a long time, as though they considered our ship some drifting, uninhabited craft — a thing fated for desolation, and therefore a fitting roosting-place for their homeless selves. And the black sea heaved and heaved, still relentlessly heaving, as if its vast tides were a conscience, and the great soul of the world were in anguish and remorse for the long sin and suffering it had caused.

Cape of Good Hope, do they call you? Rather Cape Tormentoso, as they named you long ago. For long deceived by the treacherous silences that had attended us before, we found ourselves launched into this tormented sea, where guilty beings transformed into those birds and those fish seemed condemned to swim forever without any harbor in store, or to beat that black air without any horizon. But calm, snow-white, and unchanging — still directing its fountain of feathers toward the sky — still beckoning us on from ahead — the solitary jet would at times appear.

During all this blackness of the elements, Ahab, though taking near-constant command of the drenched and dangerous deck, showed the gloomiest reserve and spoke to his mates less often than ever. In storms like these, after everything above and aloft has been secured, nothing more can be done but passively await the outcome of the gale. Then Captain and crew become practical fatalists. So, with his ivory leg inserted into its usual hole and with one hand firmly gripping a shroud, Ahab would stand for hours gazing dead to windward, while an occasional sleet or snow would drive against him and plaster itself upon his coat. Meanwhile, the Pequod would sometimes roll so fiercely that an icicle formed on one side of the helmsman's tiller would be dipped into the sea on the other. But even though drenched to the bone and half-frozen, Ahab stubbornly refused to seek shelter in the cabin, for its floor was one that he could not bear. It was dangerous enough for him to navigate any ship's deck in rough weather. But to stand on the Pequod's cabin floor was worse than standing on the backs of wild bulls. And so it was that one night, his ivory leg having received a sharp blow, he was hurled heavily against the deck. From then on, a watchman — whose task was to attend to the cabin lamp and binnacle — was stationed at the cabin door. The binnacle is called the tell-tale, because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course from his berth.
The cabin-compass is called the tell-tale because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course.
Terrible old man! thought Starbuck with a shudder. Sleeping through this gale, still you steadfastly keep your eye on your purpose.

chapters.title: Chapter 52 — The Albatross
paragraphs: Southeastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozet Islands — a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen — a sail appeared ahead: the Goney, or Albatross by name. As she slowly drew near, from my lofty perch at the foremast-head I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a newcomer in the far ocean fisheries: a whaler at sea, long absent from home.

As if the waves had been bleachers, this craft was whitened like the skeleton of a stranded walrus. All down her sides, this ghostly appearance was streaked with long channels of reddened rust, while all her spars and rigging were like thick branches of trees furred over with frost. Only her lower sails were set. It was a wild sight to see her long-bearded lookouts at those three mastheads. They seemed clad in animal skins, so torn and patched was the clothing that had survived nearly four years of cruising. Standing in iron hoops nailed to the mast, they swayed and swung over the deep. Three of the ship's officers leaned over the railing with long, bent fishing rods. They would not have looked very different from three old trees with three old crows perched on them.
"Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pale bulwarks, was in the act of putting his speaking-trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea. And the wind now rising fiercely, he struggled in vain to make himself heard without it. Meanwhile his ship was still increasing the distance between us. While the seamen of the Pequod were silently acknowledging this ominous incident at the first mere mention of the White Whale's name to another ship, Ahab paused for a moment. It almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbidden it. But seizing his own speaking-trumpet, he knew that the other vessel was too far away to be heard, so he merely stood watching her move off, always gazing at the retreating ship as long as she remained in sight.

At that moment the two ships' wakes were crossing, and instantly — as was their strange custom — schools of small harmless fish that had been peacefully swimming alongside us for days darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and lined themselves up alongside the stranger's flanks. Though in the course of his continuous voyaging Ahab must often have noticed a similar sight before, to any monomaniac man the most trivial things can carry powerful meanings.

"Swim away from me, do you?" murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed little in the words, but the tone conveyed more deep helpless sadness than the mad old man had ever before shown. But turning to the helmsman, who had been holding the ship into the wind to slow her progress, he cried out in his old lion's voice — "Up helm! Keep her off round the world!"

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings. But where does all that circumnavigation lead? Only through numberless dangers to the very point where we started, where those we left behind — safe and secure — were all the time ahead of us.

Were this world an endless plain, and by sailing eastward we could forever reach new distances and discover sights more sweet and strange than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then there would be promise in the voyage. But in pursuit of those far mysteries we dream of, or in tormented chase of that demon phantom that at some time or other swims before all human hearts — while chasing such things over this round globe, they either lead us on through barren mazes or midway leave us overwhelmed.

chapters.title: Chapter 53 — The Gam
paragraphs: The stated reason why Ahab did not go aboard the whaler we had spoken was this: the wind and sea threatened storms. But even had this not been the case, he would probably not have boarded her anyway — judging by his later conduct on similar occasions — if by hailing her he had gotten a negative answer to the question he asked. For, as it eventually turned out, he had no interest in socializing even for five minutes with any stranger captain, unless that captain could contribute some of the information he so obsessively sought. But all this might remain unexplained without some account of what a Gam is among whalemen.

If two strangers crossing the Pine Barrens in New York State, or the equally desolate Salisbury Plain in England, happen to encounter each other in such unwelcoming wilds, those two, for the life of them, cannot well avoid a mutual greeting — and stopping for a moment to exchange news, and perhaps sitting down for a while to rest together. How much more natural, then, that upon the limitless Pine Barrens and Salisbury Plains of the sea, two whaling vessels spotting each other at the ends of the earth — off lonely Fanning's Island, or the faraway King's Mills — how much more natural that under such circumstances these ships should not only exchange salutes, but take more involved steps toward socializing. And especially since it is an unavoidable thing that most whalers are away from home for at least three or four years at a stretch.

For the long-absent ship, the outward-bound vessel perhaps has letters on board. At any rate, she will be sure to share some newspapers of a date a year or two more recent than the last one in her blurred and thumb-worn files. And in return for that courtesy, the outward-bound ship would receive the latest whaling intelligence from the cruising-ground to which she may be headed — a thing of the utmost importance. And to some degree, all this holds true of whaling vessels crossing each other's paths on the cruising-ground itself, even though both are equally long absent from home. For one may have received recent mail from a friendly passing vessel, while the other has received none at all.

Nor would difference of country make any essential difference — at least so long as both parties speak the same language, as is the case with Americans and English. Though to be sure, given the small number of English whalers, such meetings do not happen very often. And when they do, there tends to be a sort of shyness between them. For your Englishman is rather reserved, and your Yankee does not appreciate that quality in anyone but himself. Besides, the English whalers sometimes display a kind of big-city superiority over the American whalers, regarding the long, lean Nantucketer with his antiquated equipment as a sort of poor rustic cousin.

So we see that of all ships separately sailing the sea, whalers have the most reason to be sociable — and they are. Whereas some merchant ships, crossing each other's path in the mid-Atlantic, will often pass without so much as a single word of acknowledgment, cutting each other on the high seas like a pair of dandies on Broadway. And all the while silently criticizing each other's rigging. As for warships, when they happen to meet at sea, they first go through such a long string of silly bowing and scraping, such a dipping of flags, that it is almost as ridiculous as two aristocrats meeting on a staircase, each insisting the other go first.

But look at the godly, honest, unpretentious, hospitable, sociable, free-and-easy whaler! What does the whaler do when she meets another whaler in any sort of decent weather? She has a Gam — a thing so utterly unknown to all other ships that they have never even heard the name. And if by chance they should hear of it, they only grin and repeat mocking stuff about "spouters" and "blubber-boilers" and similar pretty expressions. Why all merchant-seamen, and also all pirates and men-of-war sailors and slave-ship sailors, harbor such scornful feelings toward whale-ships is something that requires a separate chapter for its explanation. But for now, let us proceed.

But what is a Gam? You might wear out your index finger running up and down the columns of dictionaries and never find the word. Dr. Johnson never achieved that level of learning. Noah Webster's dictionary does not contain it. Nevertheless, this same expressive word has for many years been in constant use among some fifteen thousand true-born Americans. Certainly, it needs a definition and should be added to the dictionary. With that aim in mind, let me offer a learned definition.

GAM. Noun — A social meeting of two (or more) whale-ships, generally on a cruising-ground; when, after exchanging hails, they exchange visits by boats' crews: the two captains remaining, for the time, on board of one ship, and the two chief mates on the other.

There is another small detail about gamming that must not be forgotten here. All professions have their own little quirks of practice. So does the whale fishery. In a pirate ship, man-of-war, or slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern on a comfortable, sometimes cushioned seat, and often steers himself with a pretty little decorated tiller, hung with gay cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no stern seat, no sofa of any kind, and no tiller at all. Grand times indeed, if whaling captains were wheeled about the ocean in that fashion! In a whale-boat, the captain goes to visit another ship in the same way every other man does — practically sitting on the boat's bottom. And often, the most athletic captain will choose the bow oar for the trip. In his own boat, the visiting captain is given no special seat. He goes and comes an equal among equals — at least in this regard.

chapters.title: Chapter 54 — The Town-Ho’s Story
paragraphs: (As told at the Golden Inn.)
The Cape of Good Hope, and all the watery region around it, is much like some notable crossroads of a great highway, where you meet more travelers than in any other part.

It was not very long after speaking the Goney that another homeward-bound whaler, the Town-Ho, was encountered. She was manned almost entirely by Polynesians. In the short gam that followed, she gave us strong news of Moby Dick. To some, the general interest in the White Whale was now wildly heightened by a detail of the Town-Ho's story that seemed obscurely to involve with the whale a certain wondrous, inverted visitation of one of those so-called acts of divine judgment — a tale whose deeper meaning only a few of the Pequod's crew fully understood. To the rest of the ship's company, the story was simply about a fight between a mate and one of the crew, and that this man still remained on board, replacing the chief mate who had been killed. For all that, the Town-Ho's story was one to be told in darkness, and it is only now that I tell it in full. But let this be said at once: it was Steelkilt, the Town-Ho's crewman, who told the whole tale to Tashtego with a certain amount of secrecy on the forecastle of the Pequod, one dark night on the Japan cruising ground. But the very night Tashtego heard this amazing story, he raved in his sleep, and revealed so much of it that when he was awakened, he could not help himself. The secret was out. Nevertheless, so much of the story was withheld from the Pequod's officers that they knew nothing about Steelkilt's connection with the white whale, nor did they know how the terrible collision with that whale had been preceded by the darker conflict between two men on the Town-Ho. All they knew was the general tale of how the mate had been killed. This is the story Tashtego half-consciously told us. But for my humor's sake, I shall preserve the style in which I once narrated it at Lima, to a lounging circle of my Spanish friends on a saint's eve, smoking on the thick gold-tiled terrace of the Golden Inn.
The ancient whale-cry upon first sighting a whale from the masthead, still used by whalemen in hunting the famous Galapagos tortoise.

For my humor's sake, I shall preserve the style in which I once narrated it at Lima, to a lounging circle of my Spanish friends, one saint's eve, smoking upon the thick gold-tiled terrace of the Golden Inn. Of those fine gentlemen, the young Dons, Pedro and Sebastian, were on the closest terms with me, and hence the occasional questions they put, which are duly answered at the time.

"Some two years prior to my first learning the events which I am about to rehearse to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the northward of the Line. One morning upon handling the pumps, according to daily usage, it was observed that she made more water in her hold than common. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain, having some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and therefore being very averse to quit them, and the leak not being then considered at all dangerous, though, indeed, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather, the ship still continued her cruisings, the mariners working at the pumps at wide and easy intervals. But no good luck came; more days went by, and not only was the leak yet undiscovered, but it sensibly increased. So much so, that now taking some alarm, the captain, making all sail, stood away for the nearest harbor among the islands, there to have his hull hove out and repaired."

"Though a long passage lay ahead of her, yet if ordinary luck held, he did not at all fear that his ship would founder on the way, because his pumps were of the best. Being periodically relieved at them, his thirty-six men could easily keep the ship clear — never mind if the leak should double. In truth, since nearly the whole of this passage was attended by very good weather, the Town-Ho had all but certainly arrived at her destination in perfect safety, had it not been for the brutal overbearing of Radney, the mate, a native of Martha's Vineyard. And for the provoked vengeance of Steelkilt, a Lakeman and desperado from Buffalo."
"'Lakeman! — Buffalo! Pray, what is a Lakeman, and where is Buffalo?' said Don Sebastian, rising in his swinging grass hammock."

"On the eastern shore of our Lake Erie, Don; but — I crave your courtesy — may be, you shall soon hear further of all that. Now, gentlemen, in square-sail brigs and three-masted ships, well-nigh as large and stout as any that ever sailed out of your old Callao to far Manila, this Lakeman, in the land-locked heart of our America, had yet been nurtured by all those agrarian freebooting impressions popularly connected with the open ocean. For in their interflowing aggregate, those grand fresh-water seas of ours — Erie, and Ontario, and Huron, and Superior, and Michigan — possess an ocean-like expansiveness, with many of the ocean's noblest traits, with many of its rimmed varieties of races and of climes. They contain round archipelagoes of romantic isles, even as the Polynesian waters do; in large part, are shored by two great contrasting nations, as the Atlantic is; they furnish long maritime approaches to our numerous territorial colonies from the East, dotted all round their banks; here and there are frowned upon by batteries, and by the goat-like craggy guns of lofty Mackinaw; they have heard the fleet thunderings of naval victories; at intervals, they yield their beaches to wild barbarians, whose red painted faces flash from out their peltry wigwams; for leagues and leagues are flanked by ancient and unentered forests, where the gaunt pines stand like serried lines of kings in Gothic genealogies; those same woods harboring wild Afric beasts of prey, and silken creatures whose exported furs give robes to Tartar Emperors; they mirror the paved capitals of Buffalo and Cleveland, as well as Winnebago villages; they float alike the full-rigged merchant ship, the armed cruiser of the State, the steamer, and the beech canoe; they are swept by Borean and dismasting blasts as direful as any that lash the salted wave; they know what shipwrecks are, for out of sight of land, however inland, they have drowned full many a midnight ship with all its shrieking crew. Thus, gentlemen, though an inlander, Steelkilt was wild-ocean born, and wild-ocean nurtured; as much of an audacious mariner as any. And for Radney, though in his infancy he may have laid him down on the lone Nantucket beach, to nurse at his maternal sea; though in after life he had long followed our austere Atlantic and your contemplative Pacific — yet was he quite as vengeful and full of social quarrel as the backwoods seaman, fresh from the latitudes of buck-horn handled Bowie-knives. Yet was this Nantucketer a man with some good-hearted traits; and this Lakeman, a mariner, who though a sort of devil indeed, might yet by inflexible firmness, only tempered by that common decency of human recognition which is the meanest slave's right; thus treated, this Steelkilt had long been retained harmless and docile. At all events, he had proved so thus far; but Radney was doomed and made mad, and Steelkilt — but, gentlemen, you shall hear."

"It was not more than a day or two at most after setting course for her island harbor that the Town-Ho's leak seemed to be increasing again, but only enough to require an hour or more at the pumps each day. You should know that in a settled and civilized ocean like our Atlantic, for example, some captains think nothing of pumping their whole way across it. Though on a still, sleepy night, should the officer on watch happen to forget his duty in that respect, and the ship's pumping should cease, and the crew wake to the sound of the water washing over the cabin floor — the pumps going all day in such a case is not a thing that alarms anyone."

"Much this way it had been with the Town-Ho. So when her leak was found gaining once more, there was in truth some small concern among several of her company, especially Radney the mate. He ordered the upper sails hoisted and sheeted home anew, and every way spread to catch the breeze. Now this Radney, I suppose, was no more a coward, and no more inclined to any sort of nervous apprehension about the safety of his ship, than any other ordinary careful seaman. But coming from an island — Nantucket — where he had never met a hill bigger than a mole hill, where the horizon was the only boundary he could see, and where to his practical mind a leak in the ship was like a leak in his own body — his vigilance about the Town-Ho's leak was entirely natural. He was not half so afraid of the leak as he was of the reputation of being afraid. Still, the fact remained: Radney was afraid, and that fear drove everything he did next."

"Now, as you well know, it is not rare in this conventional world of ours — watery or otherwise — that when a person placed in command over his fellow-men finds one of them to be significantly his superior in general pride of manhood, right away he conceives an unconquerable dislike and bitterness toward that man. And if he has a chance, he will pull down and pulverize that subordinate's tower, and make a little heap of dust of it. Be that what it may, gentlemen, in Steelkilt, the Lakeman, the mate found his superior in general strength and fearlessness. And when the two were together, the contrast was a painful one for the mate."
"Spotting the mate drawing near as he was toiling at the pump with the rest, the Lakeman pretended not to notice him, and casually went on with his lighthearted joking."

"'Aye, aye, my merry lads, it's a lively leak this! Hold a cup, one of you, and let's have a taste. By the Lord, it's worth bottling! I tell you what, men, old Rad's investment must pay for it! He'd best cut away his part of the hull and tow it home. The fact is, boys, that sword-fish only started the job. He's come back again with a gang of ship-carpenters, saw-fish, and file-fish, and what not. And the whole gang is hard at work cutting and slashing at the bottom — making improvements, I suppose. If old Rad were here now, I'd tell him to jump overboard and scatter them. They're playing the devil with his property, I can tell you. But that's his lookout, not mine. I'm not paid to guard his things. Let him look after his own planks.'"
"'Damn your eyes! What's that pump stopping for?' roared Radney, pretending not to have heard the sailors' talk. 'Thunder away at it!'"

"'Aye, aye, sir,' said Steelkilt, merry as a cricket. 'Lively, boys, lively, now!' And with that the pump clanged like fifty fire-engines. The men tossed their hats off to it, and before long that peculiar gasping of the lungs was heard that marks the fullest strain of life's utmost energies."

"Leaving the pump at last, with the rest of his gang, the Lakeman went forward all panting and sat himself down on the windlass — his face fiery red, his eyes bloodshot, wiping the heavy sweat from his brow. Now what possessing devil it was, gentlemen, that drove Radney to bother such a man in that physically exhausted state, I don't know. But so it happened. Striding intolerably along the deck, the mate commanded him to get a broom and sweep down the decks, and also a shovel, and remove some offensive material left by the cattle on board."

"Now, gentlemen, sweeping a ship's deck at sea is a piece of housework which in all conditions but raging gales is regularly done every evening. It has been known to be done in the case of ships actually sinking at the time. Such, gentlemen, is the rigidity of sea customs and the instinctive love of neatness in seamen — some of whom would not willingly drown without first washing their faces. But in all ships this broom work is assigned to the boys of the crew. Besides, it was not the custom of the Town-Ho for her sailors to clean up after her cattle — that task belonged to the boys. And by boys, I do not mean children but simply the least experienced of the crew."

"But there was more than this: the order about the shovel was almost as plainly meant to sting and insult Steelkilt as though Radney had spat in his face. Any man who has been a sailor on a whale-ship will understand this. And all this, and doubtless much more, the Lakeman fully understood when the mate gave his command. But as he sat still for a moment, and as he steadily looked into the mate's malicious eye, he felt certain that the mate was deliberately provoking him to strike first, so as to have an excuse for beating him. Steelkilt knew well that the mate might lawfully do that. But while thinking all this, he slowly and deliberately swallowed his anger, though it was not easy to do so."

"Therefore, in his ordinary tone, only a little broken by the physical exhaustion he was temporarily in, he answered saying that sweeping the deck was not his business, and he would not do it. And then, without mentioning the shovel at all, he pointed to three lads as the customary sweepers, who, not being assigned to the pumps, had done little or nothing all day. To this, Radney replied with a curse, demanding instant obedience."

"Heated and irritated as he was by his convulsive labor at the pumps, for all his initial nameless impulse to hold back, the sweating Steelkilt could barely stand this behavior from the mate. But somehow still smothering the fire within him, without speaking he remained stubbornly rooted to his seat, until at last the enraged Radney shook the hammer within a few inches of his face, furiously commanding him to obey."

"Steelkilt rose, and slowly retreating around the windlass, steadily followed by the mate with his threatening hammer, deliberately repeated his refusal to obey. Seeing, however, that his restraint had not the slightest effect, by a terrible and unmistakable gesture with his twisted hand he warned off the foolish and obsessed man. But it was no use. And in this way the two went once slowly around the windlass. Then Steelkilt, quickly drawing up a heavy plank from its place, spoke these words:"

"'Mr. Radney, I will not obey you. Take that hammer away, or look to yourself.' But the doomed mate coming still closer to him, where the Lakeman stood fixed, now shook the heavy hammer within an inch of his teeth, meanwhile repeating a string of unbearable curses. Retreating not the thousandth part of an inch, stabbing him in the eye with the unflinching dagger of his glare, Steelkilt, gripping his plank tighter, made a fierce warning beneath his breath — a whisper that sounded as deadly as the click of a cocked pistol. But the mate was already raging beyond reason. The Lakeman's face spoke a command. But the mate would not obey. With one blow of the plank, Steelkilt knocked him flat on the deck, then immediately ran to the rigging."
"Before the cry could reach the stern, Steelkilt was shaking one of the backstays leading far aloft to where two of his comrades were standing their mastheads. They were both Canallers."
"'Canallers!' cried Don Pedro. 'We have seen many whale-ships in our harbors, but never heard of your Canallers. Pardon — who and what are they?'"
"'Canallers, Don, are the boatmen of our great Erie Canal. You must have heard of it.'"
"'No, Senor. Hereabouts in this dull, warm, most lazy, and hereditary land, we know but little of your vigorous North.'"
"'Is that so? Well then, Don, refill my cup. Your chicha is very fine. And before going further I will tell you what our Canallers are, for such information may shed light on my story.'"

"For three hundred and sixty miles, gentlemen, through the entire breadth of the state of New York — through numerous populous cities and thriving villages, through long, dismal, uninhabited swamps and rich cultivated fields unrivaled for fertility — by billiard-room and bar-room, through the sacred heart of great forests, on Roman arches over Indian rivers — through sun and shade, by happy hearts or broken, through all the wide contrasting scenery of those noble Northern states — winds the long Erie Canal. If it were possible for miles, the canal stretches on as straight as a pike. And every mile of it is flanked by side-stretches of the most fertile, most prosperous farm land in the Republic. The vast wealth and beauty of this great canal country gives it an almost European grandeur of appearance."
"'Is that a friar passing?' said Don Pedro, looking down into the crowded plaza with humorous concern."
"'Well for our northern friend that Dame Isabella's Inquisition is waning in Lima,' laughed Don Sebastian. 'Proceed, Senor.'"

"'A moment! Pardon!' cried another of the company. 'In the name of all us Limenos, I merely wish to say to you, sir sailor, that we have by no means overlooked your tact in not substituting present-day Lima for distant Venice in your unflattering comparison. Oh! Do not bow and look surprised — you know the proverb all along this coast: "Corrupt as Lima." It only confirms your point — churches more plentiful than billiard-rooms, and forever open — and "Corrupt as Lima." So too, Venice. I have been there. The holy city of the blessed evangelist, St. Mark! — St. Dominic, purge it! Your cup! Thanks — here I refill. Now, Senor, proceed with your story.'"

"Freely described in his own element, gentlemen, the Canaller would make a fine dramatic hero, so abundantly and colorfully wicked is he. Like Mark Antony, for days upon days along his green-turfed, flowery Nile, he lazily floats, openly enjoying himself, ripening in the sun on the deck. But ashore, all this ease is shed. The piratical look he picked up from the wild sailors he used to associate with in the Atlantic and the lawless freshwater settlements along the canal — all this tells its story. Though now a canal man, there is in him the spirit of something fiercer. He has fought river duels. He has hunted buffalo with the best of them on the plains. He has danced at the Navajos' bonfire. He may have shown himself a tough customer in the riots of the Five Points. And in the hands of the police, has sometimes been carried in a blanket like a baby, when they could get no stretcher. He has told many a straight truth in an odd way that would make a landsman stare. With the face of a desperado and the heart of a lion, he might have been a good many things in this world — if only the world would let him."

"'I see! I see!' exclaimed Don Pedro eagerly, spilling his chicha on his silver ruffles. 'No need to travel! The world's one Lima. I had thought, now, that in your temperate North the generations were cold and holy as the hills. — But the story.'"

"I left off, gentlemen, where the Lakeman shook the backstay. Hardly had he done so when he was surrounded by the three junior mates and the four harpooners, who all crowded him to the deck. But sliding down the ropes like baleful comets, the two Canallers rushed into the uproar and tried to drag their man out of it toward the forecastle. Others of the sailors joined them in this attempt, and a fierce scuffle resulted, in which the officers were eventually victorious. Steelkilt and his desperadoes were locked below. But this did not end the scene. The sailors in the forecastle had a rumor among them that the mate was purposely driving Steelkilt into a fight in order to get a reason to discipline him — all for the purpose of humiliating a man who had made him feel inferior. And when the mates came among them to get volunteers for manning the pumps — for the leak was now growing dangerous — none would volunteer, and the officers had to pump with their own hands. Even this did not shake the crew's stubbornness."
"'Come out of that, you pirates!' roared the captain, now threatening them with a pistol in each hand, just brought to him by the steward. 'Come out of that, you cutthroats!'"

"Steelkilt leaped on the barricade, and striding up and down there, defied the worst the pistols could do. But he gave the captain to understand clearly that his — Steelkilt's — death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny from all hands. Fearing in his heart that this might prove all too true, the captain backed off a little, but still commanded the rebels to return immediately to their duty."
"'Will you promise not to touch us if we do?' demanded their ringleader."
"'Turn to! Turn to! — I make no promise — to your duty! Do you want to sink the ship by knocking off at a time like this? Turn to!' And he once more raised a pistol."

"'Sink the ship?' cried Steelkilt. 'Aye, let her sink. Not a man of us turns to unless you swear not to raise a rope's end against us. What say you, men?' turning to his comrades. A fierce cheer was their response."

"The Lakeman now patrolled the barricade, all the while keeping his eye on the Captain, and throwing out sentences like these: 'It's not our fault. We didn't want it. I told him to take his hammer away. It was a boy's job. He might have known me before this. I told him not to provoke the buffalo. I believe I've broken a finger here against his cursed jaw. Aren't those mincing knives down in the forecastle there, men? Look to those handspikes, my hearties. Captain, by God, look to yourself! Say the word — don't be a fool — forget the flogging — or we're done! Say it! We only asked not to be flogged — that's all. We'll be peaceable — only say the word!'"
"'Turn to! I make no promises. Turn to, I say!'"
