"'Look here, now,' cried the Lakeman, flinging out his arm toward him, 'there are a few of us here — and I am one of them — who have shipped for the cruise, do you see? Now as you well know, sir, we can claim our discharge as soon as the anchor is down. So we don't want a fight. It's not in our interest. We want to be peaceable. We are ready to work, but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to!' roared the Captain."

"Steelkilt glanced around him a moment, and then said: 'I tell you what it is now, Captain — rather than kill you, and be hanged for such a shabby rascal, we won't lift a hand against you unless you attack us. But until you give us the word about not flogging us, we don't do a hand's turn.'"
"'Down into the forecastle, then. Down with you! I'll keep you there till you're sick of it. Down you go.'"

"'Shall we?' cried the ringleader to his men. Most of them were against it. But at length, in obedience to Steelkilt, they preceded him down into their dark den, disappearing with growls, like bears into a cave."

"As the Lakeman's bare head was just level with the planks, the Captain and his men leaped the barricade, and rapidly drawing the cover of the hatch shut, planted their group of hands upon it and loudly called for the steward to bring the heavy brass padlock belonging to the companionway. Then opening the hatch a crack, the Captain whispered something down into the dark, closed it, and turned the key."

"All night a wide-awake watch was kept by all the officers, fore and aft, especially about the forecastle hatch and the forward hatchway, where it was feared the rebels might emerge after breaking through the bulkhead below. But the hours of darkness passed in peace. The men who still remained at their duty toiled hard at the pumps, whose clinking and clanking at intervals pierced the dark night like a troubled conscience."

"At sunrise the Captain went forward, and knocking on the deck, summoned the prisoners to work; but with a yell they refused. Water was then lowered down to them, and a couple of handfuls of biscuit were tossed after it; when again turning the key upon them and pocketing it, the Captain returned to the quarter-deck. Twice every day for three days this was repeated; but on the fourth morning a confused wrangling, and then a scuffling was heard, as the customary summons was delivered; and suddenly four men burst up from the forecastle, saying they were ready to turn to. The fetid closeness of the air, and a famishing diet, united perhaps to some fears of ultimate retribution, had constrained them to surrender at discretion. Emboldened by this, the Captain reiterated his demand to the rest, but Steelkilt shouted up to him a terrific hint to stop his babbling and betake himself where he belonged. On the fifth morning three others of the mutineers bolted up into the air from the desperate arms below that sought to restrain them. Only three were left."
"'Better turn to, now?' said the Captain with a heartless jeer."
"'Shut us up again, will you!' cried Steelkilt."
"'Oh certainly,' said the Captain, and the key clicked."

"It was at this point, gentlemen, that enraged by the defection of seven of his former associates, and stung by the mocking voice that had last hailed him, and maddened by his long entombment in a place as black as the bowels of despair — it was then that Steelkilt proposed to the two Canallers, thus far apparently of one mind with him, to burst out of their hole at the next summoning of the garrison; and armed with their keen mincing knives (long, crescentic, heavy implements with a handle at each end), run amok from the bowsprit to the taffrail; and if by any devilishness of desperation possible, seize the ship. For himself, he would do this, he said, whether they joined him or not. That was the last night he should spend in that den. But the scheme met with no opposition on the part of the other two; they swore they were ready for that, or for any other mad thing — for anything, in short, but a surrender. And what was more, they each insisted upon being the first man on deck, when the time to make the rush should come. But to this their leader as fiercely objected, reserving that priority for himself; particularly as his two comrades would not yield, the one to the other, in the matter; and both of them could not be first, for the ladder would but admit one man at a time. And here, gentlemen, the foul play of these miscreants must come out."

"Upon hearing the frantic plan of their leader, each in his own separate soul had suddenly hit upon the same piece of treachery: namely, to be the first to break out so as to be the first of the three — though the last of the ten — to surrender, and thereby secure whatever small chance of pardon such behavior might earn. But when Steelkilt revealed his determination to stay and fight until the last, something changed in their faces. And while he was explaining the details to them — taking them into his full confidence — they suddenly fell upon him, and tied him hand and foot, gagging him with ropes. Then calling to the captain, they demanded release, saying they would now cooperate."

"Thinking murder was at hand and smelling in the dark for blood, the captain and all his armed mates and harpooners rushed for the forecastle. In a few minutes the hatch was opened, and bound hand and foot, the still-struggling ringleader was shoved up into the air by his treacherous allies, who at once claimed the honor of securing a man who had been fully ripe for murder. But all of them were collared and dragged along the deck like dead cattle. And the Captain, at the head of his officers, stood over the three prisoners, with a mixture of relief and contempt."

"At sunrise he summoned all hands, and separating those who had rebelled from those who had taken no part in the mutiny, he told the former that he had a good mind to flog them all round — thought, upon the whole, he would do so — he ought to — justice demanded it. But for the present, considering their timely surrender, he would let them go with a reprimand, which he then delivered in the most violent terms."

"'But as for you, you carrion rogues,' turning to the three men in the rigging — 'for you, I mean to mince you up for the try-pots.' And seizing a rope, he applied it with all his might to the backs of the two traitors, until they yelled no more, but lifelessly hung their heads sideways, like the two crucified thieves are drawn."

"'My wrist is sprained with you!' he cried at last. 'But there is still rope enough left for you, my fine bantam, who wouldn't give up. Take that gag from his mouth, and let us hear what he can say for himself.'"

"For a moment the exhausted mutineer made a trembling motion of his cramped jaws, and then painfully twisting his head around, said in a sort of hiss, 'What I say is this — and mind it well — if you flog me, I murder you!'"
"'Say you so? Then see how you frighten me' — and the Captain drew back with the rope to strike."
"'Best not,' hissed the Lakeman."
"'But I must' — and the rope was once more drawn back for the stroke."

"Steelkilt here hissed out something inaudible to all but the Captain, who, to the amazement of all hands, started back, paced the deck rapidly two or three times, and then suddenly throwing down his rope, said, 'I won't do it — let him go — cut him down, do you hear?'"

"But as the junior mates were hurrying to carry out the order, a pale man with a bandaged head stopped them — Radney, the chief mate. Ever since the blow, he had lain in his berth. But that morning, hearing the commotion on deck, he had crept out, and thus far had watched the whole scene. His mouth was in such a state that he could hardly speak. But mumbling something about being willing and able to carry out the Captain's sentence himself, he snatched the rope from the Captain's relaxed hands — in that instant, by turns maddened with pain and revenge — and advancing toward the strung-up man, ignoring Steelkilt's warning, he dealt the blow."
"'You are a coward!' hissed the Lakeman."

"'So I am, but take that.' The mate was in the very act of striking when another hiss stayed his raised arm. He paused — and then pausing no more, made good on his word, in spite of Steelkilt's threat, whatever that might have been. The three men were then cut down, all hands were turned to, and sullenly worked by the moody seamen, the iron pumps clanged as before."

"Just after dark that day, when one watch had gone below, a commotion was heard in the forecastle. The two trembling traitors came running up and besieged the cabin door, saying they dared not stay with the crew. Pleas, cuffs, and kicks could not drive them back. So at their own request they were locked down in the ship's hold for safety. Still, no sign of mutiny reappeared among the rest. On the contrary, the seamen carried out all their duties in a quiet, obedient fashion. And Steelkilt obeyed his orders, and so did all the rest of those who had been in the forecastle. As to whether the Captain quietly put away his pistols, I do not know. But I heard later that Steelkilt whispered to them all a strategy of some kind. The crew then showed a strange respect toward the mate, who grew more and more pleasant and even sociable toward them. Even Steelkilt's savage face appeared to be softening, and the Lakeman showed signs of wanting to let bygones be bygones."

"But though the Lakeman had persuaded the seamen to adopt this sort of passivity in their conduct, he kept his own counsel — at least until all was over — concerning his own proper and private revenge upon the man who had stung him in the deepest part of his heart. He was in Radney the chief mate's watch. And as if the doomed man sought to run more than halfway to meet his fate, after the scene at the forecastle he continued to push Steelkilt in small, persistent ways."

"During the night, Radney had an unseamanlike habit of sitting on the bulwarks of the quarterdeck and leaning his arm upon the gunwale of the boat that was hoisted up there, a little above the ship's side. In this position, it was well known, he sometimes dozed. There was a considerable gap between the boat and the ship, and down between them was the sea. Steelkilt calculated his time, and found that his next watch below would come at two in the morning of the third night after the flogging. He went to his hammock and looked for something. It was a piece of cord and a ball of iron — the makings of a slungshot."
"'What are you making there?' said a shipmate."
"'What do you think? What does it look like?'"
"'Like a lanyard for your bag. But it's an odd one, seems to me.'"
"'Yes, rather odd,' said the Lakeman, holding it at arm's length before him. 'But I think it will do. Shipmate, I haven't enough twine — have you any?'"
"But there was none in the forecastle."
"'Then I must get some from old Rad.' And he rose to go aft."
"'You don't mean to go begging to him!' said a sailor."

"'Why not? Do you think he won't do me a turn, when it's to help himself in the end, shipmate?' And going to the mate, he looked at him quietly and asked him for some twine to mend his hammock. It was given him — neither twine nor slungshot were seen again. But the next night an iron ball, closely netted, partly rolled from the pocket of the Lakeman's jacket as he was tucking the coat into his hammock for a pillow. Twenty-four hours later, Steelkilt and his mates would have been at work. But at this point, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned."

"But, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned. Yet complete revenge he had, and without being the avenger. For by a mysterious fate, Heaven itself seemed to step in to take out of his hands into its own the damning thing he would have done."

"It was just between daybreak and sunrise on the morning of the second day, when they were washing down the decks, that a stupid Tenerife man, drawing water in the main-chains, all at once shouted out, 'There she rolls! There she rolls!' Jesus, what a whale! It was Moby Dick."
"'Moby Dick!' cried Don Sebastian. 'St. Dominic! Sir sailor, but do whales have christenings? Whom do you call Moby Dick?'"
"'A very white, and famous, and most deadly immortal monster, Don — but that would be too long a story.'"
"'How? How?' cried all the young Spaniards, crowding around."
"'No, Dons, Dons — no, no! I cannot tell that now. Let me get more into the air, Sirs.'"
"'The chicha! The chicha!' cried Don Pedro. 'Our vigorous friend looks faint — fill up his empty glass!'"

"No need, gentlemen; one moment, and I proceed. — Now, gentlemen, so suddenly perceiving the snowy whale within fifty yards of the ship — forgetful of the compact among the crew — in the excitement of the moment, the Teneriffe man had instinctively and involuntarily lifted his voice for the monster, though for some little time past it had been plainly beheld from the three sullen mast-heads. All was now a frenzy. 'The White Whale — the White Whale!' was the cry from captain, mates, and harpooneers, who, undeterred by fearful rumors, were all anxious to capture so famous and precious a fish; while the dogged crew eyed askance, and with curses, the appalling beauty of the vast milky mass, that, lit up by a horizontal spangling sun, shifted and glistened like a living opal in the blue morning sea. Gentlemen, a strange fatality pervades the whole career of these events, as if verily mapped out before the world itself was charted. The mutineer was the bowsman of the mate, and when fast to a fish, it was his duty to sit next him, while Radney stood up with his lance in the prow, and haul in or slacken the line, at the word of command. Moreover, when the four boats were lowered, the mate's got the start; and none howled more fiercely with delight than did Steelkilt, as he strained at his oar. After a stiff pull, their harpooneer got fast, and, spear in hand, Radney sprang to the bow. He was always a furious man, it seems, in a boat. And now his bandaged cry was, to beach him on the whale's topmost back. Nothing loath, his bowsman hauled him up and up, through a blinding foam that blent two whitenesses together, till of a sudden the boat struck as against a sunken ledge, and, keeling over, spilled out the standing mate. That instant, as he fell on the whale's slippery back, the boat righted, and was dashed aside by the swell, while Radney was tossed over into the sea, on the other flank of the whale. He struck out through the spray, and, for an instant, was dimly seen through that veil, wildly seeking to remove himself from the eye of Moby Dick. But the whale rushed round in a sudden maelstrom, seized the swimmer between his jaws, and rearing high up with him, plunged headlong again, and went down."

"Meanwhile, at the first bump of the boat's bottom, the Lakeman had slackened the line so as to drop back from the whirlpool. Calmly looking on, he thought his own thoughts. But a sudden, terrific, downward jerk of the boat quickly brought his knife to the line. He cut it, and the whale was free. But at some distance, Moby Dick rose again, with some tatters of Radney's red woolen shirt caught in the teeth that had destroyed him. The four remaining boats came up to the rescue, but the whale fled, and the sailor was gone."

"In good time, the Town-Ho reached her port — a savage, solitary place where no civilized creature lived. There, led by the Lakeman, all but five or six of the forecastle men deliberately deserted among the palms. Eventually, as it turned out, they seized a large double war-canoe of the natives and set sail for some other harbor."

"The ship's company being reduced to but a handful, the captain called upon the Islanders to assist him in the laborious business of heaving down the ship to stop the leak. But to such unresting vigilance over their dangerous allies was this small band of whites necessitated, both by night and by day, and so extreme was the hard work they underwent, that upon the vessel being ready again for sea, they were in such a weakened condition that the captain durst not put off with them in so heavy a vessel. After taking counsel with his officers, he anchored the ship as far off shore as possible, loaded and ran out his two cannon from the bows, stacked his muskets on the poop, and warning the Islanders not to approach the ship at their peril, took one man with him, and setting the sail of his best whale-boat, steered straight before the wind for Tahiti, five hundred miles distant, to procure a reinforcement to his crew."

"On the fourth day of the sail, a large canoe was spotted, which seemed to have stopped at a low coral island. He steered away from it. But the savage craft bore down on him, and soon the voice of Steelkilt hailed him to heave to, or he would run him under water. The captain presented a pistol. With one foot on each prow of the yoked war-canoes, the Lakeman laughed him to scorn, assuring him that if the pistol was fired, he would immediately be sunk — the canoe being much faster than the whale-boat. He repeated his demand."
"'What do you want of me?' cried the captain."
"'Where are you bound? And for what are you bound?' demanded Steelkilt. 'No lies.'"
"'I am bound to Tahiti for more men.'"
"'Very good. Let me board you a moment — I come in peace.' With that he leaped from the canoe, swam to the boat, and climbing the gunwale, stood face to face with the captain."

"'Cross your arms, sir. Throw back your head. Now, repeat after me. As soon as Steelkilt leaves me, I swear to beach this boat on that island and remain there six days. If I do not, may lightning strike me!'"
"'A pretty scholar,' laughed the Lakeman. 'Adios, Senor!' And leaping into the sea, he swam back to his comrades."

"Watching the boat until it was fairly beached and drawn up to the roots of the coconut trees, Steelkilt set sail again, and in due time arrived at Tahiti, his own destination. There luck befriended him. Two ships were about to sail for France and were providentially in need of precisely that number of men which the sailor led. They embarked, and so forever got the start of their former captain, had he been at all disposed to pursue them."

"Some ten days after the French ships sailed, the whale-boat arrived, and the captain was forced to enlist some of the more civilized Tahitians, who had been somewhat used to the sea. Chartering a small native schooner, he returned with them to his vessel, and finding all well there, again resumed his cruising."

"Where Steelkilt now is, gentlemen, no one knows. But upon the island of Nantucket, the widow of Radney still turns to the sea which refuses to give up its dead — still in dreams sees the awful white whale that destroyed him."
"'Are you through?' said Don Sebastian quietly."
"'I am, Don.'"

"'Then I beg you, tell me if to the best of your own convictions, this story of yours is in substance really true? It is so passing wonderful! Did you get it from an unquestionable source? Bear with me if I seem to press.'"
"'Also bear with all of us, sir sailor, for we all join in Don Sebastian's request,' cried the company, with great interest."
"'Is there a copy of the Holy Gospels in the Golden Inn, gentlemen?'"
"'No,' said Don Sebastian, 'but I know a worthy priest nearby who will quickly get one for me. I go for it — but are you sure about this? This may grow too serious.'"
"'Will you be so good as to bring the priest also, Don?'"

"'Though there are no burnings at the stake in Lima now,' said one of the company to another, 'I fear our sailor friend risks the attention of the archbishop. Let us move further out of the moonlight. I see no need for this.'"
"'Excuse me for running after you, Don Sebastian — but may I also ask that you will be particular in getting the largest-sized Gospels you can.'"
"'This is the priest. He brings you the Gospels,' said Don Sebastian, gravely, returning with a tall and solemn figure."
"'Let me remove my hat. Now, venerable priest, further into the light, and hold the Holy Book before me that I may touch it."

"'So help me Heaven, and on my honor the story I have told you, gentlemen, is in substance and its great items, true. I know it to be true. It happened on this earth. I walked that ship. I knew the crew. I have seen and talked with Steelkilt since the death of Radney.'"

chapters.title: Chapter 55 — Of the Monstrous Pictures of Whales
paragraphs: Before long I shall paint for you, as well as one can without canvas, something like the true form of the whale as he actually appears to the eye of the whaleman when the whale is moored alongside the whale-ship and can fairly be stepped upon. It may be worthwhile, therefore, to first consider those curious imaginary portraits of him which even down to the present day confidently challenge the belief of the landsman. It is time to set the world right on this point. And I have no doubt the world will agree to be set right.

It may be that the original source of all those visual distortions can be found among the oldest Hindu, Egyptian, and Greek sculptures. Ever since those inventive but unscrupulous times when on the marble panels of temples, the bases of statues, and on shields, medallions, cups, and coins, the dolphin was drawn in chain-armor scales like Saladin's, and with a helmeted head like St. George's — ever since then, the same sort of license has prevailed, not only in most popular pictures of the whale, but in many supposedly scientific ones as well.

Now, by far the most ancient existing portrait purporting to be of the whale is found in the famous cave-temple of Elephanta, in India. The Brahmins maintain that in the almost endless sculptures of that ancient temple, all the trades and occupations, every conceivable pursuit of man, were depicted ages before any of them actually came into being. No wonder, then, that our noble profession of whaling should have been foreshadowed there. The Hindu whale referred to occurs in a separate sculpture panel, showing the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of the Leviathan, a creature called Matse. But though this sculpture is half man and half whale, it still does not satisfy expectations. The Hindu whale has no resemblance to the real thing.

But go to the old galleries and look at a great Christian painter's portrait of this fish, for he succeeds no better than the ancient Hindu. It is Guido's picture of Perseus rescuing Andromeda from the sea-monster or whale. Where did Guido get the model for such a strange creature? Nor does Hogarth, in painting the same scene in his own "Perseus Descending," do any better. The huge fat body of that Hogarthian monster undulates on the surface, scarcely drawing one inch of water. It has a head like a dog, and is spouting water upward from his forehead like a fountain in the park. Truly, these things are no more than signs and symbols — not real portraits of the whale.

In the illustrations and other decorations of some ancient books, you will at times encounter very curious depictions of the whale, where all manner of spouts, jets, hot springs and cold, come bubbling up from his inexhaustible brain. In the title-page of the original edition of the Advancement of Learning, you will find some curious whales.

But leaving all these amateur attempts, let us look at those pictures of whales that claim to be sober, scientific drawings, by those who know. In old Harris's collection of voyages there are some plates of whales taken from a Dutch book of voyages, published in 1671, entitled "A Whaling Voyage to Spitsbergen in the ship Jonas in the Whale, Peter Peterson of Friesland, master." In one of those plates the whales, like great rafts of logs, are shown lying among icebergs, with white bears running over their backs. In another plate, the prodigious blunder is made of giving the whale eyes the size of a man's head — and even those are set in the wrong part of the head.

Then again, there is an imposing volume written by one Captain Colnett, a Post Captain in the English navy, entitled "A Voyage round Cape Horn into the South Seas, for the purpose of extending the Spermaceti Whale Fisheries." In this book is an outline claiming to be a "Picture of a Spermaceti whale, drawn by scale from one killed on the coast of Mexico, August, 1793, and hoisted on deck." I have no doubt the captain had this faithful picture made for the benefit of his marines. To anyone who studies it, the whale in question looks much like an overgrown Guinea pig. Of course, he is a great deal worse than that.

Nor are the most careful compilations of Natural History for the education of the young and innocent free from the same kind of blunder. Look at that popular work Goldsmith's Animated Nature. In the abridged London edition of 1807, there are plates of an alleged "whale" and a "narwhal." I do not wish to seem rude, but this unsightly whale looks much like an amputated sow. And as for the narwhal, one glance is enough to astonish anyone that in this nineteenth century such a thing could be presented to students as truth.

Then again, in 1825, Bernard Germain, Count de Lacepede, a great naturalist, published a scientific whale book with several pictures of the different species of whale. All of these are not only incorrect, but the picture of the Right Whale — even Scoresby, a long-experienced man in that species — declares has no counterpart in nature.

But the crowning achievement of all this blundering was reserved for the scientific Frederick Cuvier, brother of the famous Baron. In 1836 he published a Natural History of Whales, in which he gives what he calls a picture of the Sperm Whale. Before showing that picture to any Nantucketer, you had better plan your quick escape from Nantucket. In a word, Frederick Cuvier's Sperm Whale is not a Sperm Whale, but a squash. Of course, he never had the benefit of a whaling voyage — which is how most of these one-sided scientific portraits of the whale are produced.

As for the sign-painters' whales seen in the streets, hanging over the shops of oil-dealers — what shall be said of them? They are generally monstrous whales with camel humps and very savage expressions, breakfasting on three or four boatloads of sailors. Their deformities flounder in seas of blood and blue paint.

But these many mistakes in depicting the whale are not so very surprising after all. Consider: most of the scientific drawings have been made from stranded fish. And these are about as accurate as a drawing of a wrecked ship, with its back broken, would be in correctly representing the noble vessel in all its full pride of hull and mast. Though elephants have stood for their full-length portraits, the living whale has never yet properly posed for his. The living whale, in his full majesty and significance, is only to be seen at sea in unfathomable waters. And in the great majority of cases, the hunter's first sight of the whale is from a considerable distance.

But it may be imagined that from the naked skeleton of a stranded whale, accurate hints might be gathered about his true form. Not at all. For it is one of the more curious things about this creature that his skeleton gives very little idea of his general shape. Though Jeremy Bentham's skeleton, which hangs as a chandelier in the library of one of his executors, correctly conveys the idea of a burly-browed practical old gentleman — yet the whale's skeleton could tell you nothing of that gentle curve of his back, or that blending of his body into his flukes.

For all these reasons, then, however you look at it, you must conclude that the great whale is that one creature in the world which must remain unpainted to the last. True, one portrait may come much nearer the mark than another, but none can hit it with any considerable degree of accuracy. So there is no earthly way of finding out precisely what the whale really looks like. And the only way you can get even a tolerable idea of his living shape is by going whaling yourself. But by doing so, you run no small risk of being forever stove in and sinking to the bottom. So it may go with you.

chapters.title: Chapter 56 — Of the Less Erroneous Pictures of Whales, and the True
paragraphs: Pictures of Whaling Scenes.

In connection with the monstrous pictures of whales, I am strongly tempted here to take up those still more monstrous stories about them which are found in certain books, both ancient and modern, especially in Pliny, Purchas, Hakluyt, Harris, Cuvier, and so forth. But I will let that matter pass.

I know of only four published outlines of the great Sperm Whale: Colnett's, Huggins's, Frederick Cuvier's, and Beale's. In the previous chapter Colnett and Cuvier were mentioned. Huggins's is far better than theirs, but by great odds, Beale's is the best. All of Beale's drawings of this whale are good, except the middle figure in his picture of three whales in various positions. His frontispiece, showing boats attacking Sperm Whales, though no doubt designed to be exciting, is rather bad. But his supplementary picture of a Sperm Whale, when compared to any other published version, gives something approaching a faithful likeness.

Of the Right Whale, the best outline pictures are in Scoresby. But they are drawn on too small a scale to make much impression. He has only one picture of whaling scenes, and this is a real deficiency, because it is only through such pictures, when done well, that you can get anything like a truthful idea of the living whale as seen by his living hunters.

But taken all together, by far the finest — though in some details not the most accurate — depictions of whales and whaling scenes to be found anywhere are two large French engravings, well executed, and based on paintings by one Garnery. They represent attacks on the Sperm and Right Whale respectively. In the first engraving a noble Sperm Whale is shown in the full majesty of his power, just risen beneath a boat from the ocean depths, bearing high in the air upon his back the shattered fragments of the boat and the bodies of the crew. On the other side, the harpooner is seen with his weapon aimed, ready for a dart at the beast's throat.

In the second engraving, the boat is in the act of drawing alongside the barnacle-crusted flank of a large running Right Whale, which rolls his black weedy bulk in the sea like some mossy rock-slide from the Patagonian cliffs. His jets are upright, full, and black like soot, so that from such abundant smoke in the chimney, you would think there must be a fine supper cooking in the great bowels below. Sea birds are pecking at the small crabs, shellfish, and other sea delicacies which the Right Whale sometimes carries on his pestilent back. And all the while the thick-lipped leviathan is rushing through the deep, leaving tons of tumbling white curds in his wake.

Who this painter Garnery is, or was, I do not know. But I would stake my life that he was either practically familiar with his subject or else marvelously tutored by some experienced whaleman. The French are the ones for painting action. Go and look at all the paintings of Europe, and where will you find such a gallery of living and breathing commotion on canvas as in that triumphal hall at Versailles, where the viewer fights his way through the consecutive great battles of France? Every major historical engagement is there, with one painting after another.

The natural talent of the French for capturing the picturesque seems particularly evident in their paintings and engravings of whaling scenes. With not one tenth of England's experience in the fishery, and not the thousandth part of America's, they have nevertheless furnished both nations with the only finished sketches capable of conveying the real spirit of the whale hunt. For the most part, the English and American whale artists seem content with presenting the mechanical outline of things — the unvarnished facts. But it is the French who capture the drama.

In addition to those fine engravings by Garnery, there are two other French engravings worthy of note, by someone who signs himself "H. Durand." One of them, though not precisely suited to our present purpose, nevertheless deserves mention on other grounds. It is a quiet noontime scene among the islands of the Pacific: a French whaler anchored inshore in a calm, lazily taking on water. The loosened sails of the ship and the long leaves of the palms in the background both droop together in the breathless air. This painting captures something of the peculiar tranquility of the Pacific.

chapters.title: Chapter 57 — Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in
paragraphs: Stone; in Mountains; in Stars.

On Tower Hill, as you go down to the London docks, you may have seen a crippled beggar holding up a painted board before him, depicting the tragic scene in which he lost his leg. There are three whales and three boats. And one of the boats — presumably the one containing the leg in all its original wholeness — is being crunched by the jaws of the front whale. For these ten years, they tell me, that man has held up that picture and displayed that stump to an incredulous world.

Throughout the Pacific, and also in Nantucket, and New Bedford, and Sag Harbor, you will come across lively sketches of whales and whaling-scenes, carved by the fishermen themselves on Sperm Whale teeth, or ladies' corset-stays carved out of Right Whale bone, and other like scrimshaw articles, as the whalemen call the numerous little ingenious objects they elaborately carve out of the raw material during their hours of ocean leisure. Some of them carry little boxes of dental-looking tools. The work they produce is remarkable.

Long exile from civilization inevitably restores a man to that condition in which God placed him — that is, what is called savagery. Your true whale-hunter is as much a savage as an Iroquois. I myself am a savage, owing allegiance to no one but the King of the Cannibals — and ready at any moment to rebel against him.

Now, one of the peculiar characteristics of the savage in his domestic hours is his wonderful patience and industry. An ancient Hawaiian war-club or spear-paddle, in its full complexity and elaboration of carving, is as great a testament to human perseverance as a Latin dictionary. For with nothing but a bit of broken sea-shell or a shark's tooth, that miraculous intricacy of wooden net-work has been achieved. And it has cost steady years of steady work.

As with the Hawaiian savage, so with the white sailor-savage. With the same marvelous patience, and with the same single shark's tooth of his one poor jackknife, he will carve you a bit of bone sculpture — not quite as expertly made, but as densely packed in its maze-like design as the Greek savage Achilles's shield, and full of wild spirit and suggestion, as the prints of that fine old Dutch savage, Albrecht Durer.

Wooden whales, or whales cut in profile out of the small dark slabs of the noble South Sea war-wood, are frequently found in the forecastles of American whalers. Some of them are carved with considerable accuracy.

At some old gable-roofed country houses you will see brass whales hung by the tail as door knockers. When the porter is sleepy, the anvil-headed whale would work best. But these knocking whales are seldom noteworthy as faithful likenesses. On the steeples of some old-fashioned churches you will see sheet-iron whales placed there as weather-vanes. But they are so high up, and besides are practically labeled "Hands off!" so you cannot examine them closely enough to form any real opinion.

In bony, rocky regions of the earth, where at the base of high broken cliffs masses of rock lie strewn in fantastic groupings upon the plain, you will often discover shapes like the petrified forms of whales partly merged in grass, which on a windy day breaks against them in a surf of green waves.

Then again, in mountainous countries where the traveler is continually surrounded by amphitheater-like heights, here and there from some lucky vantage point you will catch passing glimpses of whale-shaped profiles defined along the undulating ridges. But you must be a thorough whaleman to see these sights. And not only that — if you wish to return to such a sight, you must be sure to take the exact latitude and longitude of your first viewpoint, or the chance-like nature of these formations may mean you never find the same one again.

Nor, when your imagination is expanded and lifted by your subject, can you fail to trace out great whales in the starry heavens, and boats in pursuit of them — as when, long filled with thoughts of war, the Eastern nations saw armies locked in battle among the clouds. Thus at the North I have chased Leviathan round and round the Pole with the revolutions of the bright stars that first outlined him for me. And beneath the brilliant Antarctic skies I have boarded the constellation Argo-Navis and joined the chase against the starry Cetus far beyond.

With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bits and bundles of harpoons for spurs, I wish I could mount that whale and leap the topmost skies, to see whether the fabled heavens with all their countless tents really lie encamped beyond my mortal sight!

chapters.title: Chapter 58 — Brit
paragraphs: Steering northeast from the Crozets, we fell in with vast meadows of brit, the minute, yellow substance upon which the Right Whale largely feeds. For league upon league it undulated around us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe, golden wheat.

On the second day, numbers of Right Whales were seen, who — safe from the attack of a Sperm Whaler like the Pequod — with open jaws sluggishly swam through the brit. It clung to the fringing fibers of that wondrous Venetian blind in their mouths, and was in this way separated from the water that escaped at the lip.

As morning mowers, who side by side slowly and steadily advance their scythes through the long wet grass of marshy meadows — even so these monsters swam, making a strange, grassy, cutting sound and leaving behind them endless swaths of blue upon the yellow sea.

That part of the sea known among whalemen as the "Brazil Banks" does not bear that name because of shallows and soundings there, as the Banks of Newfoundland do, but because of this remarkable meadow-like appearance, caused by the vast drifts of brit continually floating in those latitudes, where the Right Whale is often hunted.

But it was only the sound they made as they parted the brit that reminded one of mowers at all. Seen from the mastheads, especially when they paused and were still for a while, their vast black forms looked more like lifeless masses of rock than anything else. And as in the great hunting countries of India, the stranger at a distance will sometimes pass elephants lying on the plains without recognizing them, mistaking them for bare, blackened humps of earth — so, often, with whales.

Indeed, in other respects, you can hardly regard any creatures of the deep with the same feelings as those of the shore. For though some old naturalists have maintained that all creatures of the land have their counterparts in the sea — and though, taking a broad general view, this may be true — yet when it comes to specifics, where, for example, does the ocean offer any fish that in temperament matches the loyal kindness of the dog? The cursed shark alone can in any way be compared to him. But as for the gentle whale — what has he in common with anything ashore?

But though, to landsmen in general, the native inhabitants of the seas have always been regarded with feelings unspeakably hostile and repelling — though we know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so that Columbus sailed over numberless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one — though by vast odds the most terrible of all mortal disasters have from time immemorial fallen indiscriminately upon tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone upon the waters — though the sea has been the sworn enemy of man since man was man — yet man has always gone to sea and always will.

The first boat we read of floated on an ocean that with Portuguese vengeance had drowned a whole world without leaving so much as a widow. That same ocean rolls now. That same ocean destroyed the wrecked ships of last year. Yes, foolish mortals — Noah's flood has not yet subsided. Two thirds of the fair world it still covers.

How do the sea and the land differ, that a miracle upon one is not a miracle upon the other? Supernatural terrors seized the Hebrews when under the feet of Korah and his company the living ground opened and swallowed them up forever. Yet not a modern sun ever sets but in precisely the same manner the living sea swallows up ships and crews.

But not only is the sea such a foe to man, who is alien to it — it is also a fiend to its own offspring. Worse than the Persian host who murdered his own guests, it does not spare the creatures it has itself produced. Like a savage tigress that, tossing in the jungle, crushes her own cubs, so the sea dashes even the mightiest whales against the rocks, and leaves them there side by side with the split wrecks of ships. No mercy, no power but its own controls it. Panting and snorting like a mad battle horse that has lost its rider, the masterless ocean overruns the globe.

Consider the subtlety of the sea — how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, invisible for the most part, treacherously hidden beneath the loveliest shades of blue. Consider also the devilish brilliance and beauty of many of its most merciless species, like the elegantly shaped bodies of many kinds of sharks. Consider, once more, the universal cannibalism of the sea: all whose creatures prey upon each other, waging eternal war since the world began.

Consider all this, and then turn to this green, gentle, and most docile earth. Consider them both — the sea and the land — and do you not find a strange parallel to something in yourself? For as this appalling ocean surrounds the green land, so in the soul of man there lies one island Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but surrounded by all the horrors of the half-known life. God keep you! Push not off from that island — you can never return!

chapters.title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — a calm, yet not a stagnant one — when the long burnished sun-glare on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the harpooner shouted, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

Upon this, the seamen rushed to the yardarms, as in swarming-time the bees rush to the branches. Bareheaded in the sultry sun, Ahab stood on the bowsprit, and with one hand pushed far behind him in readiness to wave orders to the helmsman, he cast his eager glance in the direction indicated aloft by the outstretched, motionless arm of Daggoo.

Whether the constant attendance of that one still and solitary jet had gradually worked upon Ahab, so that he was now prepared to connect the ideas of gentleness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he hunted — however this was, or whether his eagerness misled him — whichever way it might have been, no sooner did he clearly perceive the white mass than with fierce intensity he instantly gave orders for lowering.

The four boats were soon on the water, Ahab's in advance, all swiftly pulling toward their prey. Soon it went down. And while, with oars suspended, we were awaiting its reappearance — there, in the same spot where it sank, once more it slowly rose. Almost forgetting for the moment all thoughts of Moby Dick, we now gazed at the most wondrous phenomenon which the secret seas have ever revealed to humankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs in length and breadth, of a gleaming cream-color, lay floating on the water, with innumerable long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as if blindly to clutch at any unlucky object within reach. No perceptible face or front had it. No imaginable mouth. But it looked like a formless, chance-like thing of unearthly life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I almost would rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him, than to have seen you, white ghost!"
"What was it, sir?" said Flask.
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions the sperm whalemen in general have connected with the sight of this creature, it is certain that a glimpse of it being so very unusual, that fact has gone far to invest it with ominous significance. So rarely is it seen that, though every whaleman declares it to be the largest living thing in the ocean, very few of them have any but the vaguest ideas about its true nature and form. Nevertheless, they believe it furnishes the sperm whale with his only food. For though other kinds of whales feed on a diet of small organisms, the sperm whale is known to prey on nothing smaller than the squid.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppidan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classified among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward ways it would seem to belong — but only as the giant among its tribe.

chapters.title: Chapter 60 — The Line
paragraphs: With reference to the whaling scene soon to be described, as well as for the better understanding of all similar scenes presented elsewhere, I must speak here of the magical, sometimes horrible whale-line.

The line originally used in the fishery was of the best hemp, slightly coated with tar — not soaked in it, as with ordinary ropes. For while tar, as ordinarily used, makes hemp more pliable for the ropemaker and also makes the rope itself more convenient for common ship use, not only would the usual amount stiffen the whale-line too much for the close coiling it must undergo, but tar in general tends to rot rather than preserve the line. Thus the original line was merely touched with tar.

In recent years, Manila rope has in the American fishery almost entirely replaced hemp as a material for whale-lines. Though not as durable as hemp, it is stronger and far more soft and elastic. And I will add — since there is an aesthetics in all things — it is much more handsome and attractive in the boat than hemp. Hemp is a dusky, dark fellow, a sort of Indian. But Manila is like a golden-haired beauty to look at.

The whale-line is only two-thirds of an inch thick. At first sight you would not think it so strong as it really is. By experiment, each of its fifty-one yarns will suspend a weight of one hundred and twenty pounds, so that the whole rope will bear a strain of nearly three tons. In length, the common sperm whale-line measures something over two hundred fathoms. Toward the stern of the boat it is spirally coiled away in the tub — not like the pipe of a still, but in such a way that any free end can be pulled out without disturbing the rest of the coil. This way, the line is kept ready for instant use.

In English boats, two tubs are used instead of one, with the same line continuously coiled in both tubs. There is some advantage in this, because the twin tubs, being smaller, fit more easily into the boat and put less strain on it. Whereas the American tub, nearly three feet in diameter and of proportionate depth, makes rather bulky freight for a craft whose planks are but half an inch thick. For the bottom of the whale-boat is like thin ice — it will hold up a decent enough weight, but you don't want to be standing on it too long.

Both ends of the line are exposed. The lower end terminates in a loop coming up from the bottom against the side of the tub and hanging over its edge, completely free. This arrangement of the lower end is necessary for two reasons. First: to allow an additional line from a neighboring boat to be attached to it, in case the struck whale should dive so deep as to threaten to carry off the entire original line. In these instances, the line of a neighboring boat is fastened to the end of the line already attached to the whale. Second: this arrangement is necessary because of a universal law of the whale fishery — that no line can be used in active service until it has been rearranged and re-coiled from one tub into another.

Before lowering the boat for the chase, the upper end of the line is taken aft from the tub and passed around the loggerhead, then carried forward the entire length of the boat, resting crosswise upon the handle of every man's oar so that it jogs against his wrist in rowing. It also passes between the men as they alternately sit at opposite gunwales, to the grooved fittings in the extreme pointed prow of the boat, where a wooden pin the size of a common quill directs it outward. From there it hangs in a short arc over the bow, and is free to fly off at the darting of the harpoon.

Thus the whale-line wraps the whole boat in its complicated coils, twisting and writhing around it in almost every direction. All the oarsmen are caught up in its dangerous tangles, so that to the timid eye of the landsman, they look like Indian jugglers with the deadliest snakes playfully draped around their limbs. Nor can any mortal man, sitting amid those hempen intricacies for the first time, and straining his utmost at the oar, easily forget that at any unknown instant the harpoon may be thrown, and all these horrible coils will go spinning through him and snatch him into the deep.

Perhaps a very little thought will now help you understand those repeated whaling disasters — some few of which are casually recorded — of this man or that man being pulled out of the boat by the line and lost. For when the line is running out, to be seated in the boat is like being seated in the midst of the whizzing parts of a steam-engine running at full power, when every flying beam and shaft and wheel is grazing you. It is worse, for you cannot sit still in the heart of these dangers, because the boat itself is always rocking. Only by the most careful attention to the direction of the spinning line, and by occasionally jerking the oar, can you hope to escape instant destruction.

Again: as the deep calm that only apparently precedes and foretells the storm is perhaps more dreadful than the storm itself — for the calm is merely the storm's wrapper and envelope, containing it within itself, as the seemingly harmless rifle holds the fatal powder, the ball, and the explosion — so the graceful stillness of the line, as it silently coils around the oarsmen before being brought into actual play, carries more true terror than any other aspect of this dangerous business. But why say more? All men live surrounded by invisible whale-lines. All are born with halters round their necks. And a swift, sudden turn of death may come upon any of us at any moment. Only the difference is this: the whale-line makes the danger visible.

chapters.title: Chapter 61 — Stubb Kills a Whale
paragraphs: If to Starbuck the apparition of the Squid was a thing of omens, to Queequeg it was quite a different matter.
"When you see squid," said the harpooner, sharpening his harpoon in the bow of his hoisted boat, "then you quick see sperm whale."

The next day was exceedingly still and sultry, and with nothing special to occupy them, the Pequod's crew could hardly resist the drowsiness brought on by such an empty sea. For this part of the Indian Ocean through which we were then voyaging is not what whalemen call a lively ground — meaning it offers fewer sights of porpoises, dolphins, flying fish, and other lively creatures that keep you awake in more active waters.

It was my turn to stand at the foremast-head. With my shoulders leaning against the slackened rigging, I swayed idly back and forth in what seemed enchanted air. No willpower could resist it. In that dreamy mood, losing all awareness, at last my soul went out of my body, though my body still continued to sway like a pendulum long after the power that first set it in motion has been withdrawn.

Before sleep entirely took me, I had noticed that the seamen at the main and mizzen mastheads were already drowsy. So at last all three of us hung lifelessly from the spars, and for every swing we made there was a nod from below from the slumbering helmsman. The waves, too, nodded their lazy crests. And across the wide trance of the sea, the vast trade-wind kept on blowing — but so drowsily that it seemed to breathe through a dream.

Suddenly bubbles seemed to burst beneath my closed eyes. My hands gripped the rigging like vises. Some invisible, gracious force preserved me — with a shock I came back to life. And there, close under our lee, not forty fathoms off, a gigantic Sperm Whale lay rolling in the water like the capsized hull of a frigate, his broad, glossy back of an Ethiopian sheen glistening in the sun's rays like a mirror. Lazily drifting in the gentle swell, the whale's vast mild head lay dripping with the sparkling spray. At intervals, his jets would rise into the still air. The few gentle clouds aloft seemed like lazy cotton bales tossed up for the breeze to carry.
"Clear away the boats! Luff!" cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he slammed the helm down before the helmsman could reach the spokes.

The sudden shouts of the crew must have alarmed the whale. Before the boats were down, he majestically turned and swam away to leeward, but with such steady tranquility, making so few ripples as he swam, that thinking he might not yet be alarmed after all, Ahab gave orders that not an oar should be used and no man must speak above a whisper. So, seated like Ontario Indians on the gunwales of the boats, we silently sailed along, using only paddles. At times the whale turned to look at us with one slow, suspicious glance, then went on swimming.

"There go flukes!" was the cry, an announcement immediately followed by Stubb producing his match and lighting his pipe, for now a break was granted. After the full interval of the whale's deep dive had passed, the whale rose again. Being now ahead of Stubb's boat and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted on the honor of the kill. It was obvious that the whale had at last become aware of his pursuers.
Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. Now fully alive to his danger, he was going "head out" — that part projecting angled up from the mad churning foam he was brewing.

It will be seen elsewhere what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale's enormous head consists of. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part of him. So he raises it in the air with ease, and always does so when going at full speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of his head, and such the tapering cutwater formation of the lower part, that by cutting through the water at great speed, his head is completely protected from the impact of the waves.

"Start her, start her, my men! Don't hurry yourselves — take plenty of time — but start her! Start her like thunderclaps, that's all," cried Stubb, sputtering out smoke as he spoke. "Start her, now! Give them the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy — start her, all! But keep cool, keep cool — cucumbers is the word — easy, easy — only start her up like thunderclaps, that's all."

"Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!" screamed the Gay-Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies, as every oarsman in the straining boat involuntarily lurched forward with the one tremendous leading stroke the eager Indian gave.
But his wild screams were answered by others equally wild. "Kee-hee! Kee-hee!" yelled Daggoo, straining forward and backward on his seat like a pacing tiger in his cage.

"Ka-la! Koo-loo!" howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of grenadier's steak. And so with oars and yells the keels cut the sea. Meanwhile, Stubb retained his place in front, still encouraging his men to the chase, puffing smoke from his mouth the whole time. Like desperadoes they tugged and strained, until the welcome cry was heard — "Stand up, Tashtego! — give it to him!" The harpoon was hurled. "A hit, a hit!" The whale dove. Now for the rushing flight through the water! The line raced through the grooves, ran foul. Tashtego snatched his knife from its sheath, and cutting the live line near the wooden post, freed it. Then he replaced the line in the groove with fresh coils. The boat now flew through the churning water like a shark all fins.

"Wet the line! Wet the line!" cried Stubb to the tub oarsman — who, snatching off his hat, dashed seawater into it. More turns were taken, so that the line began holding fast. The boat now flew through the boiling water like a shark all fins. Stubb and Tashtego changed places — stern for bow — a staggering business in any unsteady craft.

It may here be noted that, partly to show the necessity of this act, in the old Dutch fishery a mop was used to splash the running line with water. In many other ships, a wooden bucket is set apart for that purpose. Your hat, however, is the most convenient.

From the vibrating line extending the entire length of the upper part of the boat, now tighter than a harpstring, you would have thought the craft had two keels — one cutting the water, the other the air — as the boat churned through both opposing elements at once. A continuous waterfall played at the bow. A ceaseless eddy swirled at the stern. And like a great helpless whale itself, the boat with its streaming oars drifted sidewise through the sea. A continuous cascade of spray broke over everything.

"Haul in — haul in!" cried Stubb to the bowsman! And facing the whale, all hands began pulling the boat up to him while the boat was still being towed. Soon drawing alongside his flank, Stubb firmly planted his knee in the clumsy cleat and darted lance after lance into the fleeing fish. At the word of command, the boat alternately backing off and pulling closer, Stubb delivered his thrusts from every position.

The red tide now poured from all sides of the monster like streams down a hill. His tormented body rolled not in brine but in blood, which bubbled and seethed for furlongs behind in their wake. The slanting sun playing on this crimson pond sent back its reflection into every face, so that they all glowed to each other like red men. And all the while, jet after jet of white smoke was spouting up and spiraling against the sun.

"Pull up — pull up!" he now cried to the bowsman, as the weakening whale slowed his thrashing. "Pull up! — close to!" And the boat drew alongside the fish's flank. Reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly worked his long sharp lance deep into the fish, and kept it there, carefully twisting and probing, as if cautiously feeling for some gold watch that the whale had swallowed, and which he was afraid of breaking before he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the whale. And now it was struck. For starting out of his agony, the whale threw himself in mad anguish, rolling over and over, sending the slanting sun-glance across the water, spouting thick dark blood in jets that only grew more frenzied.

And now, his fury subsiding, the whale once more rolled into view, surging from side to side, spasmodically expanding and contracting his blowhole with sharp, cracking, agonized gasps. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it were the purple dregs of red wine, shot into the frightened air, and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst.
"He's dead, Mr. Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes — both pipes smoked out!" And withdrawing his own pipe from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water, and for a moment stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.

chapters.title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the unvarying custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman or whale-killer as temporary steersman, and the harpooner pulling the foremost oar, known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, steady arm to throw the first iron into the fish. For often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy iron weapon has to be flung fifty feet or more. And no matter how powerful the arm, this distance puts real strain on it. So the harpooner needs all the rest he can get. But the very act that should give him that rest — rowing — instead drains him of the very energy he needs most. For to pull in a whale-boat is not a child's game. Often the harpooner must pull hard for several exhausting hours on end. Now, where is the point of tiring out the one man you need most? In the harpooner's oar he must pull harder than any other man in the boat. And if pulling does not fatigue his arms, the fixed, concentrated attention required to keep the oar precisely in its place surely must — since in a whale chase, oars are wielded with utmost precision. Furthermore, if the harpooner reaches his target too exhausted for a good throw, he is given barely a second to recover before the line runs. Then what happens? In practice, the line seizes him with all the strength of gravity multiplied by speed.

Again, if the dart is successful — that is, when the whale starts to run — the boathead and harpooner must likewise start running from one end of the boat to the other, to the serious danger of themselves and everyone else. It is then they swap places, and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper station in the bow.

Now, I do not care who says otherwise — all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from first to last. He should both throw the harpoon and wield the lance, and no rowing whatsoever should be expected of him, except under circumstances obvious to any fisherman. I know this would sometimes mean a slight loss of speed in the chase, but the long experience of the entire fishery would confirm this is far more than compensated for by the greater accuracy of the throw.
To ensure the greatest power in the dart, the harpooners of this world must spring to their feet from rest, not from exhaustion.

chapters.title: Chapter 63 — The Crotch
paragraphs: Out of the trunk, the branches grow. Out of them, the twigs. So, in productive subjects, grow the chapters.

The crotch mentioned on a previous page deserves separate attention. It is a notched stick of a particular form, about two feet long, which is inserted vertically into the starboard gunwale near the bow. It serves as a rest for the wooden end of the harpoon, whose other naked, barbed end projects at an angle from the bow, like a lean branch from a bare tree. The harpoon lies there like a tomahawk or any other weapon handy for instant use. Two harpoons typically rest in the crotch — one for the first throw, the other as a backup.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected to the line. The purpose is this: to throw them both, if possible, one right after the other into the same whale, so that if one should pull out during the drag, the other may still hold. It doubles the chances. But it very often happens that, owing to the confused whale-line in the boat at the time of a fast run, the second harpoon gets tangled up and cannot be thrown. The very tension of the line sometimes prevents the boatman from clearing it.

Furthermore: you should know that when the second iron is thrown overboard, it from that point becomes a dangling, sharp-edged terror, skittishly dancing about both boat and whale, tangling the lines or cutting them, and causing a prodigious commotion in all directions. Nor, in general, is it possible to recover it until the whale is fairly captured and a slack line obtained.

Consider now how it must be when four boats are all engaging one unusually strong, active, and intelligent whale — when, owing to these qualities and to the thousand coinciding accidents of such a daring enterprise, eight or ten loose second harpoons may be simultaneously dangling about him. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to replace those that are lost in the fight, and some of these are sure to be thrown and go wild. Trapped in the tangle of lines and weapons, a right whale might almost say he is being attacked with darts.

chapters.title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some distance from the ship. It was calm, so forming a tandem of three boats, we began the slow business of towing the prize back to the Pequod. And now, as we eighteen men with our thirty-six arms and one hundred eighty thumbs and fingers slowly toiled hour after hour upon that lifeless, sluggish corpse in the sea — and it seemed hardly to budge at all, except at long intervals — bitter, impatient thoughts began to fill us about the good old owner of the sea, and his way of keeping things. It was a funeral procession, and we were the pallbearers.

Darkness came on, but three lights up and down in the Pequod's main-rigging dimly guided our way, until drawing nearer we saw Ahab lowering one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. Gazing blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, he issued the usual orders for securing it for the night, then handed his lantern to a seaman and went his way into the darkness, muttering to himself.

Though, in overseeing the pursuit of this whale, Captain Ahab had shown his customary energy — to call it that — now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, or impatience, or despair, seemed to be working in him. As if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be killed, and though a thousand other whales were brought alongside, not one could be Moby Dick. And that hateful, incurable itch that tells a man he is not where he should be — that itch must have been eating at him.

A small note may as well be added here. The strongest and most reliable hold which the ship has upon the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes or tail. And since from its greater density that part is relatively heavier than any other — except the side-fins — its flexibility, even in death, causes it to sink low beneath the surface. So that a strong chain must be used to secure it. The chain is passed through the natural indentation at the narrowest part of the tail, near its base. This arrangement, however, does not prevent the tail from dropping completely below the surface at times.

If moody Ahab was now all quiet — at least as far as could be seen on deck — Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such a bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly handed over to him the sole management of affairs. One small helpful task from Starbuck was readily accepted by Stubb.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his flank!"

Here be it known that though these wild fishermen do not, as a general thing and in keeping with the great military maxim, make the enemy pay for the war expenses — at least not before cashing in on the voyage's profits — yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine taste for that particular part of the Sperm Whale known as the whale steak. It is a thick, firm slab cut from the tapering part of the body just behind the side-fin.

Around midnight that steak was cut and cooked. Lit by two lanterns of sperm oil, Stubb firmly stood up to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as if that capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only diner on whale flesh that night. Mingling their munchings with his own, thousands upon thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead whale, were feasting on his fat. A few sleepers below in their bunks were often startled by the sharp slapping of their tails against the hull, within a few inches of the sleepers' hearts. Looking over the side, you could just see them — as you might at night see the shining of silver in a graveyard — wallowing in the black waters, turning over on their backs as they scooped out huge mouthfuls of whale flesh, so that you could see their wide gaping mouths and the brightness of their teeth gleaming in the moonlight.

Though amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks will be seen longingly gazing up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to gulp down every killed man tossed to them — and though while the brave butchers above deck are thus cannibally carving each other's live flesh with their swords and cutlasses, the sharks below should all the while be surgically cutting away under the very table at which the butchers are eating — though all this is appalling, it is even worse to consider that the same sharks have been known to snap at the oars of the whaleboats. Yes, sometimes they would bite off pieces of the blades themselves. Such were the sharks that fed around Stubb's whale that night.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the feast being held so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black man, not at all pleased about having been previously roused from his warm hammock at a most unreasonable hour, came shuffling along from his galley. For like many old black men, there was something the matter with his knees, which he did not keep well oiled like his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shambling up to the capstan. His left hand held a lantern, and in his right a long cooking fork with which he occasionally rapped his limping knee as a horseman raps his riding boot.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish piece to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook. It's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're making! Cook, go and talk to them. Tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. There, take this lantern — now go and preach to them!"

Sullenly taking the offered lantern, old Fleece limped across the deck to the bulwarks. Then, with one hand dangling his light low over the sea to get a good view of his congregation, with the other hand he solemnly brandished his cooking fork, and leaning far over the side, in a mumbling voice began addressing the sharks, while Stubb, softly crawling behind, listened to what he had to say.

"Fellow creatures: I've been ordered here to say that you must stop that damn noise down there. You hear? Stop that damn smacking of your lips! Mr. Stubb says that you can fill your damn bellies up to the hatches, but by God, you must stop that damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in, slapping him on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who's that? Then preach to them yourself," he replied sullenly, turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, then — beloved fellow creatures —"
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"You is all sharks, and by nature very voracious. Yet I say to you, fellow creatures, that that voraciousness — stop that damn slapping of your tails! How do you think you can hear, if you keep up such a damn slapping and biting down there?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like gentlemen."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow creatures, I don't blame you so much for. That is nature, and can't be helped. But to govern that wicked nature, that is the point. You is sharks, for certain. But if you govern the shark in you, why then you'd be an angel. For all an angel is, is nothing more than the shark well governed. Now, look here, brothers, just try once to be civil, a helping hand to each other — a little charity between yourselves — don't be grabbing all you can, and starving the rest of the neighborhood. I know you're very hungry right now. But, fellow creatures, just think about it — can you really be filling your bellies when your neighbor's belly is empty? And is it really good behavior to be knocking each other about like that? If you're going to eat, eat peaceful-like. There's room enough for everyone."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use going on. The damn villains will keep on squabbling and slapping each other, Mr. Stubb. They don't hear a word. No use preaching to such damn gluttons as you call them, till their bellies is full. And their bellies is bottomless. And when they do get them full, they won't hear you then either, for then they sink in the sea, go fast asleep on the coral, and can't hear nothing at all."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cursed fellow creatures! Kick up the damnedest row you can! Fill your damn bellies till they burst — and then die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All attention," said Fleece, again stooping over on his fork in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What's that got to do with the steak?" said the old black man, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"About ninety, they say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"Behind the hatchway, on a ferryboat, going over the Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say the Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bless my soul, if I cook another one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old man muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever tasted. Juicy, very juicy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape Town," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When this old black man dies," said the cook slowly, changing his whole manner and tone, "he himself won't go nowhere. But some blessed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up there," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So then, you expect to go up into our main-top, do you, cook, when you are dead? But don't you know the higher you climb, the colder it gets? Main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say that at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole, cook. But no, no, cook — you don't get there except you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a tricky business, but must be done, or else it's a no-go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook — listen, now. Look here, cook — you expect to go to heaven — turn your face around — do you expect to go to heaven, cook? Answer me!"
"All attention," said the old black man, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears pointed forward at the same time.

"Well then, cook — you see this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I have put it out of sight as soon as possible. You see that, don't you? Well, for the future, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here at the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other. That done, dish it. Do you hear? And now, tomorrow night, you will cook another steak for me — and now get to bed."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Take a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."
