If you carefully examine almost any four-legged animal's spine, you will be struck by the resemblance of its vertebrae to a string of dwarfed skulls. The base of the human skull is like the first vertebra, and the vertebra like the skull in miniature. So, in the spinal cord of the whale there runs a succession of these connected skull-like shapes.

Apply this spinal branch of phrenology to the Sperm Whale. His brain-cavity is continuous with the first neck-vertebra. And in that vertebra the bottom of the spinal canal will measure ten inches across, being eight in height, and of a triangular shape with the base downward. As it passes through the remaining vertebrae, the canal tapers in size but maintains its proportions.

But leaving this hint to work as it may with the phrenologists, I would merely assume the spinal theory for a moment, in reference to the Sperm Whale's hump. This noble hump, if I am not mistaken, rises over one of the larger vertebrae, and is therefore, in some way, the outer convex mold of it. From its relative position, then, I should call this high hump the organ of firmness or indomitableness in the Sperm Whale. And that he possesses this quality in remarkable degree — all who know him will acknowledge.

chapters.title: Chapter 81 — The Pequod Meets The Virgin
paragraphs: The fated day arrived, and we duly met the ship Jungfrau, captained by Derick De Deer, out of Bremen.
Once the greatest whaling people in the world, the Dutch and Germans are now among the least. But here and there, at very wide intervals across the Pacific, you still occasionally see their flag.

For some reason, the Jungfrau seemed quite eager to pay her respects. While still some distance from the Pequod, she rounded to and dropped a boat. Her captain stood impatiently in the bow instead of the stern, urging his men toward us.
"What has he got in his hand there?" cried Starbuck, pointing to something the German was waving. "Impossible! A lamp-feeder!"

"Not that," said Stubb. "No, no, it's a coffee-pot, Mr. Starbuck. He's coming over to make us our coffee, that German. Don't you see that big tin can beside him? That's his boiling water. Oh, he's all right, that German."
"Go on with you," cried Flask. "It's a lamp-feeder and an oil-can. He's out of oil and has come begging."

However curious it may seem for an oil-ship to be borrowing oil on the whaling-ground, and however much it may contradict the old proverb about carrying coals to Newcastle, sometimes such a thing really happens. And in the present case, Captain Derick De Deer was indeed carrying a lamp-feeder, just as Flask had said.

As he climbed onto the deck, Ahab abruptly confronted him, paying no attention to what he held. But in his broken English, the German quickly showed his complete ignorance of the White Whale. He immediately turned the conversation to his lamp-feeder and oil-can, remarking that he had to turn into his hammock at night in total darkness. His last drop of Bremen oil was gone, and not a single flying-fish had been captured to make up the difference. He finished by hinting that his ship was indeed what the Fishery technically calls a clean one — that is, an empty one — well deserving the name of Jungfrau, or the Virgin.

His needs supplied, Derick departed. But he had not yet reached his ship when whales were spotted almost simultaneously from the mastheads of both vessels. Derick was so eager for the chase that without pausing to put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard, he swung his boat around and went after the great lamp-feeders themselves.

Now, since the whales had surfaced to leeward, Derick and the other three German boats that soon followed him had a considerable head start on the Pequod's boats. There were eight whales, an average pod. Aware of their danger, they were swimming abreast at great speed straight before the wind, rubbing their flanks as closely as a team of horses in harness. They left a great, wide wake behind them, as though continually unrolling a vast parchment upon the sea.

Far behind in this rapid wake swam a huge, humped old bull. His comparatively slow progress and the unusual yellowish growths covering him made him seem afflicted with jaundice or some other infirmity. Whether this whale belonged to the pod ahead was questionable, for it is not customary for such ancient leviathans to be social. Nevertheless, he stuck to their wake, though their backwater must have slowed him, because the white foam at his broad muzzle was broken and choppy, like the swell formed when two opposing currents meet. His spout was short, slow, and labored — coming forth with a choking sort of gush and spending itself in torn shreds, followed by strange subterranean rumblings inside him that seemed to find their exit at his other buried end, causing the waters behind him to bubble up.

"Who's got some medicine?" said Stubb. "He has the stomach-ache, I'm afraid. Lord, think of having half an acre of stomach-ache! Wild winds are having a mad party inside him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern. But look — did a whale ever steer so badly before? He must have lost his rudder."

As an overloaded merchant ship bearing down the coast of India with a deck full of frightened horses careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way — so did this old whale heave his aged bulk. Now and then, partly turning over on his cumbersome ribs, he exposed the cause of his unsteady wake: the unnatural stump of his starboard fin. Whether he had lost that fin in battle or had been born without it was hard to say.
"Only wait a bit, old chap, and I'll give you a sling for that wounded arm," cried cruel Flask, pointing to the whale-line near him.
"Watch he doesn't sling you with it," cried Starbuck. "Give way, or the German will have him."

With single purpose, all the rival boats were pointed toward this one whale. Not only was he the largest and therefore the most valuable, but he was nearest to them. The other whales were swimming with such great speed as to almost defy pursuit for the time being. At this point, the Pequod's boats had shot past the three German boats that launched last. But from the great head start he had, Derick's boat still led the chase, though his foreign rivals closed in with every moment. The only thing they feared was that, being already so close to the whale, he would manage to dart his iron before they could completely overtake and pass him. As for Derick, he seemed quite confident this would be the case, and occasionally shook his lamp-feeder at the other boats with a mocking gesture.

"The ungracious and ungrateful dog!" cried Starbuck. "He mocks and taunts me with the very charity box I filled for him not five minutes ago!" Then in his old intense whisper: "Give way, greyhounds! Go for it!"

"I tell you what it is, men," cried Stubb to his crew. "It's against my religion to get mad. But I'd like to eat that villainous German. Pull — won't you? Are you going to let that rascal beat you? Do you love brandy? A whole barrel of brandy to the best man. Come, why don't some of you burst a blood-vessel? Who's been dropping an anchor overboard? We don't budge an inch — we're dead in the water. Look, there's grass growing on the boat's bottom, and by the Lord, the mast is budding. This won't do, boys. Look at that German! The short and long of it is, men — will you spit fire or not?"

"Oh, see the foam he makes!" cried Flask, dancing up and down. "What a hump! Oh, do pile on the muscle — he lies like a log! Oh, my lads, do spring! Flapjacks and clams for supper, you know, my lads — baked clams and muffins! Oh, do, do spring! He's a hundred-barrel whale! Don't lose him now — don't, oh, don't! See that German! Oh, won't you pull for your pudding, my lads? Such a prize! Such a beauty! Don't you love spermaceti? There goes three thousand dollars, men! A bank! A whole bank! The Bank of England! Oh, do, do, do! What's that German about now?"

At this moment Derick was in the act of pitching his lamp-feeder at the advancing boats, and also his oil-can — perhaps with the double purpose of slowing his rivals' progress while accelerating his own through the backward momentum of the throw.

"The unmannerly Dutch mongrel!" cried Stubb. "Pull now, men, like fifty thousand shiploads of red-haired devils. What do you say, Tashtego — are you the man to snap your spine in twenty-two pieces for the honor of old Gay Head? What do you say?"
"I say, pull like god-damn," cried the Indian.

Fiercely but evenly spurred on by the Germans' taunts, the Pequod's three boats now began ranging almost abreast, and in that formation they steadily closed the gap. In that fine, loose, gallant stance of the headsman drawing near to his prey, the three mates stood up proudly, occasionally urging on the rear oarsman with an exhilarating cry: "There she slides now! Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the German! Sail over him!"

But Derick had such a decisive head start that despite all their courage, he would have won this race — had not righteous judgment descended upon him in the form of a crab that caught the blade of his middle oarsman. While this clumsy fellow was struggling to free his oar, and while Derick's boat was nearly capsizing as he thundered at his men in a mighty rage — that was the moment for Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask. With a shout, they surged forward and ranged up diagonally on the German's quarter. An instant more, and all four boats were in the whale's immediate wake, while stretching from them on both sides was the foaming swell the whale created.

It was a terrific, most pitiable, and maddening sight. The whale was now going head out, sending his spout before him in a continual tormented jet, while his one poor fin beat his side in an agony of fright. Now to this side, now to that, he swerved in his faltering flight. At every wave he broke, he either spasmodically sank into the sea or sideways rolled toward the sky his one beating fin. I have seen a bird with a clipped wing making frightened broken circles in the air, vainly trying to escape piratical hawks. But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries makes known her fear. But the fear of this vast dumb creature of the sea was chained up and enchanted in him. He had no voice save that choking respiration through his blowhole, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable — while still, in his amazing bulk, his portcullis jaw, and his omnipotent tail, there was enough to terrify the bravest man who pitied him.

Seeing now that only a few more moments would give the Pequod's boats the advantage, and rather than be cheated of his prey, Derick chose to risk what must have seemed to him an unusually long throw before his last chance escaped forever.

But no sooner did his harpooner stand up for the strike than all three tigers — Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo — instinctively sprang to their feet. Standing in a diagonal row, they simultaneously aimed their barbs and darted over the head of the German harpooner. Their three Nantucket irons entered the whale. Blinding vapors of foam and white fire! The three boats, in the first fury of the whale's headlong rush, bumped the German's aside with such force that both Derick and his baffled harpooner were spilled out and sailed over by the three flying keels.

"Don't be afraid, my butter-boxes," cried Stubb, casting a passing glance at them as he shot by. "You'll be picked up presently — all right. I saw some sharks astern — St. Bernard's dogs, you know — they relieve distressed travelers. Hurrah! This is the way to sail now. Every keel a sunbeam! Hurrah! Here we go like three tin kettles at the tail of a mad cougar! This puts me in mind of being fastened to an elephant in a carriage on a plain — makes the wheel-spokes fly, boys, when you fasten to him that way. And there's danger of being pitched out, too, when you hit a hill. Hurrah! This is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones — all a rush down an endless slope! Hurrah! This whale carries the everlasting mail!"

But the monster's run was brief. Giving a sudden gasp, he plunged straight down. With a grating rush, the three lines flew around the loggerheads with such force as to gouge deep grooves into them. The harpooners were so afraid this rapid sounding would soon exhaust the lines that they used all their skill to catch repeated smoking turns with the rope to hold on. At last — owing to the perpendicular strain from the lined chocks of the bows, where the three ropes went straight down into the blue — the gunwales of the bows were almost level with the water, while the three sterns tilted high in the air. When the whale stopped sounding, they remained in that position for a time, afraid to let out more line, though the situation was precarious. Boats have been pulled down and lost this way, yet it is this "holding on" — this hooking up by the sharp barbs embedded in the whale's living flesh — that often torments the Leviathan into rising again to meet the sharp lance of his enemies. Yet the peril aside, it is doubtful whether this is always the best course. It is reasonable to assume that the longer the wounded whale stays underwater, the more he is exhausted. Because of the enormous surface area of a full-grown sperm whale — something less than two thousand square feet — the pressure of the water is immense. We all know what an astonishing atmospheric weight we ourselves bear, even here above ground in the air. How vast, then, the burden of a whale, bearing on his back a column of two hundred fathoms of ocean! It must at least equal the weight of fifty atmospheres. One whaleman has estimated it at the weight of twenty warships, with all their guns, stores, and men on board.

As the three boats lay there on that gently rolling sea, gazing down into its eternal blue noon — and as not a single groan or cry, not so much as a ripple or a bubble, came up from its depths — what landsman would have thought that beneath all that silence and peace, the greatest monster of the seas was writhing and wrenching in agony! Not eight inches of rope were visible at the bows. Can it be believed that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the weight of an eight-day clock? Suspended? And from what? From three bits of board. Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said: "Can you fill his skin with barbed irons? Or his head with fish-spears? The sword of him that strikes at him cannot hold; the spear, the dart, nor the coat of mail. He regards iron as straw; the arrow cannot make him flee; darts are counted as stubble; he laughs at the shaking of a spear!" This the creature? This he? Oh, that prophecies should go unfulfilled! For with the strength of a thousand thighs in his tail, Leviathan had run his head under the mountains of the sea to hide from the Pequod's spears!

In that sloping afternoon sunlight, the shadows that the three boats cast beneath the surface must have been long enough and broad enough to shade half of Xerxes' army. Who can tell how terrifying those huge phantoms must have been, flitting over the wounded whale's head!

"Stand by, men — he stirs," cried Starbuck, as the three lines suddenly vibrated in the water, conducting upward to them like magnetic wires the life-and-death throbs of the whale. Every oarsman felt them in his seat. The next moment, largely relieved from the downward strain at the bows, the boats gave a sudden bounce upward, like a small ice field when a dense herd of polar bears is scared off it into the sea.
"Haul in! Haul in!" cried Starbuck again. "He's rising."

The lines, of which hardly an instant before not a hand's breadth could have been gained, were now flung back in long, quick coils, dripping, into the boats. Soon the whale broke the surface within two ship-lengths of the hunters.

His movements clearly showed his extreme exhaustion. In most land animals, there are certain valves in their veins that, when the animal is wounded, at least partly shut off the blood flow in certain directions. Not so with the whale. One of his peculiarities is a completely non-valvular blood-vessel structure, so that when pierced by even so small a point as a harpoon, a deadly drain begins at once upon his whole arterial system. When this is worsened by the extraordinary water pressure at great depth below the surface, his life may be said to pour from him in constant streams. Yet so vast is the quantity of blood in him, and so distant and numerous its interior sources, that he will keep bleeding for a considerable period — even as a river will flow during a drought whose source lies in the hidden springs of far-off hills. Even now, when the boats closed on this whale and dangerously drew over his swaying flukes, and the lances were thrust into him, they were followed by steady jets from the new wounds, which kept continually playing, while the natural spout-hole in his head only sent its frightened moisture into the air at intervals, however rapid. From this last vent no blood yet came, because no vital part had been struck. His life, as they significantly call it, was untouched.

As the boats now more closely surrounded him, the whole upper part of his body, including much that is normally submerged, was plainly revealed. His eyes — or rather the places where his eyes had been — were visible. As strange, misshapen growths gather in the knotholes of the noblest oaks when they lie fallen, so from the spots where the whale's eyes had once been, there now protruded blind bulbs, horribly pitiable to see. But pity there was none. For all his old age, his one fin, and his blind eyes, he must die and be murdered — in order to light the gay weddings and other celebrations of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional gentleness to all. Still rolling in his blood, at last he partly revealed a strangely discolored lump or swelling, the size of a bushel, low on his flank.
"A nice spot," cried Flask. "Just let me prick him there once."
"Hold off!" cried Starbuck. "There's no need of that!"

But humane Starbuck was too late. The instant the dart struck, an ulcerous jet shot from that cruel wound. Goaded by it into more than bearable agony, the whale — now spouting thick blood — blindly charged the boats with savage fury, spattering them and their gloating crews all over with showers of gore, capsizing Flask's boat and smashing the bows. It was his death stroke. For by this time, so drained was he from blood loss that he helplessly rolled away from the wreck he had made, lay panting on his side, and impotently flapped his stumped fin. Then over and over he slowly revolved like a dying world, turned up the white secrets of his belly, lay like a log, and died. It was most pitiable, that last expiring spout. As when unseen hands gradually draw the water from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled, melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground — so fell the last long dying spout of the whale.

Soon, while the crews waited for the ship to arrive, the body showed signs of sinking with all its treasures untouched. Immediately, by Starbuck's orders, lines were secured to it at different points, so that before long every boat served as a buoy, with the sunken whale suspended a few inches beneath them by the ropes. By very careful management, when the ship drew near, the whale was transferred to her side and strongly secured there by the stiffest fluke-chains. For it was clear that unless artificially held up, the body would sink at once to the bottom.

It happened that almost upon the first cut into him with the spade, the entire length of a corroded harpoon was found embedded in his flesh, on the lower part of the lump described before. But since the stumps of harpoons are frequently found in the dead bodies of captured whales, with the flesh perfectly healed around them and no sign of their location, there must have been some other unknown reason to explain the ulceration. But still more curious was the fact that a stone lance-head was found in him, not far from the buried iron, with the flesh perfectly firm around it. Who had thrown that stone lance? And when? It might have been hurled by some Northwest Indian long before America was discovered.

What other marvels might have been dug out of this monstrous cabinet there is no telling. But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries when the ship was unprecedentedly dragged sideways toward the sea, owing to the body's rapidly increasing tendency to sink. However, Starbuck, who was in charge, hung on to it to the last — hung on so stubbornly, in fact, that when at length the ship would have capsized if she kept holding on, and the command was given to break clear, the strain upon the timber-heads to which the fluke-chains and cables were fastened was so immense that it was impossible to cast them off. Meanwhile, everything in the Pequod was tilted at an angle. To cross to the other side of the deck was like walking up the steep gabled roof of a house. The ship groaned and gasped. Many of the ivory inlays in her bulwarks and cabins were popped from their places by the unnatural dislocation. In vain, handspikes and crowbars were brought to bear upon the immovable fluke-chains to pry them loose from the timber-heads. The submerged ends could not be reached at all, while every moment whole tons of weight seemed to be added to the sinking mass, and the ship seemed on the point of going over.

"Hold on, hold on, won't you?" cried Stubb to the body. "Don't be in such a devil of a hurry to sink! By thunder, men, we must do something or we're done for. No use prying there. Stop it, I say, with your handspikes, and one of you run for a prayer book and a pen-knife and cut the big chains."

"Knife? Aye, aye," cried Queequeg, and seizing the carpenter's heavy hatchet, he leaned out of a porthole and, steel against iron, began slashing at the largest fluke-chains. But only a few strokes, full of sparks, were needed before the tremendous strain did the rest. With a terrific snap, every fastening broke loose. The ship righted. The carcass sank.

Now, this occasional inevitable sinking of the recently killed sperm whale is a very curious thing. No fisherman has yet adequately explained it. Usually the dead sperm whale floats with great buoyancy, its side or belly considerably elevated above the surface. If the only whales that sank this way were old, meager, broken-hearted creatures, with their pads of fat diminished and all their bones heavy and rheumatic, then you might reasonably argue that this sinking is caused by an uncommon density in the whale. But it is not so. For young whales in the peak of health, swelling with noble energy, prematurely cut off in the warm flush and springtime of life with all their plump fat about them — even these strong, buoyant heroes sometimes sink.

It should be said, however, that the sperm whale is far less prone to this than any other species. Where one sperm whale goes down, twenty right whales do. This difference is no doubt largely due to the greater quantity of bone in the right whale. Its baleen plates alone sometimes weigh more than a ton, and from this burden the sperm whale is wholly free. But there are instances where, after many hours or several days, the sunken whale rises again, more buoyant than in life. The reason is obvious. Gases are generated inside him. He swells to prodigious size and becomes a sort of animal balloon. A warship could hardly keep him under then. In the shore whaling, in the shallows among the bays of New Zealand, when a right whale shows signs of sinking, they fasten buoys to him with plenty of rope, so that when the body has gone down, they know where to look for it when it rises again.

It was not long after the sinking of the body that a cry was heard from the Pequod's mastheads, announcing that the Jungfrau was again lowering her boats — though the only spout in sight was that of a fin-back, a species of whale that is virtually impossible to capture because of its incredible swimming speed. Nevertheless, the fin-back's spout is so similar to the sperm whale's that unskilled fishermen often mistake it. And so Derick and all his men were now in valiant chase of this uncatchable brute. The Virgin, crowding on all sail, followed after her four boats, and they all disappeared far to leeward, still in bold, hopeful pursuit.
Oh! Many are the fin-backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 82 — The Honor and Glory of Whaling
paragraphs: There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method.

The more I dive into this matter of whaling, and push my researches up to the very source of it, the more I am impressed with its great honor and antiquity — especially when I find so many great demigods and heroes, prophets of all sorts, who one way or another have shed distinction upon it. I am transported with the thought that I belong to so ancient and noble a body.

The gallant Perseus, a son of Jupiter, was the first whaleman; and to the eternal honor of our calling be it said, that the first whale attacked by our brotherhood was not killed with any sordid intent. Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we only bore arms to succor the distressed, and not to fill men's lamp-feeders. Everyone knows the fine story of Perseus and Andromeda — how the lovely Andromeda, the daughter of a king, was tied to a rock on the sea-coast, and as Leviathan was in the very act of carrying her off, Perseus, the prince of whalemen, intrepidly advancing, harpooned the monster, and delivered and married the maid. It was an admirable artistic exploit, rarely achieved by the best harpooneers of the present day; inasmuch as this Leviathan was slain at the very first dart. And let no man doubt this Arkite story; for in the ancient Joppa, now Jaffa, on the Syrian coast, in one of the Pagan temples, there stood for many ages the vast skeleton of a whale, which the city's legends and all the inhabitants asserted to be the identical bones of the monster that Perseus slew. When the Romans took Joppa, the same skeleton was carried to Italy in triumph. What seems most singular and suggestively important in this story is this: it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail.

Akin to the adventure of Perseus and Andromeda — indeed, by some supposed to be indirectly derived from it — is that famous story of St. George and the Dragon; which dragon I maintain to have been a whale. For in many old chronicles, whales and dragons are strangely jumbled together, and often stand for each other. "Thou art as a lion of the waters, and as a dragon of the sea," saith Ezekiel; hereby, plainly meaning a whale; in truth, some versions of the Bible use that word itself. Besides, it would much subtract from the glory of the exploit had St. George but encountered a crawling reptile of the land, instead of doing battle with the great monster of the deep. Any man may kill a snake, but only a Perseus, a St. George, a Coffin, have the heart in them to march boldly up to a whale.

Let not the modern paintings of this scene mislead us; for though the creature encountered by that valiant whaleman of old is vaguely represented of a griffin-like shape, and though the battle is depicted on land and the saint on horseback, yet considering the great ignorance of those times, when the true form of the whale was unknown to artists; and considering that as in Perseus' case, St. George's whale might have crawled up out of the sea on the beach; and considering that the animal ridden by St. George might have been only a large seal, or sea-horse; bearing all this in mind, it will not appear altogether incompatible with the sacred legend and the ancientest draughts of the scene, to hold this so-called dragon no other than the great Leviathan himself. In fact, placed before the strict and piercing truth, this whole story will fare like that fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines, Dagon by name; who being planted before the ark of Israel, his horse's head and both the palms of his hands fell off from him, and only the stump or fishy part of him remained. Thus, then, one of our own noble stamp, even a whaleman, is the tutelary guardian of England; and by good rights, we harpooneers of Nantucket should be enrolled in the most noble order of St. George. And therefore, let not the knights of that honorable company (none of whom, I venture to say, have ever had to do with a whale like their great patron) let them never eye a Nantucketer with disdain, since even in our woollen frocks and tarred trowsers we are much better entitled to St. George's decoration than they.

Whether to admit Hercules among us or not, concerning this I long remained dubious. For though according to the Greek mythologies, that antique Crockett and Kit Carson — that brawny doer of rejoicing good deeds — was swallowed down and thrown up by a whale, still, whether that strictly makes a whaleman of him, that might be mooted. It nowhere appears that he ever actually harpooned his fish, unless, indeed, from the inside. Nevertheless, he may be deemed a sort of involuntary whaleman; at any rate the whale caught him, if he did not the whale. I claim him for one of our clan.

But by the best contradictory authorities, this Greek story of Hercules and the whale is considered to derive from the still more ancient Hebrew story of Jonah and the whale, and vice versa. Certainly they are very similar. If I claim the demigod, then why not the prophet?

Nor do heroes, saints, demigods, and prophets alone comprise the whole roll of our order. Our grand master is still to be named; for like royal kings of old times, we find the head-waters of our fraternity in nothing short of the great gods themselves. That wondrous oriental story is now to be rehearsed from the Shaster, which gives us the dread Vishnoo, one of the three persons in the godhead of the Hindoos; gives us this divine Vishnoo himself for our Lord — Vishnoo, who, by the first of his ten earthly incarnations, has forever set apart and sanctified the whale. When Brahma, or the God of Gods, saith the Shaster, resolved to recreate the world after one of its periodical dissolutions, he gave birth to Vishnoo, to preside over the work; but the Vedas, or mystical books, whose perusal would seem to have been indispensable to Vishnoo before beginning the creation, and which therefore must have contained something in the shape of practical hints to young architects, these Vedas were lying at the bottom of the waters; so Vishnoo became incarnate in a whale, and sounding down in him to the uttermost depths, rescued the sacred volumes. Was not this Vishnoo a whaleman, then? even as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman?
Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and Vishnu! There's a membership roll for you! What club but the whaleman's can head off like that?

chapters.title: Chapter 83 — Jonah Historically Regarded
paragraphs: Reference was made to the historical story of Jonah and the whale in the preceding chapter. Now some Nantucketers rather distrust this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then there were some skeptical Greeks and Romans, who, standing out from the orthodox pagans of their times, equally doubted the story of Hercules and the whale. And some Portuguese scholars doubted the story of St. George and the Dragon. One way or another, some people will always doubt the most extraordinary stories.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman's chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this: he had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles, embellished with curious, unscientific plates, one of which represented Jonah's whale with two spouts in his head — a peculiarity only true with respect to a species of the Leviathan (the Right Whale, and the varieties of that order), concerning which the fishermen have this saying: "A penny roll would choke him"; his swallow is so very small. But to this, Bishop Jebb's anticipative answer is ready. It is not necessary, hints the Bishop, that we consider Jonah as tombed in the whale's belly, but as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough in the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale's mouth would accommodate a couple of whist-tables, and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have ensconced himself in a hollow tooth; but, on second thoughts, the Right Whale is toothless.

Another reason which Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) urged for his want of faith in this matter of the prophet, was something obscurely in reference to his incarcerated body and the whale's gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German exegetist supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a dead whale — even as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents, and crawled into them. Besides, it has been divined by other continental commentators that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he straightway effected his escape to another vessel near by, some vessel with a whale for a figure-head; and, I would add, possibly called "The Whale," as some craft are nowadays christened the "Shark," the "Gull," the "Eagle." Nor have there been wanting learned exegetists who have opined that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah merely meant a life-preserver — an inflated bag of wind — which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery doom. Poor Sag-Harbor, therefore, seems worsted all round. But he had still another reason for his want of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days' journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, very much more than three days' journey across from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet within that short distance of Nineveh? Yes. He might have carried him round by the way of the Cape of Good Hope. But not to speak of the passage through the whole length of the Mediterranean, and another passage up the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, such a supposition would involve the complete circumnavigation of all Africa in three days, not to speak of the Tigris waters, near the site of Nineveh, being too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, this idea of Jonah's weathering the Cape of Good Hope at so early a day would wrest the honor of the discovery of that great headland from Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, and so make modern history a liar.

But all these foolish arguments of old Sag-Harbor only evinced his foolish pride of reason — a thing still more reprehensible in him, seeing that he had but little learning except what he had picked up from the sun and the sea. I say it only shows his foolish, impious pride, and abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy. For by a Portuguese Catholic priest, this very idea of Jonah's going to Nineveh via the Cape of Good Hope was advanced as a signal magnification of the general miracle. And so it was. Besides, to this day, the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveller in old Harris's Voyages, speaks of a Turkish Mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which Mosque was a miraculous lamp that burnt without any oil.

chapters.title: Chapter 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform an analogous operation upon their boat — they grease the bottom. Nor is it to be doubted that, as such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no contemptible advantage; considering that oil and water are hostile, that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, took more than customary pains in that occupation, crawling under its bottom where it hung over the side, and rubbing in the unctuousness as though diligently seeking to insure a crop of hair from the craft's bald keel. He seemed to be working in obedience to some particular presentiment. Nor did it remain unwarranted by the event.
Toward noon whales were raised; but so soon as the ship sailed down to them, they turned and fled with swift precipitancy — a disordered flight, as of Cleopatra's barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats pursued, and Stubb's was foremost. By great exertion, Tashtego at last succeeded in planting one iron; but the stricken whale, without at all sounding, still continued his horizontal flight, with added fleetness. Such unintermitted strainings upon the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably extract it. It became imperative to lance the flying whale, or be content to lose him. But to haul the boat up to his flank was impossible, he swam so fast and furious. What then remained?

Of all the wondrous devices and dexterities, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties to which the veteran whaleman is so often forced, none exceed that fine manoeuvre with the lance called pitchpoling. Small sword, or broad sword, in all its exercises boasts nothing like it. It is only indispensable with an inveterate running whale; its grand fact and feature is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately darted from a violently rocking, jerking boat under extreme headway. Steel and wood included, the entire spear is some ten or twelve feet in length; the staff is much slighter than that of the harpoon, and also of a lighter material — pine. It is furnished with a small rope called a warp, of considerable length, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after darting.

But before going further, it is important to mention here that, though the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way with the lance, yet it is seldom done; and when done, is still less frequently successful, on account of the greater weight and inferior length of the harpoon as compared with the lance, which in effect become serious drawbacks. As a general thing, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale, before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb — a man who from his humorous, deliberate coolness and equanimity in the direst emergencies was specially qualified to excel in pitchpoling. Look at him: he stands upright in the tossed bow of the flying boat; wrapt in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing twice or thrice along its length to see if it be exactly straight, Stubb whistlingly gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to secure its free end in his grasp, leaving the rest unobstructed. Then holding the lance full before his waistband's middle, he levels it at the whale; when, covering him with it, he steadily depresses the butt-end in his hand, thereby elevating the point till the weapon stands fairly balanced upon his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He minds you somewhat of a juggler, balancing a long staff on his chin. Next moment, with a rapid, nameless impulse, in a superb lofty arch the bright steel spans the foaming distance, and quivers in the life-spot of the whale. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

"That drove the spigot out of him!" cried Stubb. "'Tis July's immortal Fourth; all fountains must run wine today! Would now, it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I'd have ye hold a canakin to the jet, and we'd drink round it! Yea, verily, hearts alive, we'd brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl quaff the living stuff."

Again and again to such gamesome talk, the dexterous dart is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held in skilful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry; the tow-line is slackened, and the pitchpoler dropping astern, folds his hands, and mutely watches the monster die.

chapters.title: Chapter 85 — The Fountain
paragraphs: That for six thousand years — and no one knows how many millions of ages before — the great whales should have been spouting all over the sea, and sprinkling and mistifying the gardens of the deep, as with so many sprinkling or mistifying pots; and that for some centuries back, thousands of hunters should have been close by the fountain of the whale, watching these sprinklings and spoutings — that all this should be, and yet, that down to this blessed minute (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one o'clock P.M. of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851), it should still remain a problem whether these spoutings are, after all, really water, or nothing but vapor — this is surely a noteworthy thing.

Let us, then, look at this matter, along with some interesting items contingent. Everyone knows that by the peculiar cunning of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air which at all times is combined with the element in which they swim; hence a herring or a cod might live a century, and never once raise its head above the surface. But owing to his marked internal structure, which gives him regular lungs like a human being's, the whale can only live by inhaling the disengaged air in the open atmosphere. Wherefore the necessity for his periodical visits to the upper world. But he cannot in any degree breathe through his mouth, for in his ordinary attitude, the Sperm Whale's mouth is buried at least eight feet beneath the surface; and what is still more, his windpipe has no connection with his mouth. No, he breathes through his spiracle alone; and this is on the top of his head.

If I say that in any creature breathing is only a function indispensable to vitality, inasmuch as it withdraws from the air a certain element which, being subsequently brought into contact with the blood, imparts to the blood its vivifying principle — I do not think I shall err, though I may possibly use some superfluous scientific words. Assume it, and it follows that if all the blood in a man could be aerated with one breath, he might then seal up his nostrils and not fetch another for a considerable time. That is to say, he would then live without breathing. Anomalous as it may seem, this is precisely the case with the whale, who systematically lives, by intervals, his full hour and more (when at the bottom) without drawing a single breath, or so much as in any way inhaling a particle of air; for, remember, he has no gills. How is this? Between his ribs and on each side of his spine, he is supplied with a remarkable involved Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels, which vessels, when he quits the surface, are completely distended with oxygenated blood. So that for an hour or more, a thousand fathoms in the sea, he carries a surplus stock of vitality in him, just as the camel crossing the waterless desert carries a surplus supply of drink for future use in its four supplementary stomachs. The anatomical fact of this labyrinth is indisputable; and that the supposition founded upon it is reasonable and true seems the more cogent to me when I consider the otherwise inexplicable obstinacy of that leviathan in having his spoutings out, as the fishermen phrase it. This is what I mean. If unmolested, upon rising to the surface, the Sperm Whale will continue there for a period of time exactly uniform with all his other unmolested risings. Say he stays eleven minutes, and jets seventy times — that is, respires seventy breaths; then whenever he rises again, he will be sure to have his seventy breaths over again, to a minute. Now, if after he fetches a few breaths you alarm him, so that he sounds, he will be always dodging up again to make good his regular allowance of air. And not till those seventy breaths are told will he finally go down to stay out his full term below. Remark, however, that in different individuals these rates are different; but in any one they are alike. Now, why should the whale thus insist upon having his spoutings out, unless it be to replenish his reservoir of air, ere descending for good? How obvious is it, too, that this necessity for the whale's rising exposes him to all the fatal hazards of the chase. For not by hook or by net could this vast leviathan be caught, when sailing a thousand fathoms beneath the sunlight. Not so much thy skill, then, O hunter, as the great necessities that strike the victory to thee!

In man, breathing is incessantly going on — one breath only serving for two or three pulsations; so that whatever other business he has to attend to, waking or sleeping, breathe he must, or die he will. But the Sperm Whale only breathes about one seventh or Sunday of his time.

It has been said that the whale only breathes through his spout-hole; if it could truthfully be added that his spouts are mixed with water, then I opine we should be furnished with the reason why his sense of smell seems obliterated in him — for the only thing about him that at all answers to his nose is that identical spout-hole; and being so clogged with two elements, it could not be expected to have the power of smelling. But owing to the mystery of the spout — whether it be water or whether it be vapor — no absolute certainty can as yet be arrived at on this head. Sure it is, nevertheless, that the Sperm Whale has no proper olfactories. But what does he want of them? No roses, no violets, no Cologne-water in the sea.

Furthermore, as his windpipe solely opens into the tube of his spouting canal, and as that long canal — like the grand Erie Canal — is furnished with a sort of locks (that open and shut) for the downward retention of air or the upward exclusion of water, therefore the whale has no voice — unless you insult him by saying that when he so strangely rumbles, he talks through his nose. But then again, what has the whale to say? Seldom have I known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something by way of getting a living. Oh, happy that the world is such an excellent listener!

Now, the spouting canal of the Sperm Whale, chiefly intended as it is for the conveyance of air, and for several feet laid along, horizontally, just beneath the upper surface of his head, and a little to one side — this curious canal is very much like a gas-pipe laid down in a city on one side of a street. But the question returns whether this gas-pipe is also a water-pipe — in other words, whether the spout of the Sperm Whale is the mere vapor of the exhaled breath, or whether that exhaled breath is mixed with water taken in at the mouth, and discharged through the spiracle. It is certain that the mouth indirectly communicates with the spouting canal; but it cannot be proved that this is for the purpose of discharging water through the spiracle. Because the greatest necessity for so doing would seem to be when in feeding he accidentally takes in water. But the Sperm Whale's food is far beneath the surface, and there he cannot spout even if he would. Besides, if you regard him very closely, and time him with your watch, you will find that when unmolested, there is an undeviating rhyme between the periods of his jets and the ordinary periods of respiration.

But why pester one with all this reasoning on the subject? Speak out! You have seen him spout; then declare what the spout is; can you not tell water from air? My dear sir, in this world it is not so easy to settle these plain things. I have ever found your plain things the knottiest of all. And as for this whale spout, you might almost stand in it, and yet be undecided as to what it is precisely.

The central body of it is hidden in the snowy sparkling mist enveloping it; and how can you certainly tell whether any water falls from it, when, always, when you are close enough to a whale to get a close view of his spout, he is in a prodigious commotion, the water cascading all around him? And if at such times you should think that you really perceived drops of moisture in the spout, how do you know that they are not merely condensed from its vapor? Or how do you know that they are not those identical drops superficially lodged in the spout-hole fissure, which is countersunk into the summit of the whale's head? For even when tranquilly swimming through the mid-day sea in a calm, with his elevated hump sun-dried as a dromedary's in the desert; even then, the whale always carries a small basin of water on his head, as under a blazing sun you will sometimes see a cavity in a rock filled up with rain.

Nor is it at all prudent for the hunter to be over-curious touching the precise nature of the whale spout. It will not do for him to be peering into it, and putting his face in it. You cannot go with your pitcher to this fountain and fill it, and bring it away. For even when coming into slight contact with the outer, vapory shreds of the jet, which will often happen, your skin will feverishly smart, from the acridness of the thing so touching it. And I know one who, coming into still closer contact with the spout — whether with some scientific object in view, or otherwise, I cannot say — the skin peeled off from his cheek and arm. Wherefore, among whalemen, the spout is deemed poisonous; they try to evade it. Another thing: I have heard it said, and I do not much doubt it, that if the jet is fairly spouted into your eyes, it will blind you. The wisest thing the investigator can do then, it seems to me, is to let this deadly spout alone.

Still, we can hypothesize, even if we cannot prove and establish. My hypothesis is this: that the spout is nothing but mist. And besides other reasons, to this conclusion I am impelled by considerations touching the great inherent dignity and sublimity of the Sperm Whale; I account him no common, shallow being, inasmuch as it is an undisputed fact that he is never found on soundings, or near shores; all other whales sometimes are. He is both ponderous and profound. And I am convinced that from the heads of all ponderous profound beings, such as Plato, Pyrrho, the Devil, Jupiter, Dante, and so on, there always goes up a certain semi-visible steam, while in the act of thinking deep thoughts. While composing a little treatise on Eternity, I had the curiosity to place a mirror before me; and ere long saw reflected there, a curious involved worming and undulation in the atmosphere over my head. The invariable moisture of my hair, while plunged in deep thought, after six cups of hot tea in my thin shingled attic of an August noon — this seems an additional argument for the above supposition.

And how nobly it raises our conceit of the mighty, misty monster, to behold him solemnly sailing through a calm tropical sea; his vast, mild head overhung by a canopy of vapor, engendered by his incommunicable contemplations, and that vapor — as you will sometimes see it — glorified by a rainbow, as if Heaven itself had put its seal upon his thoughts. For, d'ye see, rainbows do not visit the clear air; they only irradiate vapor. And so, through all the thick mists of the dim doubts in my mind, divine intuitions now and then shoot, enkindling my fog with a heavenly ray. And for this I thank God; for all have doubts; many deny; but doubts or denials, few along with them, have intuitions. Doubts of all things earthly, and intuitions of some things heavenly — this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who regards them both with equal eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 86 — The Tail
paragraphs: Other poets have sung the praises of the soft eye of the antelope and the lovely plumage of the bird that never lands. Less heavenly, I celebrate a tail.

If you reckon the largest sperm whale's tail to begin at the point of the trunk where it tapers to about the girth of a man, it covers an area on its upper surface alone of at least fifty square feet. The compact round root expands into two broad, firm, flat palms or flukes, gradually thinning to less than an inch in thickness. At the junction, these flukes slightly overlap, then separate from each other like wings, leaving a wide gap between them. In no living thing are the lines of beauty more exquisitely defined than in the crescent borders of these flukes. At full expansion in a full-grown whale, the tail will considerably exceed twenty feet across.

The entire structure seems a dense, webbed bed of welded sinews. But cut into it and you find three distinct layers: upper, middle, and lower. The fibers in the upper and lower layers are long and horizontal. Those in the middle are very short, running crosswise between the outer layers. This three-part structure, as much as anything else, gives the tail its power. To the student of old Roman walls, the middle layer will offer a curious parallel to the thin course of tiles always alternating with stone in those wonderful ancient ruins, which undoubtedly contribute so much to the masonry's great strength.

But as if this vast local power in the muscular tail were not enough, the whole bulk of the leviathan is knit over with a mesh of muscular fibers and filaments. These pass on either side of the loins and run down into the flukes, blending with them seamlessly and greatly adding to their might. So in the tail, the measureless force of the whole whale seems concentrated to a point. If annihilation could occur to matter, this would be the thing to do it.

Nor does this amazing strength at all cripple the graceful flexibility of its motions, where an infantlike ease undulates through a titanic power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most awesome beauty from it. Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony but often bestows it. In everything impressively beautiful, strength has much to do with the magic. Take away the tied tendons that everywhere seem bursting from the marble in the carved Hercules, and its charm would be gone. When devout Eckermann lifted the linen sheet from Goethe's naked corpse, he was overwhelmed by the massive chest, which seemed like a Roman triumphal arch. When Michelangelo paints even God the Father in human form, mark what robustness is there. And whatever they may reveal of divine love in the Son, those soft, curled Italian paintings in which his image has been most successfully embodied — so destitute of all brawniness — hint nothing of any power but the merely passive, feminine one of submission and endurance, which by all accounts form the peculiar practical virtues of his teachings.

Such is the subtle elasticity of the organ I describe that whether wielded in sport, in earnest, or in anger, whatever its mood, its movements are invariably marked by exceeding grace. No fairy's arm can surpass it.
Five great motions are peculiar to it. First, when used as a fin for propulsion. Second, when used as a club in battle. Third, in sweeping. Fourth, in lob-tailing. Fifth, in peaking flukes.

First: Being horizontal in position, the Leviathan's tail acts differently from the tails of all other sea creatures. It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority. To the whale, his tail is his sole means of propulsion. Coiled forward like a scroll beneath the body and then rapidly sprung backward — this is what gives that singular darting, leaping motion to the monster when swimming furiously. His side fins serve only to steer.

Second: It is somewhat significant that while one sperm whale fights another only with his head and jaw, in his conflicts with man he chiefly and contemptuously uses his tail. In striking at a boat, he swiftly curves his flukes away from it, and the blow is delivered only by the recoil. If made in the unobstructed air, especially if it descends on its mark, the stroke is simply irresistible. No ribs of man or boat can withstand it. Your only salvation lies in dodging it. But if it comes sideways through the water, then partly owing to the light buoyancy of the whaleboat and the springiness of its materials, a cracked rib or a smashed plank or two — a sort of stitch in the side — is generally the worst of it. These underwater side-blows are so common in the fishery that they are considered child's play. Someone strips off a shirt, and the hole is plugged.

Third: I cannot prove it, but it seems to me that in the whale the sense of touch is concentrated in the tail. In this respect, there is a delicacy in it matched only by the daintiness of the elephant's trunk. This sensitivity is chiefly shown in the action of sweeping, when with maidenly gentleness the whale slowly moves his immense flukes from side to side upon the surface of the sea. And if he feels but a sailor's whisker — woe to that sailor, whiskers and all. What tenderness there is in that preliminary touch! Had this tail any grasping power, I should think of Darmonodes' elephant that so frequented the flower market and with low bows presented bouquets to young ladies, then caressed their waists. On more accounts than one, it is a pity the whale does not possess this grasping ability. For I have heard of yet another elephant that, when wounded in a fight, curved its trunk around and extracted the dart.

Fourth: Coming upon the whale unawares in the fancied security of the open seas, you find him unbent from the vast dignity of his bulk, and kittenlike, he plays on the ocean as if it were a hearth. But still you see his power in his play. The broad palms of his tail are flipped high into the air, then brought smiting down upon the surface — the thunderous concussion resounding for miles. You would almost think a cannon had been fired. And if you noticed the light wreath of vapor from the blowhole at his other end, you would think that was the smoke from the touch-hole.

Fifth: In his normal floating posture, the leviathan's flukes lie considerably below the level of his back, completely out of sight beneath the surface. But when he is about to plunge into the depths, his entire flukes and at least thirty feet of his body are tossed erect in the air, remaining there vibrating a moment before they shoot downward out of view. Except for the sublime breach — to be described elsewhere — this peaking of the whale's flukes is perhaps the grandest sight in all of living nature. Out of the bottomless deep, the gigantic tail seems to be spasmodically grasping at the highest heaven. So in dreams, I have seen majestic Satan thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flaming Baltic of Hell. But in gazing at such scenes, it all depends on your mood. If you are in the Dantean frame, devils will come to mind. If in that of Isaiah, archangels. Standing at the masthead of my ship during a sunrise that crimsoned sky and sea, I once saw a large herd of whales in the east, all heading toward the sun, and for a moment vibrating in concert with peaked flukes. As it seemed to me then, such a grand embodiment of adoration of the gods was never seen, even in Persia, the home of fire worshippers. As Ptolemy Philopater testified of the African elephant, I then testified of the whale, pronouncing him the most devout of all beings. For according to King Juba, the military elephants of antiquity often hailed the morning with their trunks uplifted in the most profound silence.

The casual comparison in this chapter between the whale and the elephant — so far as some aspects of the tail of the one and the trunk of the other are concerned — should not suggest those two organs are equal, much less the creatures they belong to. For as the mightiest elephant is but a terrier to Leviathan, so compared with Leviathan's tail, his trunk is but the stalk of a lily. The most dreadful blow from the elephant's trunk would be as the playful tap of a fan compared with the measureless crush and crash of the sperm whale's ponderous flukes, which have repeatedly hurled entire boats with all their oars and crews into the air, much as an Indian juggler tosses his balls.*

*Though all comparison in general bulk between the whale and the elephant is absurd — inasmuch as in that regard the elephant stands in much the same relation to the whale as a dog does to the elephant — nevertheless, there are some points of curious similarity. Among these is the spout. It is well known that the elephant will often draw up water or dust in his trunk, and then, elevating it, jet it forth in a stream.

The more I consider this mighty tail, the more I deplore my inability to express it. At times there are gestures in it that, though they would well grace the hand of man, remain wholly inexplicable. In an extensive herd, so remarkable are these mystic gestures that I have heard hunters declare them akin to Freemason signs and symbols — that the whale, by these methods, was intelligently conversing with the world. Nor are there lacking other motions of the whale in his general body, full of strangeness and unaccountable to his most experienced pursuer. Dissect him how I may, then, I only go skin deep. I do not know him, and never will. But if I cannot even understand the tail of this whale, how can I understand his head? Much more, how can I comprehend his face, when he has none? You shall see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen. But I cannot fully make out his back parts either. And hint what he will about his face — I say again he has no face.

chapters.title: Chapter 87 — The Grand Armada
paragraphs: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast wall, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several passages for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

Those narrow Straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java. Standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory known to seamen as Java Head, they closely resemble the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire. And considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that eastern sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance — however ineffective — of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis. Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships that for centuries past, by night and day, have passed between Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive such ceremony, they by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.

Since time out of mind, the pirate boats of the Malays, lurking among the low, shaded coves and islets of Sumatra, have sailed out upon passing vessels, fiercely demanding tribute at spear-point. Though by repeated bloody punishments at the hands of European warships their boldness has of late been somewhat checked, even now we occasionally hear of English and American vessels that have been ruthlessly boarded and plundered in those waters.

With a fair, fresh wind, the Pequod was now drawing near to these straits. Ahab intended to pass through them into the Java Sea, and thence, cruising northward over waters known to be frequented by the sperm whale, sweep inshore by the Philippine Islands and reach the far coast of Japan in time for the great whaling season there. By this route, the circumnavigating Pequod would sweep almost all the known sperm whale cruising grounds of the world before descending upon the equator in the Pacific — where Ahab, though everywhere else frustrated in his pursuit, firmly counted on giving battle to Moby Dick in the sea he was most known to frequent, at a season when he might most reasonably be expected to haunt it.

But how now? In this far-ranging quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Mark this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

Now, as many sperm whales had been captured off the western coast of Java, near the Straits of Sunda, and since most of the surrounding waters were generally recognized by fishermen as an excellent cruising ground, the Pequod's lookouts were repeatedly hailed and warned to stay wide awake as she gained upon Java Head. But though the green palmy cliffs of the land soon loomed on the starboard bow, and with delighted nostrils the fresh cinnamon was sniffed in the air, yet not a single spout was sighted. Almost giving up all thought of finding any whales in these parts, the ship had nearly entered the straits when the customary cheering cry was heard from aloft, and before long a spectacle of singular magnificence greeted us.

But here it must be noted that owing to the relentless activity with which sperm whales have lately been hunted over all four oceans, they now frequently gather in extensive herds, instead of almost invariably sailing in small, separate groups as in former times. Sometimes these herds embrace so great a multitude that it would almost seem as if numerous nations of them had sworn a solemn pact for mutual assistance and protection. To this massing of sperm whales may be attributed the fact that even in the best cruising grounds, you may now sometimes sail for weeks and months without being greeted by a single spout — and then be suddenly confronted by what seems thousands upon thousands.

Broad on both bows, at a distance of two or three miles, forming a great semicircle that embraced one half of the level horizon, a continuous chain of whale-spouts was playing and sparkling in the noonday air. Unlike the straight perpendicular twin-jets of the right whale, which divide at the top and fall over in two branches like the drooping boughs of a willow, the single forward-slanting spout of the sperm whale presents a thick curled bush of white mist, continually rising and falling away to leeward.

Seen from the Pequod's deck as she would rise on a high hill of the sea, this host of vapory spouts, individually curling up into the air and viewed through a blending atmosphere of bluish haze, looked like the thousand cheerful chimneys of some dense city, glimpsed on a balmy autumn morning by some horseman on a hill.

As marching armies approaching an unfriendly mountain pass accelerate their march, all eagerness to put that perilous passage behind them and once more expand in comparative safety upon the plain — even so did this vast fleet of whales now seem hurrying forward through the straits, gradually contracting the wings of their semicircle and swimming on in one solid but still crescent-shaped formation.

Crowding on all sail, the Pequod pressed after them. The harpooners handled their weapons and cheered loudly from the bows of their still-suspended boats. If the wind only held, they had little doubt that chased through these Straits of Sunda, the vast host would only spread out into the eastern seas to witness the capture of not a few of their number. And who could tell whether, in that gathered caravan, Moby Dick himself might not be temporarily swimming, like the worshipped white elephant in a Siamese coronation procession! So with every sail set, we drove these leviathans before us — when suddenly, the voice of Tashtego was heard, loudly directing attention to something in our wake.

Corresponding to the crescent ahead of us, we saw another behind us. It seemed formed of detached white vapors, rising and falling somewhat like whale-spouts, only they did not fully come and go but constantly hovered without quite disappearing. Leveling his glass at this sight, Ahab quickly spun in his pivot-hole, crying: "Aloft there, and rig whips and buckets to wet the sails! Malays, sir, and after us!"

As if lurking too long behind the headlands, waiting until the Pequod had fairly entered the straits, these rascally Asians were now in hot pursuit to make up for their overcautious delay. But when the swift Pequod, with a fresh leading wind, was herself in hot chase — how very kind of these tawny philanthropists to help speed her on to her own chosen pursuit, serving as mere riding-crops and spurs to her. As Ahab paced the deck with glass under arm, in his forward turn beholding the monsters he chased and in his backward turn the bloodthirsty pirates chasing him — some such thought seemed his. And when he glanced upon the green walls of the watery passage through which the ship was sailing, and considered that through that gate lay the route to his vengeance, and saw how through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end — and not only that, but a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on with their curses — when all these thoughts had passed through his brain, Ahab's brow was left gaunt and furrowed, like a black sand beach after some stormy tide has been gnawing it without being able to drag the firm thing from its place.

But thoughts like these troubled very few of the reckless crew. When, after steadily dropping the pirates astern, the Pequod at last shot past the vivid green Cockatoo Point on the Sumatra side, emerging upon the broad waters beyond, the harpooners seemed more grieved that the swift whales had been gaining on the ship than glad that the ship had so victoriously gained upon the Malays. But still driving on in the whales' wake, at length they seemed to slow their speed. Gradually the ship neared them. The wind dying away, word was passed to launch the boats. But no sooner did the herd — by some wonderful instinct of the sperm whale — become aware of the three boats coming after them, though still a mile behind, than they rallied again. Forming in close ranks and battalions, so that their spouts all looked like flashing lines of stacked bayonets, they moved on with redoubled speed.

Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the battle against Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. Best, therefore, withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

Though many of the whales, as has been said, were in violent motion, as a whole the herd neither advanced nor retreated but collectively remained in one place. As is customary in such cases, the boats separated at once, each making for some lone whale on the outskirts of the shoal. In about three minutes, Queequeg's harpoon was flung. The stricken whale darted blinding spray in our faces, then ran away with us like light, steering straight for the heart of the herd. Though such a move by a harpooned whale is by no means unprecedented and indeed is almost always expected to some degree, it presents one of the more dangerous episodes of the fishery. For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid farewell to cautious living and exist only in a delirious rush.

As, blind and deaf, the whale plunged forward, as if by sheer speed to rid himself of the iron leech fastened to him — as we tore a white gash in the sea, menaced on all sides by the crazed creatures rushing to and fro around us — our beset boat was like a ship mobbed by icebergs in a tempest, striving to steer through their complicated channels and straits, not knowing at what moment it might be locked in and crushed.

But not a bit daunted, Queequeg steered us expertly — now sheering off from this monster directly across our route, now edging away from that one whose colossal flukes were suspended overhead — while all the time Starbuck stood in the bow, lance in hand, pricking aside whatever whales he could reach with short thrusts, for there was no time for long ones. Nor were the oarsmen quite idle, though their usual duty was now entirely suspended. They chiefly attended to the shouting part of the business. "Out of the way, Commodore!" cried one to a great whale that suddenly rose bodily to the surface and for an instant threatened to swamp us. "Hard down with your tail, there!" cried a second to another that, close to our gunwale, seemed calmly cooling himself with his own fan-like extremity.

All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called drags. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is attached to the middle of this block, and the other end, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drag is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so when you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence the drag comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drag. They were hampered like prisoners with chain and ball. But upon flinging the third, the clumsy wooden block caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three shirts in and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

It would have been nearly impossible to throw these drag-harpoons had our whale's pace not greatly slowed as we advanced into the herd. Moreover, as we went still further from the circumference of commotion, the chaos seemed to be waning. So when at last the jerking harpoon pulled free and the towing whale vanished sideways, we glided with the tapering force of his parting momentum between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal — as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake. Here the storms raging in the gaps between the outermost whales were heard but not felt. In this central expanse, the sea presented that smooth satin-like surface called a sleek, produced by the subtle moisture thrown off by the whale in his quieter moods. Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion. And still in the distracted distance we saw the tumults of the outer concentric circles — successive pods of whales, eight or ten in each, swiftly going round and round like multiplied teams of horses in a ring, so closely shoulder to shoulder that a titanic circus-rider might easily have arched over the middle ones and ridden round on their backs. Owing to the density of the whales reposing more immediately around the trapped center of the herd, no possible chance of escape was presently offered to us. We had to watch for a breach in the living wall that hemmed us in — the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up. Keeping to the center of the lake, we were occasionally visited by small, tame cows and calves: the women and children of this routed host.

Now, including the occasional wide intervals between the revolving outer circles and the spaces between the various pods in any one of those circles, the entire area at this point must have contained at least two or three square miles. At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because, as if the cows and calves had been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and as if the wide extent of the herd had prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping — or possibly, being so young, innocent, and inexperienced — however it may have been, these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at. Like household dogs, they came snuffling right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.
