But far beneath this wondrous world upon the surface, another and still stranger world met our eyes as we gazed over the side. For suspended in those watery vaults floated the forms of nursing mother whales, and those that by their enormous girth seemed shortly to become mothers. The lake, as I have hinted, was to a considerable depth exceedingly transparent. And as human infants while suckling will calmly and fixedly gaze away from the breast, as if leading two different lives at the same time — while yet drawing mortal nourishment, still spiritually feasting upon some unearthly memory — even so did the young of these whales seem to look up toward us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of seaweed in their newborn sight. Floating on their sides, the mothers also seemed quietly eyeing us. One of these little infants, that from certain signs seemed hardly a day old, might have measured some fourteen feet in length and six feet around. He was a little frisky, though his body seemed scarcely recovered from the cramped position it had so recently occupied in the womb, where, tail to head and all ready for the final spring, the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar's bow. The delicate side-fins and the palms of his flukes still freshly retained the plaited, crumpled appearance of a baby's ears newly arrived from foreign parts.
"Line! Line!" cried Queequeg, looking over the gunwale. "Him fast! Him fast! Who line him? Who struck? Two whale — one big, one little!"
"What ails you, man?" cried Starbuck.
"Look here," said Queequeg, pointing down.

As when the struck whale that from the tub has reeled out hundreds of fathoms of rope — as, after deep sounding, he floats up again and shows the slackened curling line buoyantly rising and spiraling toward the air — so now Starbuck saw long coils of the umbilical cord of Madame Leviathan, by which the young cub seemed still tethered to its mother. Not seldom in the rapid turns of the chase, this natural line, with the maternal end loose, becomes entangled with the hemp one, so that the cub is trapped. Some of the subtlest secrets of the seas seemed revealed to us in this enchanted pond. We saw young Leviathan courtship in the deep.*

*The sperm whale, like all other species of Leviathan but unlike most other fish, breeds indiscriminately at all seasons. After a gestation that may probably be set at nine months, it produces but one at a time, though in some few known instances giving birth to twins — a contingency provided for in suckling by two teats, curiously situated one on each side of the anus, though the breasts themselves extend upward from that point. When by chance these parts in a nursing whale are cut by the hunter's lance, the mother's pouring milk and blood discolor the sea in rivaling streams for yards. The milk is very sweet and rich. It has been tasted by man, and it might go well with strawberries. When overflowing with mutual affection, the whales greet each other in human fashion.

And thus, though surrounded by circle upon circle of terrors and frights, did these inscrutable creatures at the center freely and fearlessly indulge in all peaceful pursuits — yea, serenely reveling in tenderness and delight. But even so, amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still forever centrally float in mute calm. And while ponderous planets of unceasing woe revolve around me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe myself in an eternal mildness of joy.

Meanwhile, as we lay entranced, the occasional sudden frantic scenes in the distance showed the activity of the other boats, still engaged in dragging the whales on the frontier of the host, or possibly carrying on the war within the first circle, where there was room enough and some convenient retreats. But the sight of the enraged dragged whales now and then blindly darting to and fro across the circles was nothing to what at last met our eyes. It is sometimes the custom, when fast to a whale more than usually powerful and alert, to try to hamstring him by severing or maiming his gigantic tail-tendon. This is done by throwing a short-handled cutting-spade with a rope attached for hauling it back. A whale wounded in this way — as we afterward learned — but not effectively, had broken away from the boat, carrying along with him half of the harpoon line. In the extraordinary agony of the wound, he was now dashing among the revolving circles like the lone mounted desperado Arnold at the Battle of Saratoga, carrying dismay wherever he went.

But agonizing as this whale's wound was, and appalling a spectacle in itself, the peculiar horror he seemed to inspire in the rest of the herd was owing to a cause which at first the intervening distance hid from us. But at length we saw that by one of the unimaginable accidents of the fishery, this whale had become entangled in the harpoon line he towed. He had also run off with the cutting-spade in him. While the free end of the rope attached to that weapon had permanently caught in the coils of the harpoon line wound around his tail, the cutting-spade itself had worked loose from his flesh. So, tormented to madness, he was now churning through the water, violently flailing with his flexible tail and tossing the keen spade about him, wounding and killing his own companions.

This terrific sight seemed to rouse the whole herd from their frozen fright. First, the whales forming the margin of our lake began to crowd a little and jostle against each other, as if lifted by spent waves from afar. Then the lake itself began faintly to heave and swell. The submarine nurseries and bridal chambers vanished. In tighter and tighter orbits, the whales in the more central circles began to swim in thickening clusters. Yes, the long calm was departing. A low advancing hum was soon heard. And then, like the tumultuous masses of block-ice when the great river Hudson breaks up in spring, the entire host of whales came tumbling upon their inner center, as if to pile themselves up in one common mountain. Instantly Starbuck and Queequeg changed places, Starbuck taking the stern.

"Oars! Oars!" he intensely whispered, seizing the helm. "Grip your oars and clench your souls now! My God, men, stand by! Shove him off, Queequeg — the whale there! Prick him! Hit him! Stand up — stand up, and stay so! Spring, men — pull, men! Never mind their backs — scrape them! Scrape away!"

The boat was now all but jammed between two vast black hulks, leaving a narrow strait between their long bodies. But by desperate effort we at last shot into a temporary opening, then pulled hard, earnestly watching for another way out. After many similar narrow escapes, we at last swiftly glided into what had just been one of the outer circles but was now crossed by random whales, all violently making for the center. This lucky escape was cheaply purchased by the loss of Queequeg's hat, which, while he stood in the bow pricking the fleeing whales, was snatched clean from his head by the air-current made by the sudden tossing of a pair of broad flukes close by.

Riotous and disordered as the universal commotion now was, it soon resolved itself into what seemed a systematic movement. Having clumped together at last in one dense body, the whales renewed their forward flight with increased speed. Further pursuit was useless, but the boats still lingered in their wake to pick up whatever dragged whales might be dropped behind, and also to secure one that Flask had killed and marked. The mark is a pennanted pole, two or three of which are carried by every boat. When additional prey is at hand, these are inserted upright into the floating body of a dead whale, both to mark its place on the sea and as a token of prior possession, should the boats of any other ship draw near.

The result of this hunt was somewhat illustrative of that wise saying in the fishery: the more whales, the less fish. Of all the dragged whales, only one was captured. The rest managed to escape for the time, but only to be taken, as will later be seen, by some other vessel than the Pequod.

chapters.title: Chapter 88 — Schools and Schoolmasters
paragraphs: The previous chapter gave an account of an immense body or herd of sperm whales, and there was also given the probable cause behind those vast gatherings.

Now, though such great bodies are at times encountered, as has been seen, even today small separate bands are occasionally observed, ranging from twenty to fifty individuals each. Such bands are known as schools. They are generally of two sorts: those composed almost entirely of females, and those mustering none but young, vigorous males — or bulls, as they are familiarly called.

In gallant attendance upon the school of females, you invariably see a male of full-grown size, but not old, who upon any alarm shows his chivalry by falling to the rear and covering the flight of his ladies. In truth, this gentleman is a luxurious sultan, swimming about the watery world, surrounded by all the comforts and pleasures of the harem. The contrast between this sultan and his consorts is striking, because while he is always of the largest proportions, the ladies, even at full growth, are not more than one-third the bulk of an average-sized male. They are comparatively delicate, indeed — I daresay not exceeding half a dozen yards around the waist. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that on the whole they are hereditarily entitled to plumpness.

It is very curious to watch this harem and its lord in their indolent wanderings. Like fashionable society, they are forever on the move in leisurely search of variety. You meet them on the equator in time for the full bloom of the feeding season, having just returned perhaps from spending the summer in the northern seas, and so cheating summer of all its unpleasant weariness and warmth. By the time they have lounged up and down the equatorial promenade awhile, they start for the eastern waters in anticipation of the cool season there, and so evade the other excessive temperature of the year.

When serenely traveling on one of these journeys, if any strange suspicious sights are seen, the lord whale keeps a wary eye on his interesting family. Should any rudely bold young Leviathan happen that way and presume to draw confidentially close to one of the ladies — with what prodigious fury the lord assails him and chases him away! High times indeed, if unprincipled young rakes like him are to be permitted to invade the sanctity of domestic bliss. Though do what the lord will, he cannot keep the most notorious seducer out of his bed, for alas, all fish bed in common. As on shore, the ladies often cause the most terrible duels among their rival admirers. Just so with the whales, who sometimes come to deadly battle, and all for love. They fence with their long lower jaws, sometimes locking them together and striving for supremacy like elks that warring interweave their antlers. Not a few are captured bearing the deep scars of these encounters: furrowed heads, broken teeth, scalloped fins, and in some instances wrenched and dislocated mouths.

But suppose the invader of domestic bliss takes himself away at the first rush of the harem's lord. Then it is very amusing to watch that lord. Gently he insinuates his vast bulk among them again and revels there awhile, still in tantalizing proximity to young Lothario, like pious Solomon devoutly worshipping among his thousand concubines. Granting other whales to be in sight, the fishermen will seldom give chase to one of these grand sultans, for these grand sultans are too lavish with their strength, and hence their oil-yield is small. As for the sons and daughters they beget, those sons and daughters must take care of themselves — at least with only the mother's help. For like certain other roving lovers that might be named, the lord whale has no taste for the nursery, however much for the bower. And so, being a great traveler, he leaves his anonymous babies all over the world, every baby an exotic. In good time, nevertheless, as the ardor of youth declines — as years and gloom increase, as reflection lends her solemn pauses — in short, as a general weariness overtakes the sated sultan, a love of ease and virtue replaces the love of maidens. Our lord enters upon the impotent, repentant, lecturing stage of life, forswears and disbands the harem, and grown to an exemplary, sulky old soul, goes about all alone among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers and warning each young Leviathan from his amorous errors.

Now, as the harem of whales is called by the fishermen a school, so is the lord and master of that school technically known as the schoolmaster. It is therefore not in strict character — however admirably satirical — that after going to school himself, he should then go abroad teaching not what he learned there but the folly of it. His title of schoolmaster would very naturally seem derived from the name of the harem itself. But some have guessed that the man who first gave this name to this sort of sultan whale must have read the memoirs of Vidocq, and informed himself what sort of country schoolmaster that famous Frenchman was in his younger days, and what was the nature of those secret lessons he taught some of his pupils.

The same seclusion and isolation to which the schoolmaster whale retreats in his advancing years is true of all aged sperm whales. Almost universally, a lone whale — as a solitary Leviathan is called — proves to be an ancient one. Like the venerable moss-bearded Daniel Boone, he will have no one near him but Nature herself. And her he takes to wife in the wilderness of waters — and the best of wives she is, though she keeps so many moody secrets.

The schools composed of nothing but young, vigorous males, previously mentioned, offer a strong contrast to the harem schools. For while those female whales are characteristically timid, the young males — or forty-barrel-bulls, as they call them — are by far the most combative of all Leviathans and proverbially the most dangerous to encounter, excepting those wondrous gray-headed, grizzled whales sometimes met, who will fight you like grim fiends aggravated by gout.

The forty-barrel-bull schools are larger than the harem schools. Like a mob of young college men, they are full of fight, fun, and mischief, tumbling round the world at such a reckless, rollicking rate that no prudent insurance man would cover them any more than he would a riotous student at Yale or Harvard. They soon outgrow this wildness, though, and when about three-quarters grown, they break up and separately go about in quest of settlements — that is, harems.

Another difference between the male and female schools is still more characteristic of the sexes. Say you strike a forty-barrel-bull: poor devil! All his comrades abandon him. But strike a member of the harem school, and her companions swim around her with every sign of concern, sometimes lingering so near and so long as to fall prey themselves.

chapters.title: Chapter 89 — Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
paragraphs: The mention of the marker-pole in the chapter before last calls for some account of the laws and regulations of the whale fishery, of which the marker may be considered the grand symbol and badge.

It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would constantly arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

Perhaps the only formal whaling code authorized by legislation was that of Holland, decreed by the States-General in 1695. But though no other nation has ever had any written whaling law, the American fishermen have been their own legislators and lawyers in this matter. They have provided a system which for terse completeness surpasses Justinian's Pandects and the bylaws of the Chinese Society for the Suppression of Meddling with Other People's Business. Yes, these laws might be engraved on a Queen Anne's farthing, or the barb of a harpoon, and worn around the neck, so small are they.
I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
II. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it.
But what causes trouble with this masterful code is the admirable brevity of it, which requires a vast volume of commentary to explain it.

First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a marker or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the marking party plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

These are the learned commentaries. But the commentaries of the whalemen themselves sometimes consist of hard words and harder knocks — the fists doing the arguing. True, among the more upright and honorable whalemen, allowances are always made for special cases where it would be an outrageous moral injustice for one party to claim possession of a whale previously chased or killed by another. But others are by no means so scrupulous.

Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when they had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally claimed it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of celebration, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. Wherefore the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

Mr. Erskine was counsel for the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine went on to illustrate his position by alluding to a recent adultery case, in which a gentleman, after in vain trying to curb his wife's unfaithfulness, had at last abandoned her upon the seas of life. But in the course of years, repenting of that step, he brought an action to recover possession of her. Erskine was on the other side and had then supported the case by saying that though the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and had once had her fast, and only by reason of the great force of her wayward plunging had at last abandoned her — yet abandon her he did, so that she became a Loose-Fish. And therefore when a subsequent gentleman re-harpooned her, the lady then became that subsequent gentleman's property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her.
Now in the present case Erskine argued that the examples of the whale and the lady were mutually illustrative of each other.

These arguments and counter-arguments being duly heard, the very learned judge officially decided as follows: As for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives. But with regard to the disputed whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants — the whale because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture, and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it acquired property in those articles, and hence anybody who afterward took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterward took the fish; therefore, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

An ordinary man looking at this decision of the very learned judge might possibly object to it. But plowed down to the bedrock of the matter, the two great principles laid down in the twin whaling laws previously quoted — applied and explained by Lord Ellenborough in the above-cited case — these two laws touching Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish will, on reflection, be found the fundamentals of all human law. For notwithstanding its complicated decorative sculpture, the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two pillars to stand on.

Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and American slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last penny but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a nameplate for a marker — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of a hundred thousand pounds, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that vast sum but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?
But if the doctrine of Fast-Fish is pretty generally applicable, the kindred doctrine of Loose-Fish is still more widely so. It is internationally and universally applicable.

What was America in 1492 but a Loose-Fish, in which Columbus struck the Spanish standard by way of marking it for his royal master and mistress? What was Poland to the Czar? What Greece to the Turk? What India to England? What at last will Mexico be to the United States? All Loose-Fish.

What are the Rights of Man and the Liberties of the World but Loose-Fish? What all men's minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish? What to the pompous pedantic quibblers are the thoughts of thinkers but Loose-Fish? What is the great globe itself but a Loose-Fish? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish, too?

chapters.title: Chapter 90 — Heads or Tails
paragraphs: "De balena vero sufficit, si rex habeat caput, et regina caudam." — Bracton, l. 3, c. 3.

Latin from the books of the Laws of England, which taken with the context means that of all whales captured by anybody on the coast of that land, the King, as Honorary Grand Harpooner, must have the head, and the Queen be respectfully presented with the tail. A division which, in the whale, is much like halving an apple — there is no remainder. Now as this law, under a modified form, is to this day in force in England, and as it offers in various respects a strange anomaly touching the general law of Fast and Loose Fish, it is here treated in a separate chapter, on the same courteous principle that prompts the English railways to provide a separate car specially reserved for royalty. In the first place, as curious proof that the above-mentioned law is still in force, I proceed to lay before you something that happened within the last two years.

It seems that some honest sailors of Dover, or Sandwich, or some one of the Cinque Ports, had after a hard chase succeeded in killing and beaching a fine whale which they had originally spotted far off from the shore. Now the Cinque Ports are partially or somehow under the jurisdiction of a sort of policeman or official called a Lord Warden. Holding the office directly from the crown, I believe, all the royal revenues from the Cinque Port territories become his by assignment. Some writers call this office a sinecure. But not so. Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in pocketing his privileges — which are his chiefly by virtue of that same pocketing of them.

Now when these poor sun-burnt sailors, barefoot and with their trousers rolled high up on their weather-beaten legs, had wearily hauled their fat fish high and dry, promising themselves a good hundred and fifty pounds from the precious oil and bone — and in their imaginations already sipping fine tea with their wives and good ale with their friends, upon the strength of their respective shares — up steps a very learned and most Christian and charitable gentleman, with a copy of Blackstone under his arm. Laying it upon the whale's head, he says: "Hands off! This fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish. I seize it as the Lord Warden's." Upon this, the poor sailors in their respectful consternation — so truly English — knowing not what to say, fell to vigorously scratching their heads all round, meanwhile ruefully glancing from the whale to the stranger. But that did nothing to mend the matter or soften the hard heart of the learned gentleman with his copy of Blackstone. At length one of them, after long scratching about for his ideas, made bold to speak:
"Please, sir, who is the Lord Warden?"
"The Duke."
"But the Duke had nothing to do with taking this fish?"
"It is his."
"We have been at great trouble and peril and some expense, and is all that to go to the Duke's benefit — we getting nothing at all for our pains but our blisters?"
"It is his."
"Is the Duke so very poor as to be forced to this desperate way of getting a livelihood?"
"It is his."
"I thought to relieve my old bed-ridden mother by part of my share of this whale."
"It is his."
"Won't the Duke be content with a quarter or a half?"
"It is his."

In a word, the whale was seized and sold, and his Grace the Duke of Wellington received the money. Thinking that viewed in certain lights the case might by a bare possibility in some small degree be deemed, under the circumstances, a rather hard one, an honest clergyman of the town respectfully addressed a note to his Grace, begging him to take the case of those unfortunate sailors into full consideration. To which the Duke in substance replied — both letters were published — that he had already done so, and received the money, and would be obliged to the reverend gentleman if in the future he would decline meddling with other people's business. Is this the still-militant old man, standing at the corners of the three kingdoms, on all hands demanding charity from beggars?

It will readily be seen that in this case the Duke's alleged right to the whale was a delegated one from the Sovereign. We must then inquire on what principle the Sovereign is originally invested with that right. The law itself has already been set forth. But Plowdon gives us the reason for it. Says Plowdon, the whale so caught belongs to the King and Queen "because of its superior excellence." And by the soundest commentators this has ever been held a compelling argument in such matters.
But why should the King have the head and the Queen the tail? A reason for that, you lawyers!

In his treatise on "Queen-Gold," or Queen's pin-money, an old King's Bench author, one William Prynne, writes thus: "The tail is the Queen's, that the Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with whalebone." Now this was written at a time when the black limber bone of the Greenland or right whale was widely used in ladies' corsets. But this same bone is not in the tail; it is in the head — which is a sad mistake for a learned lawyer like Prynne. But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.

There are two royal fish so styled by the English law writers: the whale and the sturgeon, both royal property under certain limitations, and nominally supplying the tenth branch of the crown's ordinary revenue. I know not that any other author has hinted at the matter, but by inference it seems to me that the sturgeon must be divided in the same way as the whale, the King receiving the highly dense and elastic head peculiar to that fish — which, symbolically considered, may possibly be humorously based on some presumed resemblance. And thus there seems a reason in all things, even in law.

chapters.title: Chapter 91 — The Pequod Meets The Rose-Bud
paragraphs: "In vain it was to rake for Ambergris in the paunch of this Leviathan, insufferable stench denying not inquiry." — Sir T. Browne, V.E.

It was a week or two after the last whaling scene recounted, and when we were slowly sailing over a sleepy, hazy, midday sea, that the many noses on the Pequod's deck proved more vigilant discoverers than the three pairs of eyes aloft. A peculiar and not very pleasant smell was detected in the sea.
"I'll bet something now," said Stubb, "that somewhere nearby are some of those dragged whales we stabbed the other day. I thought they'd turn belly-up before long."

Presently, the haze ahead slid aside, and there in the distance lay a ship whose furled sails indicated that some sort of whale must be alongside. As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colors from her peak. And by the eddying cloud of vulture sea-birds that circled, hovered, and swooped around her, it was plain that the whale alongside must be what the fishermen call a blasted whale — that is, a whale that has died unmolested on the sea and so floated as an unclaimed corpse. You can well imagine what an unsavory odor such a mass must give off — worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living cannot bury the dead. So intolerable is it considered by some that no greed could persuade them to moor alongside it. Yet there are those who will still do it, notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of rose-water.

Coming still nearer with the dying breeze, we saw that the Frenchman had a second whale alongside. This second whale seemed even more of a stench-bouquet than the first. In truth, it turned out to be one of those problematical whales that seem to dry up and die with a sort of prodigious indigestion, leaving their dead bodies almost entirely bankrupt of anything like oil. Nevertheless, in the proper place we shall see that no knowledgeable fisherman will ever turn up his nose at such a whale as this, however much he may shun blasted whales in general.
The Pequod had now swept so close to the stranger that Stubb swore he recognized his cutting spade-pole entangled in the lines knotted around the tail of one of these whales.

"There's a pretty fellow now," he banteringly laughed, standing in the ship's bow. "There's a jackal for you! I well know that these Frenchmen are poor devils in the fishery — sometimes lowering their boats for breakers, mistaking them for sperm whale spouts. Yes, and sometimes sailing from their port with their hold full of tallow candles and cases of snuffers, foreseeing that all the oil they'll get won't be enough to dip the captain's wick into. Aye, we all know these things. But look here, here's a Frenchman that is content with our leavings — the dragged whale there, I mean. Aye, and content too with scraping the dry bones of that other precious fish he has there. Poor devil! Pass round a hat, someone, and let's make him a present of a little oil for dear charity's sake. For what oil he'll get from that dragged whale there wouldn't be fit to burn in a jail — no, not in a condemned cell. And as for the other whale, why, I'll agree to get more oil by chopping up and boiling out these three masts of ours than he'll get from that bundle of bones. Though, now that I think of it, it may contain something worth a good deal more than oil. Yes — ambergris. I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It's worth trying. Yes, I'm for it." And so saying he started for the quarter-deck.

By this time the faint breeze had become a complete calm, so that like it or not, the Pequod was now fairly trapped in the smell, with no hope of escaping unless the wind picked up again. Coming out of the cabin, Stubb called his boat's crew and pulled off for the stranger. Drawing across her bow, he saw that in accordance with the fanciful French taste, the upper part of her stem-piece was carved in the likeness of a huge drooping stalk, was painted green, and for thorns had copper spikes projecting from it here and there — the whole terminating in a symmetrical folded bulb of a bright red color. Upon her headboards, in large gilt letters, he read "Bouton de Rose" — Rose-button, or Rose-bud. And this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship.
Though Stubb did not understand the "Bouton" part of the inscription, the word "rose" and the bulbous figurehead put together sufficiently explained the whole to him.
"A wooden rose-bud, eh?" he cried with his hand to his nose. "That will do very well. But how like all creation it smells!"
Now in order to communicate directly with the people on deck, he had to pull around the bow to the starboard side, and thus come close to the blasted whale and talk over it.
Arriving at this spot, with one hand still to his nose, he bawled: "Bouton-de-Rose, ahoy! Are there any of you Bouton-de-Roses that speak English?"
"Yes," replied a Guernseyman from the bulwarks, who turned out to be the chief mate.
"Well then, my Bouton-de-Rose-bud, have you seen the White Whale?"
"What whale?"
"The White Whale — a sperm whale — Moby Dick. Have you seen him?"
"Never heard of such a whale. Cachalot Blanche! White Whale — no."
"Very good, then. Goodbye now, and I'll call again in a minute."

Then rapidly pulling back toward the Pequod, and seeing Ahab leaning over the quarter-deck rail awaiting his report, he cupped his two hands into a trumpet and shouted: "No, sir! No!" Upon which Ahab retired, and Stubb returned to the Frenchman.
He now noticed that the Guernseyman, who had just gotten into the chains and was using a cutting-spade, had slung his nose in a sort of bag.
"What's the matter with your nose there?" said Stubb. "Broken it?"
"I wish it was broken, or that I didn't have any nose at all!" answered the Guernseyman, who did not seem to relish the job he was at very much. "But what are you holding yours for?"
"Oh, nothing! It's a wax nose — I have to hold it on. Fine day, isn't it? Air rather garden-like, I should say. Throw us a bunch of posies, will you, Bouton-de-Rose?"
"What in the devil's name do you want here?" roared the Guernseyman, flying into a sudden rage.

"Oh, keep cool — cool? Yes, that's the word! Why don't you pack those whales in ice while you're working at them? But joking aside, though — do you know, Rose-bud, that it's all nonsense trying to get any oil out of such whales? As for that dried-up one there, he hasn't a drop in his whole carcass."

"I know that well enough. But, d'you see, the Captain here won't believe it. This is his first voyage — he was a Cologne manufacturer before. But come aboard, and maybe he'll believe you, if he won't believe me. And so I'll get out of this dirty mess."

"Anything to oblige you, my sweet and pleasant fellow," replied Stubb, and with that he soon climbed onto the deck. There a queer scene presented itself. The sailors, in tasseled caps of red yarn, were getting the heavy tackles ready for the whales. But they worked rather slowly and talked very fast, and seemed in anything but a good humor. All their noses projected upward from their faces like so many bowsprits. Now and then pairs of them would drop their work and run up to the masthead to get some fresh air. Some, thinking they would catch the plague, dipped oakum in coal-tar and at intervals held it to their nostrils. Others, having broken the stems of their pipes almost short off at the bowl, were vigorously puffing tobacco smoke so that it constantly filled their nostrils.

Stubb was struck by a shower of outcries and curses coming from the captain's cabin aft. Looking in that direction, he saw a fiery face thrust from behind the door, which was held slightly open from within. This was the tormented surgeon, who after in vain protesting against the day's proceedings, had retreated to the captain's cabin to avoid the stench — but still could not help yelling out his pleas and objections from time to time.

Noting all this, Stubb saw his opportunity. Turning to the Guernseyman, he had a little chat with him, during which the mate expressed his contempt for his captain as a conceited fool who had brought them all into so stinking and unprofitable a mess. Sounding him carefully, Stubb further perceived that the Guernseyman had not the slightest suspicion concerning the ambergris. He therefore kept quiet on that subject, but otherwise was quite frank and friendly with him, so that the two quickly hatched a little plan for both outwitting and mocking the captain, without his at all suspecting their true intentions. According to this plan, the Guernseyman, under cover of being an interpreter, was to tell the captain whatever he pleased, but as if it came from Stubb. And as for Stubb, he was to utter whatever nonsense came to mind during the interview.

By this time their intended victim appeared from his cabin. He was a small, dark, but rather delicate-looking man for a sea-captain, with large whiskers and mustache, and he wore a red cotton velvet vest with watch-seals at his side. To this gentleman, Stubb was now politely introduced by the Guernseyman, who at once ostentatiously put on the manner of interpreting between them.
"What shall I say to him first?" said he.
"Why," said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, "you may as well begin by telling him that he looks sort of babyish to me, though I don't pretend to be a judge."

"He says, Monsieur," said the Guernseyman in French, turning to his captain, "that only yesterday his ship spoke a vessel whose captain and chief mate, with six sailors, had all died of a fever caught from a blasted whale they had brought alongside."
Upon this the captain started, and eagerly wanted to know more.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman to Stubb.
"Why, since he takes it so easily, tell him that now I've eyed him carefully, I'm quite certain that he's no more fit to command a whale-ship than a monkey. In fact, tell him from me he's a baboon."
"He vows and declares, Monsieur, that the other whale, the dried one, is far more deadly than the blasted one. In short, Monsieur, he begs us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish."
Instantly the captain ran forward, and in a loud voice commanded his crew to stop hoisting the cutting-tackles and at once cast loose the cables and chains confining the whales to the ship.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman, when the captain had returned to them.
"Why, let me see. Yes, you may as well tell him now that — that — in fact, tell him I've tricked him, and" — aside to himself — "perhaps somebody else."
"He says, Monsieur, that he's very happy to have been of any service to us."
Hearing this, the captain declared that they were the grateful parties — meaning himself and the mate — and concluded by inviting Stubb down to his cabin to drink a bottle of Bordeaux.
"He wants you to take a glass of wine with him," said the interpreter.
"Thank him heartily, but tell him it's against my principles to drink with the man I've tricked. In fact, tell him I must go."

"He says, Monsieur, that his principles won't admit of his drinking. But that if Monsieur wants to live another day to drink, then Monsieur had best drop all four boats and pull the ship away from these whales, for it's so calm they won't drift."

By this time Stubb was over the side, and getting into his boat, he hailed the Guernseyman to this effect: that having a long tow-line in his boat, he would do what he could to help them by pulling out the lighter whale from the ship's side. While the Frenchman's boats were engaged in towing the ship one way, Stubb benevolently towed his whale the other way, ostentatiously letting out an unusually long tow-line.

Presently a breeze sprang up. Stubb pretended to cast off from the whale. Hoisting his boats, the Frenchman soon increased his distance, while the Pequod slid in between him and Stubb's whale. Whereupon Stubb quickly pulled to the floating body, and hailing the Pequod to give notice of his intentions, at once proceeded to reap the fruit of his cunning trick. Seizing his sharp boat-spade, he commenced an excavation in the body, a little behind the side fin. You would almost have thought he was digging a cellar there in the sea. And when at length his spade struck against the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in rich English soil. His boat's crew were all in high excitement, eagerly helping their chief and looking as anxious as gold-hunters.

And all the time numberless birds were diving, ducking, screaming, yelling, and fighting around them. Stubb was beginning to look disappointed, especially as the horrible stench increased, when suddenly from out the very heart of this plague there stole a faint stream of perfume. It flowed through the tide of bad smells without being absorbed by it, as one river will flow into and along with another without at all blending with it for a time.
"I have it! I have it!" cried Stubb with delight, striking something in the underground regions. "A purse! A purse!"

Dropping his spade, he thrust both hands in and drew out handfuls of something that looked like ripe Windsor soap, or rich mottled old cheese — very oily and fragrant. You might easily dent it with your thumb. It is of a hue between yellow and ash-gray. And this, good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist. Some six handfuls were obtained. But more was unavoidably lost in the sea, and still more might have been secured were it not for impatient Ahab's loud command to Stubb to stop and come on board, else the ship would bid them goodbye.

chapters.title: Chapter 92 — Ambergris
paragraphs: Now this ambergris is a very curious substance, and so important as an article of commerce that in 1791 a certain Nantucket-born Captain Coffin was examined at the bar of the English House of Commons on the subject. For at that time, and indeed until comparatively recently, the precise origin of ambergris remained, like amber itself, a mystery to the learned. Though the word ambergris is merely the French compound for gray amber, the two substances are quite distinct. For amber, though at times found on the seacoast, is also dug up in some far inland soils, whereas ambergris is never found except upon the sea. Besides, amber is a hard, transparent, brittle, odorless substance, used for pipe mouthpieces, beads, and ornaments. But ambergris is soft, waxy, and so highly fragrant and spicy that it is widely used in perfumery, in pastilles, precious candles, hair-powders, and pomade. The Turks use it in cooking and also carry it to Mecca, for the same purpose that frankincense is carried to St. Peter's in Rome. Some wine merchants drop a few grains into claret to flavor it.

Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should treat themselves to an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale! Yet so it is. By some, ambergris is supposed to be the cause of the whale's indigestion, and by others the effect. How to cure such indigestion would be hard to say, unless by administering three or four boatloads of pills and then running out of harm's way, as laborers do when blasting rocks.

I have forgotten to say that there were found in this ambergris certain hard, round, bony plates, which at first Stubb thought might be sailors' trouser buttons. But it afterward turned out that they were nothing more than pieces of small squid bones embalmed in that manner.

Now that the incorruption of this most fragrant ambergris should be found in the heart of such decay — is this nothing? Think of that saying of St. Paul in Corinthians, about corruption and incorruption: how we are sown in dishonor but raised in glory. And likewise call to mind that saying of Paracelsus about what it is that makes the best musk. Also do not forget the strange fact that of all foul-smelling things, Cologne water, in its earliest manufacturing stages, is the worst.

I should like to conclude the chapter with the above appeal, but cannot, owing to my anxiety to refute a charge often made against whalemen, and which, in the estimation of some already biased minds, might be considered as indirectly supported by what has been said of the Frenchman's two whales. Elsewhere in this volume the slanderous claim has been disproved that the business of whaling is throughout a slovenly, untidy one. But there is another thing to address. They hint that all whales always smell bad. Now how did this nasty rumor originate?

I believe it is plainly traceable to the first arrival of the Greenland whaling ships in London, more than two centuries ago. Because those whalemen did not then, and do not now, render their oil at sea as the southern ships have always done. Instead, cutting up the fresh blubber in small bits, they thrust it through the bungholes of large casks and carry it home that way — the shortness of the season in those icy seas and the sudden, violent storms to which they are exposed forbidding any other course. The consequence is that upon breaking into the hold and unloading one of these whale cemeteries in the Greenland dock, a stench is released similar to that rising from excavating an old city graveyard for the foundations of a hospital.

I partly suspect also that this wicked charge against whalers may likewise be attributed to the existence on the coast of Greenland, in former times, of a Dutch village called Schmerenburgh or Smeerenberg — which latter name is the one used by the learned Fogo Von Slack in his great work on Smells, a textbook on that subject. As its name implies (smeer, fat; berg, to put up), this village was founded to provide a place for the blubber of the Dutch whale fleet to be rendered without being taken home to Holland. It was a collection of furnaces, fat-kettles, and oil sheds, and when the works were in full operation, they certainly gave off no very pleasant odor. But all this is quite different with a South Sea sperm whaler. In a voyage of perhaps four years, after completely filling her hold with oil, she does not perhaps spend fifty days in the business of boiling out. And in the state that it is casked, the oil is nearly scentless. The truth is that, living or dead, if but decently treated, whales as a species are by no means foul-smelling creatures. Nor can whalemen be detected, as the people of the Middle Ages claimed to detect a Jew in the company, by the nose. Nor indeed can the whale possibly be otherwise than fragrant, when, as a general thing, he enjoys such excellent health — taking abundant exercise, always out of doors, though, it is true, seldom in the open air. I say that the motion of a sperm whale's flukes above water gives off a perfume, as when a musk-scented lady rustles her dress in a warm parlor. What then shall I liken the sperm whale to for fragrance, considering his magnitude? Must it not be to that famous elephant, with jeweled tusks and redolent with myrrh, which was led out of an Indian town to do honor to Alexander the Great?

chapters.title: Chapter 93 — The Castaway
paragraphs: It was only some few days after encountering the Frenchman that a most significant event befell the most insignificant of the Pequod's crew — an event most lamentable, and which ended in providing the sometimes madly merry and predestined craft with a living and ever-accompanying prophecy of whatever shattered fate might prove her own.

Now, on a whale-ship, not everyone goes in the boats. Some few hands are held back as ship-keepers, whose job it is to work the vessel while the boats are chasing the whale. As a general thing, these ship-keepers are as hardy as the men in the boats' crews. But if there happens to be an unduly slender, clumsy, or timid fellow on the ship, that fellow is certain to be made a ship-keeper. It was so on the Pequod with the little negro Pippin — Pip, for short. Poor Pip! You have heard of him before. You must remember his tambourine on that dramatic midnight, so gloomy-jolly.

In outward appearance, Pip and Dough-Boy made a matched pair, like a black pony and a white one of equal size though different color, driven in one wild harness. But while hapless Dough-Boy was by nature dull and sluggish in his wits, Pip, though over tender-hearted, was at bottom very bright, with that pleasant, warm, jolly brightness peculiar to his people — a people who ever enjoy all holidays and festivities with finer, freer relish than any other race. For blacks, the year's calendar should show nothing but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year's Days. Nor smile while I write that this little black boy was brilliant, for even blackness has its brilliance: behold that lustrous ebony, paneled in kings' cabinets. But Pip loved life and all life's peaceful securities, so that the panic-striking business in which he had somehow become entangled had most sadly dimmed his brightness — though, as will soon be seen, what was thus temporarily subdued in him was destined in the end to be luridly illuminated by strange wild fires, that falsely showed him off to ten times the natural luster with which, in his native Tolland County in Connecticut, he had once enlivened many a fiddler's dance on the green and, at melodious twilight, with his gay laughter had turned the round horizon into one star-belled tambourine. So, though in the clear light of day a pure diamond drop suspended against a blue-veined neck will glow with healthy beauty, yet when the cunning jeweler would show you the diamond in its most impressive luster, he lays it against a gloomy background and then lights it up not by the sun but by some unnatural gas. Then come those fiery blazes, infernally superb. Then the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell. But let us get to the story.
It came to pass that in the ambergris affair, Stubb's rear oarsman happened to sprain his hand so badly as to be temporarily disabled. And so Pip was put in his place.

The first time Stubb lowered with him, Pip showed much nervousness. But happily, that time he escaped close contact with the whale, and therefore came off not altogether badly — though Stubb, observing him, afterward took care to urge him to nurture his courage to the utmost, for he might often find it necessary.

Now upon the second lowering, the boat paddled up to the whale. As the fish received the darted harpoon, it gave its customary jolt, which happened in this instance to be right under poor Pip's seat. The involuntary shock of the moment caused him to leap, paddle in hand, out of the boat. And in such a way that part of the slack whale-line, coming against his chest, he carried it overboard with him, becoming entangled in it when he plunged into the water. That instant the struck whale started on a fierce run. The line swiftly straightened, and — presto! — poor Pip came foaming up to the bow of the boat, remorselessly dragged there by the line, which had taken several turns around his chest and neck.

Tashtego stood in the bow. He was full of the fire of the hunt. He despised Pip for a coward. Snatching the boat-knife from its sheath, he held its sharp edge over the line, and turning toward Stubb, cried: "Cut?" Meanwhile, Pip's blue, choking face plainly pleaded: Do, for God's sake! All passed in a flash. In less than half a minute, the whole thing happened.
"Damn him, cut!" roared Stubb. And so the whale was lost and Pip was saved.

As soon as he recovered himself, the poor little negro was assailed by yells and curses from the crew. Calmly letting these irregular damnations blow over, Stubb then in a plain, businesslike, but still half-humorous manner, cursed Pip officially. And that done, unofficially gave him much wholesome advice. The substance was: Never jump from a boat, Pip, except — but all the rest was indefinite, as the soundest advice ever is. Now, in general, "Stick to the boat" is the true motto in whaling. But cases will sometimes arise when "Leap from the boat" is still better. Moreover, as if realizing at last that if he gave Pip fully conscientious advice, he would be leaving him too wide a margin to jump in for the future, Stubb suddenly dropped all counsel and concluded with a flat command: "Stick to the boat, Pip, or by the Lord, I won't pick you up if you jump. Mind that. We can't afford to lose whales because of the likes of you. A whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama. Bear that in mind, and don't jump anymore." Hereby perhaps Stubb indirectly hinted that though man loved his fellow, yet man is a money-making animal, a tendency that too often interferes with his kindness.

But we are all in the hands of the Gods, and Pip jumped again. It was under very similar circumstances to the first time, but now he did not carry the line overboard with him. And so when the whale started to run, Pip was left behind on the sea, like a hurried traveler's forgotten trunk. Alas! Stubb was but too true to his word. It was a beautiful, bountiful, blue day. The spangled sea was calm and cool, stretching flatly away on all sides to the horizon, like gold-beater's skin hammered out to the extreme. Bobbing up and down in that sea, Pip's dark head showed like a head of cloves. No boat-knife was lifted when he fell so rapidly astern. Stubb's inexorable back was turned upon him, and the whale was struck. In three minutes, a whole mile of shoreless ocean lay between Pip and Stubb. Out from the center of the sea, poor Pip turned his crisp, curling, black head to the sun — another lonely castaway, though the loftiest and the brightest.

Now in calm weather, to swim in the open ocean is as easy for the practiced swimmer as to ride in a carriage on shore. But the awful loneliness is intolerable. The intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity — my God! Who can tell it? Notice how when sailors in a dead calm bathe in the open sea, they hug their ship and only swim along her sides.

But had Stubb really abandoned the poor little negro to his fate? No — he did not mean to, at least. Because there were two boats in his wake, and he supposed, no doubt, that they would quickly come up to Pip and pick him up. Though, indeed, such consideration toward oarsmen endangered through their own timidity is not always shown by the hunters in similar cases. And such cases occur not infrequently. Almost invariably in the fishery, a coward, so called, is marked with the same ruthless contempt peculiar to military navies and armies.

But it so happened that those boats, without seeing Pip, suddenly spotted whales close to them on one side, turned, and gave chase. And Stubb's boat was now so far away, and he and all his crew so intent upon their whale, that Pip's ringed horizon began to expand around him miserably. By the merest chance, the ship itself at last rescued him. But from that hour the little negro went about the deck an idiot — such, at least, they said he was. The sea had mockingly kept his finite body up but drowned the infinite of his soul. Not drowned entirely, though. Rather carried down alive to wondrous depths, where strange shapes of the unwarped primal world glided to and fro before his passive eyes. And the miser-merman, Wisdom, revealed his hoarded heaps. And among the joyous, heartless, ever-youthful eternities, Pip saw the multitudinous, God-omnipresent coral insects that out of the firmament of waters heaved the colossal orbs. He saw God's foot upon the treadle of the loom, and spoke it. And therefore his shipmates called him mad. So man's insanity is heaven's sense. And wandering from all mortal reason, man comes at last to that celestial thought which, to reason, is absurd and frantic — and, weal or woe, feels then uncompromised, indifferent as his God.
For the rest, do not blame Stubb too harshly. The thing is common in that fishery. And in the sequel of the narrative, it will be seen what like abandonment befell myself.

chapters.title: Chapter 94 — A Squeeze of the Hand
paragraphs: That whale of Stubb's, so dearly purchased, was duly brought to the Pequod's side, where all those cutting and hoisting operations previously described were regularly gone through, even to the bailing of the Heidelburgh Tun, or Case.

While some were occupied with this latter duty, others were employed in dragging away the larger tubs as soon as they were filled with sperm. And when the proper time arrived, this same sperm was carefully processed before going to the try-works, of which more later.

It had cooled and crystallized to such a degree that when, with several others, I sat down before a large bath of it, I found it strangely congealed into lumps, here and there rolling about in the liquid part. It was our business to squeeze these lumps back into fluid. A sweet and oily duty! No wonder that in old times this sperm was such a favorite cosmetic. Such a cleanser! Such a sweetener! Such a softener! Such a delicious emollient! After having my hands in it for only a few minutes, my fingers felt like eels and began, as it were, to coil and spiral.

As I sat there at my ease, cross-legged on the deck — after the bitter exertion at the windlass, under a blue tranquil sky, the ship under lazy sail and gliding so serenely along — as I bathed my hands among those soft, gentle globules of infiltrated tissue, woven almost within the hour, as they richly broke to my fingers and discharged all their richness, like fully ripe grapes their wine, as I breathed in that uncontaminated aroma, literally and truly like the smell of spring violets — I declare to you that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow. I forgot all about our horrible oath. In that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it. I almost began to credit the old superstition that sperm is of rare virtue in calming the heat of anger. While bathing in that bath, I felt divinely free from all ill-will, or irritation, or malice of any sort whatsoever.

Squeeze! Squeeze! Squeeze! All the morning long I squeezed that sperm till I myself almost melted into it. I squeezed that sperm till a strange sort of madness came over me, and I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-workers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules. Such an overflowing, affectionate, friendly, loving feeling did this work beget that at last I was continually squeezing their hands and looking up into their eyes sentimentally — as much as to say: Oh, my dear fellow beings, why should we any longer harbor any social bitterness, or know the slightest ill-humor or envy! Come, let us squeeze hands all round. Nay, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other. Let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.

Would that I could keep squeezing that sperm forever! For now, since by many prolonged, repeated experiences I have perceived that in all cases man must eventually lower, or at least shift, his idea of attainable happiness — not placing it anywhere in the intellect or the imagination but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country — now that I have perceived all this, I am ready to squeeze case eternally. In visions of the night, I saw long rows of angels in paradise, each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti.
Now, while speaking of sperm, it is fitting to mention other things related to it in the business of preparing the sperm whale for the try-works.

First comes white-horse, so called, which is obtained from the tapering part of the fish and also from the thicker portions of his flukes. It is tough with congealed tendons — a wad of muscle — but still contains some oil. After being severed from the whale, the white-horse is first cut into portable blocks before going to the mincer. They look much like blocks of marble.

Plum-pudding is the term bestowed upon certain fragmentary parts of the whale's flesh, here and there adhering to the blanket of blubber and often sharing considerably in its oiliness. It is a most refreshing, sociable, beautiful object to behold. As its name implies, it is of an exceedingly rich, mottled tint, with a streaked snowy and golden background dotted with spots of the deepest crimson and purple. It is plums of rubies in pictures of citron. Despite all reason, it is hard to keep yourself from eating it. I confess that once I stole behind the foremast to try it. It tasted something as I should imagine a royal cutlet from the thigh of Louis le Gros might have tasted, supposing him to have been killed the first day after the venison season, and that particular season contemporary with an unusually fine vintage of Champagne.

There is another substance, a very singular one, which turns up in the course of this business, but which I find very difficult to adequately describe. It is called slobgollion — a name original with the whalemen, and so is the nature of the substance. It is an indescribably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm after a prolonged squeezing and subsequent decanting. I hold it to be the wondrously thin, ruptured membranes of the case, fused together.

Gurry, so called, is a term properly belonging to right whalemen but sometimes used by the sperm fishermen as well. It designates the dark, glutinous substance which is scraped off the back of the Greenland or right whale, and much of which covers the decks of those inferior souls who hunt that ignoble Leviathan.

Nippers. Strictly, this word is not native to the whale's vocabulary. But as applied by whalemen, it becomes so. A whaleman's nipper is a short, firm strip of tough material cut from the tapering part of Leviathan's tail. It averages an inch in thickness and is otherwise about the size of the iron part of a hoe. Moved edgewise along the oily deck, it works like a leather squeegee, and by nameless magic, attracts along with it all impurities.

But to learn all about these obscure matters, your best course is to go straight down into the blubber-room and have a long talk with its inmates. This place has previously been mentioned as the receptacle for the blanket-pieces when stripped and hoisted from the whale. When the time comes to cut up its contents, this room becomes a scene of terror to all newcomers, especially at night. On one side, lit by a dull lantern, a space has been cleared for the workmen. They generally go in pairs — a pike-and-gaff man and a spademan. The whaling-pike is similar to a warship's boarding-weapon of the same name. The gaff is something like a boat-hook. With his gaff, the gaffman hooks onto a sheet of blubber and tries to hold it from slipping as the ship pitches and lurches about. Meanwhile, the spademan stands on the sheet itself, chopping it perpendicularly into portable horse-pieces. This spade is as sharp as a whetstone can make it. The spademan's feet are shoeless. The thing he stands on will sometimes irresistibly slide away from him like a sled. If he cuts off one of his own toes, or one of his assistant's, would you be very much surprised? Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.

chapters.title: Chapter 95 — The Cassock
paragraphs: Had you stepped aboard the Pequod at a certain point in this post-mortem of the whale and strolled forward near the windlass, I am quite sure you would have studied with no small curiosity a very strange, puzzling object lying lengthwise in the lee scuppers. Not the wondrous cistern in the whale's huge head; not the wonder of his unhinged lower jaw; not the miracle of his symmetrical tail — none of these would so surprise you as half a glimpse of that unaccountable cone, longer than a Kentuckian is tall, nearly a foot in diameter at the base, and jet-black as Yojo, the ebony idol of Queequeg. And an idol, indeed, it is — or rather, in old times, its likeness was. Such an idol as that found in the secret groves of Queen Maachah in Judea, and for worshipping which King Asa, her son, deposed her, destroyed the idol, and burnt it as an abomination at the brook Kedron, as darkly set forth in the fifteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings.

Look at the sailor called the mincer, who now comes along and, assisted by two helpers, heavily shoulders the grandissimus, as the mariners call it, and with bowed shoulders staggers off with it as if he were a soldier carrying a dead comrade from the field. Laying it upon the forecastle deck, he proceeds to remove its dark skin cylindrically, as an African hunter skins a boa. This done, he turns the skin inside out like a trouser leg, gives it a good stretching so as almost to double its diameter, and at last hangs it, well spread, in the rigging to dry. Before long it is taken down. Removing some three feet from the pointed end and then cutting two slits for armholes at the other end, he lengthwise slips himself bodily into it. The mincer now stands before you invested in the full ceremonial garments of his calling. From time immemorial to all his order, this investiture alone will adequately protect him while employed in the peculiar functions of his office.

That office consists in mincing the horse-pieces of blubber for the pots — an operation conducted at a curious wooden horse planted endwise against the bulwarks, with a capacious tub beneath it into which the minced pieces drop, fast as the sheets from a hurried speaker's desk. Arrayed in decent black, occupying a conspicuous pulpit, intent on Bible leaves — what a candidate for an archbishop, what a lad for a Pope, this mincer!*

*Bible leaves! Bible leaves! This is the invariable cry from the mates to the mincer. It commands him to be careful and cut his work into the thinnest possible slices, inasmuch as by doing so the business of boiling out the oil is much accelerated and its quantity considerably increased, besides perhaps improving it in quality.

chapters.title: Chapter 96 — The Try-Works
paragraphs: Besides her hoisted boats, an American whaler is outwardly distinguished by her try-works. She presents the curious anomaly of the most solid masonry joined with oak and hemp to constitute the completed ship. It is as if a brick kiln were transported from an open field to her planks.

The try-works are set between the foremast and mainmast, the roomiest part of the deck. The timbers beneath are of unusual strength, fitted to bear the weight of an almost solid mass of brick and mortar, some ten feet by eight and five feet high. The foundation does not penetrate the deck, but the masonry is firmly secured to the surface by ponderous iron knees bracing it on all sides and bolting it down to the timbers. On the flanks it is encased with wood, and at the top completely covered by a large, sloping, battened hatchway. Removing this hatch, we expose the great try-pots, two in number, each of several barrels' capacity. When not in use, they are kept remarkably clean — sometimes polished with soapstone and sand till they shine within like silver punch-bowls. During night watches, some cynical old sailors will crawl into them and coil up for a nap. While polishing them — one man in each pot, side by side — many confidential conversations are carried on over the iron rims. It is a place also for deep mathematical meditation. It was in the left-hand try-pot of the Pequod, with the soapstone diligently circling round me, that I was first indirectly struck by the remarkable fact that in geometry all bodies sliding along a cycloid, my soapstone for example, will descend from any point in precisely the same time.

Removing the fire-board from the front of the try-works, the bare masonry of that side is exposed, penetrated by the two iron mouths of the furnaces directly underneath the pots. These mouths are fitted with heavy iron doors. The intense heat of the fire is prevented from reaching the deck by means of a shallow reservoir extending under the entire enclosed surface of the works. By a tunnel inserted at the rear, this reservoir is kept filled with water as fast as it evaporates. There are no external chimneys — they open directly from the rear wall. And here let us go back for a moment.
It was about nine o'clock at night that the Pequod's try-works were first fired up on this present voyage. It fell to Stubb to oversee the business.

"All ready there? Off hatch, then, and start her. Cook, fire the works." This was an easy thing, for the carpenter had been stuffing his shavings into the furnace throughout the passage. Here let it be said that in a whaling voyage, the first fire in the try-works has to be fed for a time with wood. After that, no wood is used except as a means of quick ignition for the staple fuel. In a word, after being boiled out, the crisp, shriveled blubber, now called scraps or fritters, still contains considerable oily properties. These fritters feed the flames. Like a self-consuming martyr, once ignited the whale supplies his own fuel and burns by his own body. Would that he consumed his own smoke! For his smoke is horrible to inhale, and inhale it you must, and not only that but you must live in it for the time. It has an unspeakable, wild, Hindu odor about it, such as may lurk in the vicinity of funeral pyres. It smells like the left wing of the day of judgment. It is an argument for the pit.

By midnight the works were in full operation. We were clear of the carcass; sail had been made; the wind was freshening; the wild ocean darkness was intense. But that darkness was licked up by the fierce flames, which at intervals forked forth from the sooty flues and illuminated every lofty rope in the rigging, as with the famed Greek fire. The burning ship drove on, as if remorselessly commissioned to some vengeful deed. So the pitch-and-sulfur-laden fire-ships of the bold Greek hero Canaris, issuing from their midnight harbors with broad sheets of flame for sails, bore down upon the Turkish frigates and folded them in conflagrations.

The hatch, removed from the top of the works, now provided a wide hearth in front of them. Standing on this were the hellish shapes of the pagan harpooners, always the whale-ship's stokers. With huge pronged poles they pitched hissing masses of blubber into the scalding pots, or stirred up the fires beneath, till the snaky flames darted curling out of the doors to catch them by the feet. The smoke rolled away in sullen heaps. With every pitch of the ship there was a pitch of the boiling oil, which seemed all eagerness to leap into their faces. Opposite the mouth of the works, on the far side of the wide wooden hearth, was the windlass. This served as a sea-sofa. Here lounged the watch, when not otherwise employed, staring into the red heat of the fire till their eyes felt scorched in their heads. Their swarthy features, now all grimed with smoke and sweat, their matted beards, and the contrasting barbaric brilliance of their teeth — all these were strangely revealed in the capricious flare of the works. As they told each other their unholy adventures, their tales of terror told in words of mirth — as their wild laughter forked upward out of them, like flames from the furnace — as the harpooners wildly gesticulated in front of them with their huge pronged forks and dippers — as the wind howled on and the sea leaped and the ship groaned and dove and yet steadily shot her red hell further and further into the blackness of the sea and the night, and scornfully bit the white bone in her mouth and viciously spat round her on all sides — then the rushing Pequod, freighted with savages and laden with fire and burning a corpse and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the material counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.

So it seemed to me as I stood at her helm, and for long hours silently guided the way of this fire-ship on the sea. Wrapped in darkness myself for that interval, I only the better saw the redness, the madness, the ghastliness of others. The continual sight of the fiendish shapes before me, capering half in smoke and half in fire, at last bred kindred visions in my soul, as soon as I began to yield to that unaccountable drowsiness that always came over me at a midnight helm.

But that night in particular, a strange and ever since inexplicable thing occurred to me. Starting from a brief standing sleep, I was horribly conscious that something was fatally wrong. The jawbone tiller struck my side, which was leaning against it. In my ears was the low hum of sails just beginning to shake in the wind. I thought my eyes were open. I was half conscious of putting my fingers to the lids and mechanically stretching them still further apart. But despite all this, I could see no compass before me to steer by, though it seemed but a minute since I had been watching the card by the steady binnacle lamp. Nothing seemed before me but a jet-black gloom, now and then made ghastly by flashes of redness. Uppermost was the impression that whatever swift, rushing thing I stood on was not so much bound to any haven ahead as rushing from all havens astern. A stark, bewildered feeling, as of death, came over me. Convulsively my hands grasped the tiller, but with the crazy notion that the tiller was somehow, in some enchanted way, inverted. My God! What is the matter with me? I thought. Lo! In my brief sleep I had turned myself about, and was facing the ship's stern, with my back to the prow and the compass. In an instant I whirled back around, just in time to prevent the vessel from flying up into the wind and very probably capsizing her. How glad and how grateful the relief from this unnatural hallucination of the night, and the fatal danger of being caught by the lee!

Look not too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with your hand on the helm! Turn not your back to the compass. Heed the first hint of the hitching tiller. Believe not the artificial fire when its redness makes all things look ghastly. Tomorrow, in the natural sun, the skies will be bright. Those who glared like devils in the forking flames, the morning will show in far other, at least gentler, light. The glorious, golden, glad sun — the only true lamp! All others but liars!

Nevertheless, the sun does not hide Virginia's Dismal Swamp, nor Rome's accursed Campagna, nor the wide Sahara, nor all the millions of miles of deserts and of griefs beneath the moon. The sun does not hide the ocean, which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two-thirds of this earth. So therefore, that mortal man who has more of joy than sorrow in him — that mortal man cannot be true, or is undeveloped. With books the same. The truest of all men was the Man of Sorrows, and the truest of all books is Solomon's, and Ecclesiastes is the fine hammered steel of woe. "All is vanity." ALL. This willful world has not yet grasped unchristian Solomon's wisdom. But he who dodges hospitals and jails and walks fast crossing graveyards and would rather talk of operas than hell — who calls Cowper, Young, Pascal, Rousseau poor devils all of sick men, and throughout a carefree lifetime swears by Rabelais as supremely wise and therefore jolly — not that man is fitted to sit down on tombstones and break the green damp mold with the unfathomably wondrous Solomon.

But even Solomon, he says, "the man that wanders out of the way of understanding shall remain" — that is, even while living — "in the congregation of the dead." Give not yourself up, then, to fire, lest it invert you, deaden you — as for the time it did me. There is a wisdom that is woe. But there is a woe that is madness. And there is a Catskill eagle in some souls that can alike dive down into the blackest gorges and soar out of them again and become invisible in the sunny spaces. And even if he forever flies within the gorge, that gorge is in the mountains; so that even in his lowest swoop the mountain eagle is still higher than other birds upon the plain, even though they soar.

chapters.title: Chapter 97 — The Lamp
paragraphs: Had you gone down from the Pequod's try-works to the Pequod's forecastle, where the off-duty watch were sleeping, for one single moment you would have almost thought you were standing in some illuminated shrine of canonized kings and counselors. There they lay in their triangular oaken bunks, each mariner a chiseled stillness, a score of lamps flashing upon his hooded eyes.

In merchant ships, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his bed — this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his bunk an Aladdin's lamp and lies down in it, so that in the blackest night the ship's dark hull still houses an illumination.

See with what perfect freedom the whaleman takes his handful of lamps — often but old bottles and vials, though — to the copper cooler at the try-works and refills them there, as mugs of ale at a vat. He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unprocessed and therefore untainted state — a fluid unknown to solar, lunar, or astral lamps on shore. It is sweet as early grass butter in April. He goes and hunts for his oil, so as to be sure of its freshness and genuineness, even as the traveler on the prairie hunts up his own supper of game.

chapters.title: Chapter 98 — Stowing Down and Clearing Up
paragraphs: Already it has been told how the great leviathan is spotted from afar at the masthead; how he is chased over the watery moors and slaughtered in the valleys of the deep; how he is then towed alongside and beheaded; and how — on the principle that entitled the headsman of old to the garments in which the beheaded was killed — his great padded overcoat becomes the property of his executioner; how, in due time, he is condemned to the pots, and like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, his spermaceti, oil, and bone pass unscathed through the fire. But now it remains to conclude the last chapter of this part of the description by rehearsing — singing, if I may — the romantic proceeding of decanting off his oil into the casks and lowering them down into the hold, where once again leviathan returns to his native depths, sliding along beneath the surface as before — but, alas, never more to rise and blow.

While still warm, the oil, like hot punch, is received into the six-barrel casks. And while perhaps the ship is pitching and rolling this way and that in the midnight sea, the enormous casks are rolled around and upended, sometimes perilously scooting across the slippery deck like so many landslides, till at last they are wrestled into place and secured. And all around the hoops, rap, rap, go as many hammers as can play upon them, for now, by necessity, every sailor is a cooper.
